title: Shipley's Dozen: Jaguars Enter Trade Deadline As NFL's Most Dominant Team After Ravens Blowout
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are living the good life.
The Jaguars are 6-2 through eight games, are entering a mini bye week after a gritty road win and some tough injuries, and their Thursday Night blowout of the Baltimore Ravens puts them square in the mix for the AFC's top seed.
“I was extremely proud of their process throughout the week. I told the guys it was one of the best short weeks I’ve been a part of in terms of their preparation and their detail," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the 33-10 win. "We didn’t have a ton of guys looking lost tonight. You just had a lot of guys just business-like, doing their job, and had some individual performances of guys making plays."
In today's Shipley's Dozen column, we take a look at why the Jaguars are the NFL's most dominant team through the first half of the season, trade deadline takes , and much more. Remember: Shipley's Dozen comes out the morning after each Jaguars game.
There is pretty much zero stat that doesn't reinforce the fact that the Jaguars have been the NFL's most dominant team since Liam Coen was hired. They are 19-6 in that span, and of their six losses only one of them has been by multiple scores. The Jaguars have lost as many games in London as in Jacksonville. They have outscored their last two opponents 75-17. They will not have the NFL's best record after Week 9, because that will belong to the Buffalo Bills or Minnesota Vikings. But they are the NFL's most dominant team.
Simply put, blowouts do not happen at the NFL level the way they have happened with Jacksonville over the last two seasons. It was their fourth win by 20-plus points in 2026, while no other team even has three such wins entering Week 9 Sunday. It was also the fourth time the Jaguars held their opponent to 10 points or fewer in 2026, the most such games in the NFL. Consider some of these other stats:
The Jaguars went with a two-man platoon to replace injured star nose tackle Davon Hamilton on a short week. The Jaguars had Matt Dickerson make the start at the spot next to Arik Armstead, with third-round rookie defensive tackle Albert Regis getting his most playing time in a game to date as his backup. The duo played 22 snaps against the run before the game got out of hand and the backups were put in, and honestly the rotation was closer than I anticipated it would be.
Out of those 22 snaps, Dickerson played 13 to Regis' nine. It is worth noting, though, that Dickerson took the first four snaps of the game at nose tackle and after that point, him or Regis more or less rotated at an even pace. Neither was Hamilton, of course, but they each had some positive reps, including Regis having his biggest flash in the NFL yet with a tackle for no gain on Derrick Henry. They still need to add someone, but they had a good night.
https://t.co/JVwmWxMKfp pic.twitter.com/6AwEV48qsm
I have covered Trevor Lawrence his entire career, and I have seen him make some absolutely bonkers passes in the past. I mean, even during the Urban Meyer year and the lost 2024 season, he was making at least one or two pass a game that made you think this guy could get a completion at any area of the field when he was on. He has clearly had a lot of highlight throws this season during an MVP-like run , but this one he had to Brenton Strange between three defenders broke my brain.
RIDICULOUS tight window throw here from Trevor Lawrence. pic.twitter.com/3eHN5FGfl5
For most quarterbacks, this wouldn't be a good decision. For most quarterbacks, it would not even be a thought that enters the mind. But Lawrence isn't most quarterbacks, because he has proven he can make these sicko throws at a high rate. He is playing out of his mind right now, and I think we just saw the most impressive pass of his entire season.
Liam Coen was wrongly passed over as Coach of the Year last season. He would have to fend off media darling Ben Johnson and his epic trick plays to win it this season, but that doesn't matter as much as it matters that Coen has quickly become one of the best head coaches in the NFL. Coen, Johnson, Kyle Shanahan, Mike Macdonald, and Sean McVay look like the five best coaches in football right now, putting them in whatever order you want.
What makes Coen and the Jaguars unique is that they have proven they can win different ways. They have aired it out, leaned on the run, leaned on three-receiver sets, leaned on 12 and 13 personnel. They are a different team every week, but the results stay the same. That says as much about their dominance under Coen as anything else.
If you go purely off metrics, Thursday was the worst single-game performance by the Jaguars' ground attack during the Liam Coen era. The Jaguars had just 77 rushing yards, rushed for 2.6 yards per carry, did not have a run go over six yards, and had the worst cumaltitve rushing EPA of any Jaguars game during the Coen era. It was also the first game this season the Jaguars also did not have a single run of 10 yards.
Why was the running game so rough? Perhaps due to Bhayshul Tuten not being 100%, perhaps due to the line, perhaps due to the fact the Jaguars went into chew the clock mode early. Perhaps it was all of it, and perhaps it was none of it at all. The simple fact is we have not seen the Jaguars running game look that lifeless down-to-down at any other point, so I would not quite call it a concern.
The Jaguars will enter the final weekend before the trade deadline knowing what they need and who they want. It does take two to tango, though, and the Jaguars should root for a few different results to convince teams to become sellers. Losses at the trade deadline can often inspire change, and the Jaguars should hope these three teams lose in Week 9 and start a fire sale: the Philadelphia Eag,es (Moro Ojomo), the Carolina Panthers (Derrick Brown), and the Arizona Cardinals (Roy Lopez, Budda Baker).
That the Ravens ... didn't even really try? I get the screens. I even get the Wildcat stuff, though perhaps not to that extent. But they didn't call anything other than the one shot play to try to pick up first downs and score touchdowns. The Jaguars put this game away when they went up 17-3, and it never looked like Jesse Minter's team wanted it after that. The Jaguars went into their stadium and bullied them into unplugging their controller and turning the Xbox off.
The Jaguars getting annoyed with the rain. The Jaguars have played in a ton of rainy games this season, and it has certainly had its impact. Liam Coen said after the game that he would have liked to pass the ball more, but the conditions forced the Jaguars, and the Ravens, to play a sloppy, ground-based game where most plays felt like theywere just running into walls. The Jaguars need a dry game for once.
Bhayshul Tuten. After not practicing in the days leading up to the game due to a foot/ankle injury he sustained last week against the Colts, Tuten was the lead work horse for the first 2.5 quarters of the game on Thursday. He showed some real grit and toughness to fight through it the way he did, and he got another touchdown on top of it.
This is more of an AFC South preview this week since the Jaguars are entering Friday as the only team to have played thus far. The Jaguars could have as big of a lead as four games by the end of Sunday afternoon depending on how the slate of games play out, and the big hope this weekend should be a knockout blow to the Houston Texans.
The Texans would be more or less done for good at 2-6, though they are facing an 0-7 Chargers team that looks like the biggest mess in the NFL. The Chargers have to win eventually, so maybe this is the week, but it feels unlikely. The Colts will play the Dallas Cowboys in a game that would drop them to 2-7 with a loss, but they have already waved the white flag on the season.
As for the Titans, who the Jaguars play next week, they are on a bye. The Sunday rooting guide in terms of the AFC South will more or less come in the form of…

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Primetime Trouncing of Ravens: Cam Little Goes Perfect
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are all smiles after their latest blowout win.
The Jaguars took care of business on the road on Thursday Night, taking down the Baltimore Ravens with a 33-10 win that was not really as close as the score indicated. The Jaguars were never in danger of losing this one, and they did exactly what they were supposed to do.
So, who earned the game balls this week as the Jaguars improved to 6-2 after yet another win? We break it down below.
For the second week in a row, Trevor Lawrence was able to get things popping right out of the gate. Lawrence has been playing like an MVP all season long and he once again was able to get off to a hot start on Thursday. He threw for nearly 200 yards and two touchdowns before the rain really came in and turned it into a running attack. This included a 52-yard completion to rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher, the rookie tight end's third big play in the last three games.
"To go down two weeks in a row now to start the season – which is something that we’ve been struggling at [and] has been a point of emphasis – starting faster and being better on the first drive of the game," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game.
"I’m kind of yelling at [Trevor Lawrence] to run out of bounds, and he just finds 'Boerk' [Nate Boerkircher], and I just think he was very on when it was really a game. Like when it was mattering and things were going and it’s a back-and-forth football game early on, he was extremely sharp, accurate, and he played a really solid football game for us.”
Lawrence has been Steady Eddie for the Jaguars all year long, and Thursday was another example. The Jaguars have rarely needed Lawrence to make big plays at the end of games this year, and that is largely due to the amount of big plays he is making at the start of games ... such as the big completion to Boerkircher.
Ventrell Miller gets the nod this week after recording a team-high seven tackles and a key pass-breakup. Had Miller not tipped a pass during the first-half, it would have surely resulted in an explosive gain for the Ravens. Add in a few stellar tackles in space, and Miller once again looked like an ascending young linebacker who can only improve moving forward.
There are a few other players who also deserve consideration. Foyesade Oluokun had seven tackles, including the Jaguars' only sack of the night. Montaric Brown and Jourdan Lewis each had interceptions, while Travon Walker recorded two tackles for loss despite not being 100%. But it was Miller who was consistently getting the Jaguars off the field both against the run and the pass, and it is Miller who wins this week's defensive game ball.
The conditions were not exactly favorable for things like kicking or passing the ball, especially as the rain came down even harder during the second-half. That didn't stop Cam Little, though, with the Jaguars' third-year kicker making all four of his field goals and all three of his extra points. Little is now 14-of-16 on field goals this season, and he has not missed a kick since Week 3 against the New England Patriots.
“Dialed," Coen said about Little's performance. "I was very pleased with his – he has a lot of confidence. He has a lot of confidence right now. We have a lot of confidence in him, and he’s hitting it really good right now.”

title: 7 Winners, 3 Losers from Jaguars' Domination of Ravens: Trevor Lawrence, Parker Washington Lead the Way
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- All things considered, that was one of the easier games of the Liam Coen era.
The Jacksonville Jaguars took apart a depleted Baltimore Ravens team with a 33-10 win on Thursday Night Football, with the favored Jaguars doing what everyone expected them to do entering Week 9. As a result, the Jaguars are 6-2 and in a good spot moving into their mini-bye.
So, who were the winners and losers from the latest Jaguars blowout win? We break it all down below.
Trevor Lawrence didn't light up the box score, but that is largely because he didn't need to. Lawrence has gotten used to going into chew the clock mode during second-half of games, but that is largely because of how well he and the offense are operating when the game is, well, still a game. Lawrence looks like a clear MVP candidate , and the only thing that might be standing in his way is the Jaguars' own offensive dominance.
Trevor Lawrence has averaged 5.1 dropbacks per game in the 4th quarter this season, the fewest among qualified QB. Lawrence has 36 total dropbacks in the 4th quarter.
Lawrence hit a few throws during the first-half, where he had nearly 200 passing yards, that showed he has developed a full skill-set. He is beating defenses before the snap, beating the blitz after the snap, and is doing a little bit of everything else in between. Lawrence is the real deal and then some, and there is no more hiding that.
If there was ever a reminder that the Jaguars' passing game starts and ends with Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers, this was it. Washington and Meyers combined for 13 of Lawrence's 26 targets, with the rest of the Jaguars' receivers cdombining for two catches for five yards. Brian Thomas Jr. did not even see a pass go his way, but that didn't stop Washington and Meyers for record 126 receiving yards, including a 50-yard touchdown from Washington.
PARKER WASHINGTON TO THE CRIB. JAXvsBAL on Prime Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/M79mYxS3b2
Washington and Meyers are more than good enough to each be the focal point of the offense, which is a moving target that is bound to change a bit more each week. But when the Jaguars' offense does go through its wide receivers, it is very clear which receivers are going to get the bulk of the work between these two.
The Jaguars needed their entire defensive front to step up against the Ravens considering the loss of Davon Hamilton , and that is exactly what the Jaguars got against Derrick Henry. One player who flashed consistently in the place of Hamilton was Albert Regis, the Jaguars' third-round nose tackle who has been a healthy scratch for the last few weeks. Regis showed good effort, some real range as a tackler for a defensive tackle, and some juice as well. It was a strong showing from the rook.
The Jaguars' defense has been much improved in the back-end since they officially got Montaric Brown back healthy. It has allowed the Jaguars to utilize their entire cornerback room with a four-man rotation that allows them to put players in different spots depending on the situation and foe. On Thursday, we saw this rotating come up big for the Jaguars on two different occasions.
Brown and Lewis each recorded an interception, with it being Brown's first interception of the season and the third interception from Lewis. Both interceptions set up field goals, and they were strong signs that the Jaguars' secondary is taking steps forward, one way or another. It was a strong night for both cornerbacks in general, and Jarrian Jones deserves some love too for a quarterback hit and a pass breakup.
Montaric Brown INT! pic.twitter.com/EgwLFjcTrt
It has been a good last few weeks for second-year linebacker Jalen McLeod on special teams, and he made the biggest play of his NFL career thus far during the second-half on Thursday. McLeod made a terrific tackle on a coverage unit and ended up forcing the ball out for the first forced fumble of his career, with the Jaguars scooping up the fumble and eventually kicking a field goal shortly after as a result. That is now three turnovers forced in the last two weeks by second-year Jaguars, which is becoming a bit of a trend for James Gladstone's team moving forward.
Brian Thomas Jr's stat line over the Jaguars' last four games: 1 catch for 12 yards and a touchdown on seven targets. Thomas did not get a ton of playing time seemingly on Thursday as the Jaguars went with 12 and 13 personnel more than 11, and this meant there were limited chances for Thomas to get in on the action. Considering the Jaguars' relatively conservative game-plan on offense, that left little for Thomas to do.
The Jaguars' wide receiver ended Thursday with zero targets despite nine other players getting targets, with Travis Hunter, LeQuint Allen, Chris Rodriguez, Josh Cameron, and Tanner Koziol all getting more looks than him. It remains to be seen if this was his last game as a Jaguar, but this game was clearly not about showcasing his talent ahead of the trade deadline.
Jaguars rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon looks like a rookie, which is far from a bad thing. Still, the Jaguars are hopeful Super Bowl contenders and even rookies will have to be held to a high standard for the Jaguars to reach their ultimate goals. Pregnon is a big part of that, and the Jaguars will likely see much better performances from him moving forward than they saw from him on Thursday.
Part of this was due to penalties, with Pregnon getting called for three different false starts. He also had some issues when left on an island in pass-protection, making this a game for Pregnon that has to be about lessons and development. Pregnon is getting some valuable experience, and he did do some good things in the running game, but this wasn't his best game.
Even in a game where the Jaguars sat Bhayshul Tuten down with a few minutes left in the third-quarter to rest him after he entered the game banged up, there still just wasn't much there for LeQuint Allen to do. Allen was seemingly set to enter the year as the No. 3 running back before a training camp injury sidelined him for a few weeks, and he hasn't quite taken the role back from Ameer Abdullah since.
Allen was targeted twice as a check-down in the passing game, but those were the only looks he got with the ball despite the Jaguars' other three running backs toting the ball for 29 carries and two other catches. Allen is a gifted pass-blocker and a key part of the Jaguars' culture, but it seems like his role is set to be capped out there.

title: 8 Instant Observations on Jaguars' Blowout of Ravens: King Henry Gets Slayed
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are 6-2 and hitting their stride.
The Jaguars were big favorites entering Thursday's game, and for good reason after their 33-10 domination over the Baltimore Ravens. The Jaguars have kept it rolling, and here is everything we saw from them on Thursday.
Jesse Minter is one of the best defensive minds in football. He has produced elite units at both the college and the NFL level, and there is a good reason the Ravens tabbed him as the man to replace the legendary John Harbaugh. With that said, there is a decent chance that Minter checks underneath his bed and his closet for Liam Coen offenses after how Coen's unit have performed against Minter's defenses over the years.
Coen-led offenses scored 75 points in two games against Minter's defense over the last two seasons. After the way the Jaguars were able to hit explosive plays when they needed to on Thursday with relative ease, there is no questioning which coach gets the better of their peer whenever Coen and Minter line up on opposite sidelines. Coen offenses have simply gotten the job done every time, and this was another example.
The Ravens went with an offense that looked more like Ribault High School than an NFL unit, largely because of their injury issues at quarterback. With the Ravens starting third-string undrafted free agent quarterback Joe Fagnano
 under center after injuries to Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley, offensive coordinator Declan Doyle went with a ton of Wildcat and screens to try to take the ball out of his hand. This meant a ton of Derrick Henry, especially early on.
Henry was getting a few solid gains against the Jaguars, more than they normally give up. That should be expected after the loss of Davon Hamilton to a season-ending injury, but it is not like Henry killed them, either. Henry had more success against the Jaguars' run defense than he would have if Hamilton was in the game, but he also did not have any long breakaway run that broke things open. He ran hard, but the Jaguars would likely take this run-game performance each and every time against Henry. Justice Hill had a 65-yard run at the end of the game with the backups in, but this was still a strong game by the run defense.
The Jaguars came out with a ton of 13 personnel on the first drive of the game. It paid off big near the goal-line, of course, but it was just as big at the very start. The Jaguars hit rookie tight end Nate Boerkircher for a big play for the third time in three games with a 52-yard catch to set up the opening drive touchdown, yet another evolution in the Jaguars' usage of the rookie tight end. The Jaguars entered the game with the second-best EPA/dropback in 2+ tight end formations, and this played a big role to start the game.
This is the biggest area where the Jaguars' scheme has grown this year. After mainly being an 11 personnel team a year ago, the Jaguars have really started to lean into their talented and developing tight end room. The Boerkircher pick was panned to a hyperbolic level in April, and the Jaguars are starting to show why it was such a priority for them.
Jaguars linebacker Foyesade Oluokun has been playing some darn good football all season, but especially since the bye week. Oluokun had nine tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack last week, and he was key against the Ravens on Thursday. Oluokun had a big third-down sack in the first-half to get the Jaguars' defense off the field after the Ravens had some momentum, and he didn't stop there.
Oluokun and the Jaguars had a tough task tonight against a Derrick Henry-led attack that featured a lot of Wildcat and unbalanced lines. Oluokun has been playing some of the best football of his career in 2026, and Week 9 was just another example of his game aging like fine wine over the last few seasons. With Ventrell Miller also playing at a high level, the Jaguars have one of the more underrated LB duos in the NFL. The Jaguars need help at a few depth spots on defense, but not at linebacker.
The Jaguars only had four drives in the first half due to the Ravens killing the clock with a run-heavy attack, but that didn't really stop Trevor Lawrence from producing early on. Lawrence had two passes of 50 yards or more in the first-half with his 52-yard throw to Boerkircher and his 50-yard touchdown pass to Parker Washington before halftime. Before Lawrence's big throw to Washington, he had one of his best throws of the season on a tight-window throw to Brenton Strange for a first-down that he threw between three Ravens defenders. Three!
RIDICULOUS tight window throw here from Trevor Lawrence. pic.twitter.com/3eHN5FGfl5
Lawrence should have already been an MVP candidate entering the game. After the flashes he showed in Thursday's game before the rain started really coming down, Lawrence should be right in the mix with Joe Burrow, Josh Allen, and anyone else. Lawrence is making high-level throws at a consistent clip and he is the biggest reason the Jaguars are 6-2 right now.
Have a day, Jaylon Jones. The Jaguars' cornerback and special teamer was signed to the roster after Week 4 with the expectation of him making a very real impact on special teams to replace former core special teamer Christian Braswell. Jones has not played a ton of football for the Jaguars after a hamstring injury early on in his Jaguars tenure, but he was easy to spot on the field during Thursday's win.
Jones made a pair of tackles on coverage units Thursday that showed why he can be exactly the kind of depth piece the Jaguars need moving forward. They need Antonio Johnson and Jarrian Jones on defense instead of special teams, so anything Jones can do for them on special teams is a big boost for them moving forward.
With the Jaguars set to be without star nose tackle Davon Hamilton for the rest of the season, they will need third-round rookie Albert Regis to develop quickly. Regis had barely played up to this point in the season and has been a healthy scratch for the last few weeks, but he was needed on Thursday night after Hamilton went on IR and the Jaguars had no real time to add any true outside reinforcements.
Regis certainly stood out when given a chance to play on Thursday night. He made several impressive plays against the run, showing off the motor and anchor the Jaguars liked in the third-round of the NFL Draft in April. It looked like the best performance he has had so far as a pro, and the Jaguars badly needed it to happen.
If there was one rookie who has been thrown to the fire who did not have a great night, it felt like it was left guard Emmanuel Pregnon. Pregnon has done some solid things for the Jaguars as an every-week starter at guard, and the fact that he has been so reliable for the Jaguars in terms of his availability has been big for a unit that has had some moving pieces. With that said, Sunday felt like one of his weaker games.
Pregnon had a few issues with penalties, which has been an issue throughout the season. He even had one on a PAT attempt, which kind of sums up some of his issues with false starts, holds, and more. Add in a few pressures allowed and this feels like one of the games to forget for the rookie guard.

title: Jaguars' Bhayshul Tuten Will Play vs. Ravens, Which Leaves One Big Question
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Make it 27 out of 28.
Jacksonville Jaguars running back Bhayshul Tuten is active for the team's Thursday Night Football battle with the Baltimore Ravens, making him the first player in the Coen era to suit up for a game despite not practicing that week. The previous 27 player sin the Coen era who had not practiced before a game did not play that week.
Getting Tuten back is a big deal considering the Jaguars should have the upper hand on paper when it comes to running the ball against the Baltimore Ravens. T he big question now, though, is whether he leads the backfield like he has each week.
Tuten has been the Jaguars' clear RB1 each week, getting more carries than backup running back Chris Rodriguez Jr. in 6-of-7 games. But will Rodriguez get more volume tonight now that Tuten has been injured coming off a short week? The Jaguars have clear trust in the veteran back who they added in free agency, and this seems like a favorable matchup.
Tuten has been the Jaguars' star at running back and if the Jaguars just roll with his usual workload, he could be in for another big performance. If the Jaguars hold him back, we could see something closer to the split backfield many though it would be coming into the season, myself included.
Tuten is coming off the best game of his NFL career in Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts, recording his first-ever 100-yard rushing game. In the process, he became the first Jaguars running back to have 100-plus rushing yards, 50-plus receiving yards, a rushing touchdown and a receving touchdown in a game.
In seven games this season, Tuten has led the Jaguars' offense with 110 carries for 492 yards and three touchdowns. Add in his 15 catches for 181 yards and three touchdowns, and Tuten is the Jaguars' most productive skill player from scrimmage. In 2026, Tuten ranks tied sixth in touchdowns scored (six) and eighth in scrimmage yards (673) and rushing yards (492) in the AFC.
“It’s really cool. It's one of the really special parts about coaching, seeing guys like Tuten who come in as a rookie and they put their head down and work, and they work, and they work, and it doesn't maybe materialize immediately, but over the course of time, we see it on the practice field, it shows up then on Sundays, and he's still just scratching the surface," Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski said earlier this week.
"And he knows, and we know, there's even so much more that he can do and accomplish. But it's so special to see a guy like that who does it for all the right reasons, selflessly, cares about his teammates, runs so hard, works hard in pass protection, works hard in the pass game. And maybe we didn't give him the opportunities, but to see some of those things actually materialize on Sunday is really special."
Meanwhile, the Jaguars will have the following players inactive: wide receiver CJ Williams, cornerback Alijah Huzzie, safety Cam'Ron Silmon-Craig, defensive end Wesley Williams. The Jaguars will have rookie nose tackle Albert Regis active and ready to go to help replace Davon Hamilton.

title: Short Week Set Up Could Give Jaguars Fascinating Trade Deadline Window
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have much bigger things on their plate Thursday night than the NFL Trade Deadline. But that could change in a quick 24 hours.
The Jaguars need to take care of business on Thursday Night Football against the Baltimore Ravens before they do anything else. The Jaguars are big favorites against a third-string undrafted free agent at quarterback, however, and they should be 6-2 by the end of the night if they are the team they have shown to be.
If/when the Jaguars make it to Friday with another win, they can turn their focus completely to the trade deadline , set for next Tuesday. With obvious needs at a few positions on defense and the never-ending speculation on Brian Thomas Jr., the trade deadline could prove to be eventful for Jacksonville for a few reasons.
Could one of those reasons be in part due to the Jaguars' schedule, though? With the Jaguars playing on Thursday Night Football, they could get a window to attack the trade deadline that other teams have used in recent seasons.
With the Jaguars playing on Thursday night, they can get a few days head start on the deadline. Most moves happen between the end of Sunday's games and the day of the deadline each season, which means that any previous trade movements in the weeks ahead typically do not mean much when it comes to how much action there is on the actual deadline.
In short, deadlines force moves. With this being the final week of games before the deadline, this is the week where many teams have to make decisions to either address their needs toward a playoff push or start selling off roster pieces in a lost season. We have seen each happen over the last two seasons.
In four of the last five seasons, teams playing on Thursday Night Football ended up making deals at the deadline after playing on Thursday. Sometimes, like in 2022 with the Ravens, it was a blockbuster in the form of adding Roquan Smith. Sometimes like last season, it was the Dolphins dealing Jaelan Phillips after falling to 2-7 following a Thursday Night loss to ... the Ravens.
Deadline Trades from TNF Teams
This is not to say we should look too deeply into the trend, but it is worth noting that teams who play on Thursday at least get clarity a bit earlier than the other 28 teams that are set to play before the trade deadline on Tuesday. There are a few teams among those 28 who are worth watching, too.
Could the Arizona Cardinals go into sell mode if a loss to the Seattle Seahawks on the road drops them to 3-6? They have pieces at EDGE, defensive tackle, and safety. The same goes for the Los Angeles Chargers, who would drop to 0-8 with a loss to the Houston Texans. Perhaps the team worth watching the most is the Philadelphia Eagles, who would be 2-7 with a loss to the New York Giants, which could make them more inclined to move a piece like Moro Ojomo.
The Jaguars can underline their targets and know exactly what and who they need a few days earlier than the rest of these teams, especially when it comes to taking a look at their run defense without Davon Hamilton. The Jaguars feel like a real candidate to make a move over the next week, and Thursday could prove to be a big piece of the equation.

title: What the Chiefs Can (and Can't) Prove Against the Jets
full_text:
Coming off of a pair of back-to-back losses against likely playoff teams, the Kansas City Chiefs are in a unique place this Sunday against the New York Jets. The Chiefs can't entirely exorcise the demons of their losses to the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos because, well, the Jets aren't good enough to prove what they need to prove. However, that's a bit of an oversimplification.
There are a few things the Chiefs can show to be true with a good day against the 2-6 Jets, and a few other things that will require a series of better performances in bigger games.
Rookie second-round defensive end R Mason Thomas had a career-low number of snaps in Seattle before hitting another low mark last week in Denver . For a Chiefs team desperately needing more firepower in its pass rush, that's a confusing development for a player who has shown real sparks in the early weeks of his NFL career.
I don't believe that Thomas' role dipped due to a tumble down the depth chart; I can clearly imagine a world where defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo simply favored his more experienced edge defenders who are more stout against the run in the last two games, but that excuse won't hold up for a third time. Thomas needs to continue getting experience on the field, and that should resume with a larger role against New York.
Jets quarterback Geno Smith has been sacked 23 times this year, tied for the second-most in the NFL. Smith is largely playing pretty well in his second stint with the Jets, but he's shown a willingness to hold on to the ball (while throwing only three interceptions so far this season).
The Chiefs' pass rush has been toothless too often this year, recording just eight sacks in seven games, with four of those coming in Week 1. Yes, it would be a good sign to see them bring Smith down early and often on Sunday, but that's a matchup where the Chiefs should be able to pad their stats. Even if they do find their footing against Smith, they'll have to do it again against better offenses down the stretch.
Left tackle Kahlil Benson has earned plenty of credit for his performance as an undrafted rookie who had no experience playing left tackle before being thrust into action to begin this season, while right tackle Jaylon Moore hasn't lived up to his salary cap hit. Both tackles have struggled by some key metrics , and the Chiefs' passing game hasn't felt comfortable or consistent for most of the year.
Particularly with rookie No. 2 overall pick David Bailey and third-year first-round pick Will McDonald IV rushing Patrick Mahomes on Sunday, it would be a great time for Benson and Moore to show that there's still room for improvement on the bookends of the offensive line.
Following the high-profile losses to the Seahawks and Broncos, the Chiefs have an upcoming three-game stretch against the Jets, Falcons and Cardinals. The Chiefs could win all three of those games by reasonable margins, and it still wouldn't be enough to write off the issues we've seen from the last two weeks. After those three games, Kansas City faces off with the Bills, Rams, Bengals, Patriots and 49ers. That will be the stretch that defines their standing among the NFL's contenders.
A win—perhaps even a blowout win?—over the Jets would stop the bleeding for the time being. If the Chiefs can show that some of the issues of the season so far are improving game-to-game, it would be a building block for the work that still needs to be done. Frankly, the Chiefs have no choice but to beat the Jets. A loss at Arrowhead Stadium, marking the third game of a brutal losing streak? There's no room for that as an aspiring Super Bowl contender.

title: How Serious is the Chiefs' Offensive Tackle Problem?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' offensive tackle situation in the 2026 season has been... complicated. But has it been actively detrimental to the KC offense? Well, that's complicated too. Let's start from the top.
The season of O-line uncertainty began at left tackle, where undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson—a player who did not sign to the Chiefs' 90-man roster until May 4 —has started every game at one of the sport's most impactful positions, protecting Patrick Mahomes' blindside since Week 1.
Benson joined the team after a strong showing during rookie minicamp, then climbed the depth chart all the way to a battle for the starting right tackle spot in training camp. (Oh yeah, it's worth remembering that Benson was a lifelong right tackle, playing exclusively on the right side during his collegiate career.)
By the waning days of camp, it appeared that veteran Jaylon Moore would hold on to his starting right tackle spot. Then, starting left tackle Josh Simmons suffered a back injury. Very long story, very short : Simmons hasn't played in a game this season and currently sits on the injured reserve list, with his future timeline remaining uncertain.
Benson was named AFC Offensive Rookie of the Month in September , giving the youngster a bit of recognition for his ability to step into a very difficult situation, playing decent ball on his unnatural side of the line. Meanwhile, Moore has started at right tackle in every game except for the Chiefs' Week 7 loss in Seattle, when he was out with a concussion, leaving Joshua Ezeudu to start in his place.
Anecdotally, I've found most Chiefs fans to be relatively impressed with Benson's performance at left tackle while being largely unsatisfied with Moore's performance on the right side. The offense has been solid enough this season (with the exception of the Sunday night beatdown in Seattle and the scoreless fourth quarter in Denver), but it certainly hasn't been an unstoppable force, ranking 11th in points per game this season , even with a molten-hot start from running back Kenneth Walker to begin the year.
How can we properly assess the impact the tackles have had on the offense? This week, a pair of charts caught my eye.
OT percentile grades in run & pass blocking pic.twitter.com/Xato64hyeI
That graphic, from Judah Fortgang on Twitter , charts qualifying offensive tackles from around the league relative to their pass blocking and run blocking grades from Pro Football Focus . (Obvious disclaimer: PFF grades aren't always the gospel truth, but they're rarely total hogwash, particularly in a larger sample size like this.) You'll find the Chiefs' two starters, Benson and Moore, on the far left side of the graphic. That's not where you want to be.
Benson has the fifth-worst pass-blocking grade from PFF among qualifying tackles this season, but he's dead last in Fortgang's pass block grade percentile chart. He fares significantly better as a run blocker, right around the middle of the pack. Moore fares slightly better in pass block grading but slightly worse on the ground; still not good.
Another chart focuses on how their individual performances have impacted the offense.
How often OT are left 1-on-1 in pass blocking and their grades on those plays pic.twitter.com/gUGT6NElVS
This second graphic from Fortgang specifically looks at how often offensive tackles are left one-on-one in pass blocking situations and how they fare on those plays. In this case, you'll see Benson and Moore both at the bottom of the graphic (still bad), but in very different places on the x-axis.
From eyeballing this chart, you can see that Benson is left on an island at the sixth-highest rate in the league—an astronomical spot for the inexperienced rookie. Unfortunately, he also has the worst one-on-one grade of any qualifying tackle in the league by these metrics. The story of that chart is telling you that Benson is largely left one-on-one, to the tune of league-worst results.
Meanwhile, Moore has a much lower one-on-one rate, but he has the third-worst one-on-one grade when he is left to handle his assignment on his own.
Again, I want to emphasize two things before getting to the concerning takeaway. First, these grades shouldn't be the only data point used to evaluate the Chiefs' tackles (but I would say that they're a fair representation of what we've seen on film). Second, it's still reasonable to be impressed with what Benson has done in extraordinary circumstances. Asking an undrafted rookie right tackle to operate like a franchise left tackle is a remarkably steep task, and Benson has been good enough for the Chiefs to keep a functional offense in most circumstances.
Still, I believe that the impact of the questionable tackle play has shown up in big moments.
Mahomes is his O-line's best friend. Even when he's under duress, Mahomes is extremely good at mitigating the pressure while keeping his eyes downfield, giving him a chance to make a play even after the trenches have been lost. Think back to all the times Mahomes has escaped a collapsing pocket this season. Then, you have the times he has left the pocket by design, with the play call creating a moving target for opposing pass rushers, trying to give the tackles a schematic advantage while defensive ends are left guessing. Then think of how many times Mahomes has been able to sit in the pocket, survey his options, and deliver the ball without incident.
GOT 'EM. 📺: CBS pic.twitter.com/9eSUKJJwjA
Even Mahomes isn't without fault here. Particularly in Seattle with Ezeudu at right tackle, Mahomes stepped into pressure that may not have otherwise arrived. That, to me, looked like a quarterback who isn't entirely trusting his surroundings.
When the Chiefs' offense designs passing plays to run away from Benson's side of the line, that seems indicative of both the problem Kansas City currently has, and of the way they've mitigated it so far. Benson can be asked to "die a slow death" while Mahomes buys time to his right, asking Moore to hold his spot long enough for Mahomes to reset and fire. When it works, it looks great. When any part of that equation fails, you see a hurried, out-of-sync, unconfident passing game that still hasn't found its footing.
It's not all on the tackles; the pass-catchers are hurting more often than they're helping, and the interior offensive line bears some of the responsibility as well. This also isn't for the sake of stirring up more vitriol for Benson or Moore; Benson is overachieving any reasonable expectations anyone could have had for his rookie season, and Moore is underperforming on his contract, so he's already getting plenty of blame from many fans. But if the Chiefs want to get back to the best version of Mahomes and the ideal version of their passing game, they'll need a better second half of the season from their bookends on the offensive line.

title: 5 Realistic Trade Targets for Chiefs Ahead of the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
The annual NFL trade deadline has produced many a deal in the past, especially in the final hours of eligibility. Clubs like the Kansas City Chiefs have consistently been linked to rumors in recent weeks, with the noise only amplifying as more time passes.
It's one thing to connect a team to a candidate, but it's another for said deal to actually manifest. Everyone knows which positions would benefit from being addressed in KC — what names make the most sense?
Let's dive into five realistic Chiefs trade targets for the 2026 NFL trade deadline should general manager Brett Veach want to take a swing or two.
The Chiefs' need for a wideout is well-documented, even with Rashee Rice back from the hamstring injury he sustained in Week 4. Given that Tyquan Thornton is out for most or all of what's left of the regular season, the state of the receiver room is lackluster at best. Would calling the Cleveland Browns about Jerry Jeudy be the right play?
As far as financials are concerned, Spotrac reveals that Jeudy's new team would only be on the hook for $750,000 the rest of the way in 2026. Next season, he carries a $5.8M cap hit but just under $23M in total cash. Non-guaranteed money plays a role in the calculus.
The former first-round pick broke out in 2024 when he made the Pro Bowl for the first time and hauled in 90 passes for 1,229 yards and four touchdowns. Unfortunately, it's been tough sledding for him since then. He turned 106 targets into just 602 yards last season and has yet to find the end zone across eight games this year.
Still, Jeudy's capable of lining up on the boundary of the formation and should be right in his athletic prime. He won't save the season, although he could help it to some degree if all he needs in a change of scenery (and a reunion with Chiefs receivers coach Chad O'Shea).
This is an interesting case. Set to turn 32 in December, Calvin Ridley's best football is surely behind him. Long gone are the days of him being one of football's premier big-play threats and lighting up the stat sheet for the Atlanta Falcons, Jacksonville Jaguars or Tennessee Titans. With that said, could escaping the latter team help salvage whatever's left of his career in terms of production?
Ridley currently sits fourth among all Titans wideouts with 218 snaps, yet he's managed just six receptions for 91 yards. Perhaps a look back to last season is a better reflection of his ceiling after the age of 30, as he caught 17 passes for 303 yards (17.8 yards per reception) in 2025. According to Pro Football Focus , his yards per route run figure is way down to 0.73 after being 1.89 and 1.86 the two years prior.
Burning a Day 3 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft for someone of Ridley's pedigree wouldn't be the worst idea in the world, even if he turns out to be a cooked product. The receiving team in a trade would be on the hook for $2.84M via cap hit before deciding what to do with 2027 ($22.5M in cash).
Former San Francisco 49ers standout Jauan Jennings was a hot commodity entering this past offseason. Many folks in Chiefs circles wanted the club to take a swing on him, but it's safe to say he hasn't lived up to the one-year, $8M deal he inked with the Minnesota Vikings. In parts of six games, the 29-year-old has only six catches for 54 yards. Twenty of those yards came on one snag.
It's clear that things weren't panning out in Minnesota, so much so that there was nearly a deal to send Jennings back to San Fran as the calendar flipped from October to November:
The #49ers and #Vikings recently had a trade agreement in place for WR Jauan Jennings to return to San Francisco, but Jennings made it clear he didn’t want to go back, and the deal fell through, per @JayGlazer . pic.twitter.com/aqCgTn5l0M
One contributing factor for Jennings' struggles could be his alignment. He's spent 59.5% of his time in the slot, his highest mark since 2023. That's enabled him to be more of a post-catch threat, but his ideal role seems to be more in line with the one he held in his old stomping grounds.
That doesn't fit with what Kansas City typically opts for, in this writer's view, even with just $3.3M being due in the event of a trade.
Behold, the name that's had the attention of just about everyone on Chiefs social media. There's been plenty of buzz surrounding Colts wideout Josh Downs, especially since his team's season has done nothing but go further down the drain in recent weeks. With the 25-year-old set to become a free agent at the conclusion of his rookie contract, he's an affordable rental who could make a significant impact in the right contest.
Is that context Kansas City, though? That's the popular debate right now.
On one hand, the connection between quarterback Daniel Jones and Downs has produced 0.35 EPA per play and a 10.3-yard average depth of target. There's no denying Downs' ability to find soft spots in zone coverage and get open. There is , however, questioning of his fit with the Chiefs considering how the rotation is presently constructed.
Downs has lined up in the slot for just under 70% of his 2026 snaps, and that marks was 78.8% in 2025 and over 80% in his first two seasons. That clashes directly with Rashee Rice, who's a slot-heavy receiver (45.7% this year). There are ways to work around that for the right player, with the right price making it even more worth doing.
You didn't think we'd get out of here without listing a defensive player, did you?
Defensive end A.J. Epenesa is someone those who follow the Chiefs should be quite familiar with, as he spent over half a decade with the Buffalo Bills and squared off against Kansas City multiple times. He's a well-built lineman with a track record of being a formidable run defender, although a slip in his play the last couple of seasons led to Buffalo bidding him farewell.
Epenesa has since latched on with the Philadelphia Eagles, where he has yet to even crack the 75-snap mark and has been credited with only four pressures and three "stops" by PFF . Still, he'd be an extremely cheap get for a team seeking one piece to round out its defensive line rotation.
The question then becomes whether the Chiefs, who are already making waiver wire claim Jack Pyburn a game-day inactive, have the 53-man roster spot for him . Consider this more of an insurance policy sort of move than something Veach needs to jump on immediately.

title: Chris Jones Has an Interesting Explanation for Chiefs’ Frustrating Sack Drought
full_text:
It's no secret that the Kansas City Chiefs' defensive line has not performed up to expectations this season. They are currently tied for the worst mark in the NFL with nine sacks, and that sluggish start was exacerbated by a three-game sack drought earlier in the year.
Defensive linemen like Chris Jones have consistently insisted that results would come in due time , but that simply hasn't been the case. He's currently in the midst of one of the longest dry spells of his 11-year career in KC and has yet to record a full sack in 2026. Frustrations are mounting for the Chiefs defense after it blew an 11-point lead in the fourth quarter of last week's loss to the Denver Broncos. The team now sits second in the AFC West despite holding a 1.5-game lead a couple of weeks ago. Regardless, Jones' confidence has not wavered amid this recent slide.
During a media appearance on Wednesday , Jones reiterated why he believes the sacks will eventually come.
"It's all about perspective from my angle. We've got 10 games [left], right?" Jones said. "So, continue to chop wood. This year is an awkward year for all of us. Sacks started off slow, but you've got to continue to do what you've been doing. Eventually, they're going to start coming, and when they come, they come in bunches."
Jones and the media have been butting heads for quite a while whenever he is questioned about his unit's lack of production.
However, his wording to call the current campaign an "awkward" one is certainly telling of the challenges he has faced. There is no doubt that he and fellow star pass rushers like George Karlaftis are feeling the weight of the struggles. Later in his press conference, Jones would go on to explain why counting sacks is not always indicative of a defense .
"I think the sack part is kind of overrated," Jones continued. "People look at stats and they're not actually looking at the intricacies of the game. When you watch it play-by-play, watch what the team is actually doing, we get a lot of seven-man protection. You can't get too involved in the back-and-forth with the sacks and stats."
Although Jones argues that the defensive line has been better than fans have credited it for, the advanced metrics don't necessarily tell the same story. According to ESPN Research , the Chiefs' 6% pressure rate generated against Bo Nix last Sunday was the lowest of any NFL team since Week 5 in 2024 and a franchise low for the Chiefs dating back 14 years.
Toward the end of his presser, Jones declared that he has no interest in discussing sacks until the regular season concludes. "We'll talk about this at the end of the year," Jones told reporters. "I don't play for stats. I play for letters: Ws and Ls."
As Jones mentioned, a lot of factors come into play when evaluating the D-line's performance, including pass protection and how quickly the ball is getting out. However, Chiefs fans surely can't feel great that the pass-rushing unit isn't getting home to the quarterback at a time when the team is fighting to win the division.

title: What's Going On With R Mason Thomas?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' pass rush has struggled so far this season, and if you've been watching the unit particularly closely, you may be ready to argue that "has struggled" is an understatement.
The Chiefs did not record a sack in four of their first seven games of this season, and their only sack against the Denver Broncos in Week 8 was aided by Bo Nix short-circuiting when he spiked the ball behind him while under pressure. (By the way, that play was one of only two total times Nix was pressured on Sunday.)
ESPN Research: Chiefs pressured Bo Nix on 2 of 34 dropbacks (6%), the lowest for any team since 2024 Week 5, and the lowest for the Chiefs since 2012 Week 8 Chiefs had a 48.5% pressure rate on Nix in Week 1
George Karlaftis has recorded two sacks this season. No other Chief has more than one. Chris Jones hasn't recorded a box score stat in two weeks —a remarkable fact even as he still faces more than his fair share of double-teams. Second-year third-round pick Ashton Gillotte is establishing himself as a solid player, but not a disruptive pass-rusher. Former first-round pick Felix Anudike-Uzomah showed some flashes through the first few weeks, recording a sack in Week 1 and four quarterback hits through the first five games of the year , but he's been quieter since the bye week.
Most of those players currently feel like relatively straightforward known quantities. Good players! But largely already defined in their role for an NFL rotation. That's part of what makes rookie second-round pick R Mason Thomas so alluring, and also what makes his last two weeks so confusing.
Through the first five games of the season, Thomas played between 41.5% and 59.5% of the team's defensive snaps , with a few splash plays to show for it. Against the Seahawks, he played only 29% (20 snaps). In Denver, just 27% (17 snaps). Why the decrease in the last two games?
While this year's No. 40 overall pick has certainly had his share of poor snaps against the run , Seattle and Denver were both struggling to move the ball on the ground before their matchups with the Chiefs, and Thomas was given a larger workload at the very beginning of his NFL career, including in KC's Week 1 win over Denver when he played 27 snaps (53%) against those same Broncos.
To be fair, Thomas' workload has decreased, not disappeared, in the last two weeks. Still, it's hard to find a logical reason for him to be taken off the field as often as he has been.
Sure, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo often prefers veteran players in a vacuum, and he seems to have a penchant for bigger edge defenders who can be trusted to stay stout against the run—again, not Thomas' strength. But the Chiefs specifically need quick pressures from their four-man rush, which is something that Thomas can provide.
Thomas has played 17 fewer defensive snaps than Gillotte and 29 fewer than Anudike-Uzomah this season, which is still a substantial sample size for the rookie. In that time, according to Next Gen Stats , Thomas has led the Chiefs in pressure rate by a substantial margin.
Chiefs leaders in QB pressure rate through 7 games ( @NextGenStats ) R Mason Thomas (17%) George Karlaftis (12%) FAU (9.6%) Ashton Gillotte (7.5%) Khyiris Tonga (7.1%) Chris Jones (6.7%) Peter Woods (2.2%)
There's room for all of these players in Kansas City's struggling defensive line rotation. Gillotte can keep his running-down snaps. Karlaftis is strong on his edge. Anudike-Uzomah has also been rushing from the interior. Across the board, Kansas City needs more ways to pressure the quarterback, and Thomas' skill set is completely unique on this roster.
Thomas is not perfect. He's not a finished product. I'm not even calling him the best defensive end on the team—that title still belongs to Karlaftis and his well-rounded suite of tools. But as all eyes turn to the NFL's trade deadline, I still believe that the Chiefs' best chance for a second-half pass-rushing resurgence comes with a larger dose of Thomas. He should be given every opportunity to learn and get after the quarterback here in his rookie season, with hopes of his game coming together in time for the playoff push.
. @ByNateTaylor cooking on @ChiefsHMA “R Mason Thomas in 81 plays as a pass rusher has 20 wins. Ranks 13th in pass rush win rate when giving true chances to rush the passer in dropback settings.”
Again, this is currently still a short-term issue that could end up being just a two-game blip on the radar. I don't believe that Thomas has been soft-benched by Spagnuolo, sent to the doghouse, been entirely demoted, or anything of that sort. But those recent snap counts should still be a wake-up call for the Chiefs' defensive coaching staff. If Thomas can stumble into an insignificant workload just because of the flow of a particular game, they need to make a concerted effort to be sure it doesn't happen again.

title: Chiefs On SI Mailbag: What Could Kansas City Realistically Do at the Trade Deadline?
full_text:
After back-to-back frustrating losses—a blowout in Seattle and a meltdown in Denver —the Kansas City Chiefs are in a strange place. They're still clearly among the contenders in the AFC , but that's part of the strange feeling surrounding Chiefs Kingdom. They're among the rest of the contenders, not rising to a tier above them.
With a week until the NFL's trade deadline, what could the Chiefs do to bolster their roster in the next seven days, and where does the team stand now? That's what we'll unpack in today's Chiefs On SI mailbag.
In your opinion, what trades or position upgrades should the Chiefs make at the deadline? And realistically, which ones will they actually make? What’s your gut saying? - @MrEd315
The Chiefs clearly haven't gotten enough out of their pass catchers or pass rushers so far this season, so that's the place to begin. On the defensive line, however, I don't know if there's an external option that truly makes sense.
I'd be surprised to see the Chiefs make a huge swing for a player like Josh Sweat unless his price tag is much lower than expected, and if they look for a lower-tier player, they have to be an improvement (and earn Steve Spagnuolo's trust) over players like Felix Anudike-Uzomah and Ashton Gillotte, who are having nice seasons so far.
Wide receiver has some openings. I'd keep calling the Colts about Josh Downs until the price drops as far as it'll go, and I'd be interested in Brian Thomas Jr. as a multi-year solution while he's a buy-low candidate. I'd make room for someone like Dontayvion Wicks at a fair price too. There are a few creative mid-level answers out there... but my gut feeling?
My gut feeling is that it might not matter all that much. Andy Reid's comments last week , if taken at face value, remind us that the best chance for an improvement this season may have to come from a player who was on the team in training camp.
What are the top three realistic fixes the Chiefs can make in the middle of this season that give them the best shot to win the Super Bowl? Offensive line help? WR? - @mattlacasse.bsky.social
Since we just talked about trade options, I want to take this question to three internal solutions the Chiefs could find without reaching for outside help.
First, keep ramping up Cyrus Allen's workload. It wasn't perfect on Sunday in Denver, and it won't be perfect in the weeks to come. But he's more dynamic than Jalen Royals or Andrew Armstrong, and Xavier Worthy's apparent mistakes haven't kept him off the field.
Second, lean into the ground-and-pound production we saw during the first several weeks of the season. With Rashee Rice back, the offense should be multidimensional enough to keep defenses guessing, and the under-center offense is worth returning to. Go under center and hand it to Walker. Go under center and run some play-action. These last two weeks have felt like a regression to some of the problems of 2025. (And as a bonus, use that under-center offense to be aggressive on 4th-and-short. No more questionable kicks or unnecessary punts.)
Third, get as many pass-rushing snaps for R Mason Thomas as possible. If the Chiefs' pass rush is going to take a meaningful step forward, I think Thomas would be the most likely candidate for a substantial breakout. The rookie defensive end played a season-low 17 snaps (27%) in Denver after playing a then-low 20 snaps (29%) in Seattle. He doesn't need to be on the field for every likely rushing down, but he needs opportunities to get after the quarterback.
Is there something going on with Chris Jones? Dude's production has completely disappeared. - @ZachTakes
I have been (and still remain) extremely hesitant to sound the alarm on Chris Jones; he's one of the three most important players of the Chiefs' dynasty and has shown an incredible ability to be disruptive, even when facing tremendous attention from opposing offenses. I'm still holding out hope for a late-season/playoff-push stretch of games where Jones turns back the clock, but it's impossible to pretend that he's performing at his usual standard.
I think that's partially the encroachment of Father Time having an impact on the 32-year-old and partially an indictment on the rest of the Chiefs' defensive front, revealing how much they've relied on Jones to be elite for so many years. Still, that doesn't feel like enough to explain the fact that he hasn't recorded a statistic in two weeks . He had a calf issue reported on the Chiefs' injury reports through Week 4, but he's been clear of that designation since the bye.
I still believe that there will be game-changing moments from Jones down the stretch of this season, but I have to acknowledge that it's been a long time since we've seen one.
Did Reid decide to attempt a field goal in the fourth quarter as a way to assess if a change was needed this week?
 - @SoCal1186
I sure hope that wasn't the logic. Even without Harrison Butker's recent history front of mind, kicking a field goal there was the wrong choice. According to Next Gen Stats , punting the ball away in that scenario would have added the most win probability (raising it to 74.3%), while going for it would've put KC's win probability at 72.5%. Attempting the field goal was the least-analytically-sound decision at 71.5%.
If you don't care about analytics, you could rely on the eye test, your gut, and your recent memory to surmise that a 54-yard field goal in the rain was probably not going in from the struggling Butker. If he had hit that field goal, the Broncos would've still had solid starting field position after the kickoff, needing a touchdown to take the lead, and I think Butker would've still needed a few more clean weeks before he could be viewed as "back." However you slice it, I just don't think sending him out there in that scenario was a good decision.

title: Chiefs Rookie and Sophomore Power Rankings: Day 3 Pick on the Rise After Week 8?
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs outplayed the Denver Broncos for a huge chunk of their Week 8 meeting, only to give the game away near the end and fail to recover before the clock hit zeroes. That doesn't mean there wasn't plenty of good to take away from the contest, though, particularly regarding the club's young players.
Multiple first and second-year pieces continued to make names for themselves on Sunday, ranging from early-round NFL Draft selections by general manager Brett Veach to lesser-discussed pickups. Where does everyone stand as a new week of play begins?
Following Week 8, let's break down the Chiefs' rookies and sophomores by ranking each qualifying 53-man roster member in tiers. Be sure to return to this series each week to see who's moving and shaking.
Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott, whose practice window was recently opened , isn't included due to him still being on the physically unable to perform list .
Left tackle Josh Simmons sits this one out after going to injured reserve . The same applies to running back Brashard Smith .
The secondary duo of cornerbacks Nohl Williams and Mansoor Delane could be one of the Chiefs' most important tandems for the next couple of years. Williams has certainly held up his end of the bargain this year. Delane missed more time with a lingering shoulder injury , which head coach Andy Reid acknowledged will be a thing for a while.
"It's just a matter of being strong, strong enough to get out there," Reid said on Monday. "So there's a good chance he'll be able to get — or at least a chance — that he'll be able to get himself out there this week. But again, it's just how strong it is. We will see; that's going to be a day-to-day thing. If he can do it, he can do it. If not, (Kristian) Fulton did a nice job in there.”
Second-round defensive end R Mason Thomas had one of Kansas City's many Week 8 penalties, albeit while also recording a batted pass on the Broncos' third drive and continuing to flash plenty of athletic upside. Second-year man Ashton Gillotte, who's come on strong in recent weeks, played terrific run defense all afternoon and into the evening.
The (positive) story of the game, however, was fifth-round running back Emmett Johnson. His 15-yard rush featuring multiple broken tackles and his fourth-quarter kickoff return were both nice, but his value in the passing game managed to outshine everything else. Johnson finished with five receptions for 128 yards and a touchdown, potentially earning an increased role in the process.
Emmett Johnson has been the best RB of Week 8. pic.twitter.com/gUEU7EuAjB https://t.co/zwPbXZSinX
The book is clearly out on undrafted tackle Kahlil Benson, but that can't be held against him too much considering he's being asked to fill a role he isn't suited for over this many games. Speaking of role, rookie wideout Cyrus Allen played a career-high 31 offensive snaps in Week 8 and had a couple of catches, including a big-time one on third down. The glaring red flag from his performance, unfortunately, was a missed connection on a deep ball he just didn't seem prepared for.
Defensive tackle Peter Woods, the second of Kansas City's two first-round picks, left Sunday's defeat to Denver with a neck injury. He's still flying under the radar overall, preventing him from going back to the upper tier of Chiefs youngsters. With Woods hurt, August waiver wire addition Bryson Eason was on the field for 20 defensive snaps (32.3% of those available) but didn't notch a tackle.
Once L'Jarius Sneed went to injured reserve, KC was immediately tasked with producing a slot replacement on defense. Fourth-round pick Jadon Canady wasn't a huge part of the solution, although his seven snaps played were significant nonetheless. The 23-year-old had a solid third-and-7 tackle on receiver Marvin Mims to open the second half and also closed on a play later in the third frame.
Wide receiver Jalen Royals' workload wasn't expected to increase with Rashee Rice back from a hamstring injury. Now that Allen is flashing some of his ability and the Chiefs are still rumored to be shopping for a wideout on the trade market, that'll only become more so the case.
For the first time since Week 1, former Clemson tight end Jake Briningstool converted on his lone target of the game and had a positive reception. That marked his second straight outing with just five offensive snaps.
Safety Xavier Nwankpa hasn't seen the field on defense since the last time the Chiefs won a game. Linebacker Jeffrey Bassa, who's made a nice special teams play or two for Dave Toub this year, still can't really crack the rotation for Steve Spagnuolo's unit.
As usual, nothing to see here. After being active but not registering a snap in Week 7, tackle Diego Pounds sat out this one. Quarterback Garrett Nussmeier assumed his weekly role as the emergency third signal-caller, with defensive end Jack Pyburn once again being organizational depth who won't play in games barring an injury to someone else.

title: Chiefs Stock Watch: Kansas City Failed Patrick Mahomes in Week 8 Defeat to Broncos
full_text:
Life comes at you quickly in the NFL, and the Kansas City Chiefs are perhaps the best example of that right now. In a matter of just two Sundays, the team's gone from riding high as an undefeated powerhouse to a club that's licking its wounds after suffering back-to-back losses.
Week 7's defeat at the hands of the Seattle Seahawks was a beatdown, but Week 8's shortcoming against the Denver Broncos raised the panic level even more. Despite some inspired performances from multiple players, others served as big enough culprits to drag everyone else down with them.
Let's dive into the good and bad from Week 8's Chiefs loss against Denver and single out three players whose stock is trending up, as well as three who could use a better showing in Week 9 and beyond.
These players stood out for positive reasons on Sunday, potentially changing the trajectory of their seasons in the process.
After going consecutive contests with no touchdown passes and an interception, quarterback Patrick Mahomes found himself on the wrong end of the post-Week 7 edition of this column. That came with a sentiment that he wouldn't be there for long, which wound up being the case thanks to his rebound effort on Sunday in the Mile High City.
Mahomes completed a staggering 30 of his 41 pass attempts for 321 yards and a trio of touchdowns, also going without a turnover for the first time in nearly a month. The two-time MVP was crisp, efficient and did a nice job of extending plays when needed. According to RBSDM , No. 15 was good for 0.24 EPA per play, and that might've been selling him short.
Kansas City let an improved Mahomes outing go to waste, which is a shame for everyone involved.
Entering Sunday's play, rookie running back Emmett Johnson had failed to receive a single rushing attempt in two of his previous three games. In the one contest he did get some work in, it was a three-tote, six-yard output against the Los Angeles Chargers. That left many to wonder whether the fifth-round pick would see an increased role at any point, only for the course to completely reverse on Sunday.
Johnson experienced by far his best game as a professional, and he did it in multiple ways. As a receiver, he made the most of his five targets by ripping off five catches for 128 yards and his first regular-season touchdown. He also broke off about as fun and hard-earned a 15-yard rush as you'll ever see. His work didn't stop there — he had a nice kickoff return on special teams, too.
The Nebraska product's blend of tough running, contact balance, smarts and improving pass protection make him closer to a starting-caliber player than someone who should be buried on the depth chart. Kansas City's completely revamped its halfback room in the best of ways.
Being a nose tackle in the pros is a pretty thankless job. Oftentimes, it's your name not being called that means you're fulfilling your role at a high level. Everyone knew that'd be primarily the case when Khyiris Tonga signed with the Chiefs earlier this year, but he's making a name for himself. After a six-tackle performance against Seattle, the 30-year-old picked up right where he left off.
Tonga finished with just two tackles in Week 8, but one was a run stop on halfback J.K. Dobbins that stood out on tape. He also batted a pass in the second half of play and, per Pro Football Focus , was credited with a pressure on quarterback Bo Nix. On an afternoon and evening that saw several members of the Chiefs fall short, Tonga Time was out in full force.
This group of three didn't meet the appropriate level of expectations in Week 8 and desperately needs to recover moving forward.
Another week, another instance of star center Creed Humphrey failing to do perhaps the simplest part of his complex job. How concerning is it that a four-time Pro Bowler and two-time All-Pro has been charged with a career-high six fumbles before the season is even halfway over? Humphrey acknowledged last week that he was working on resolving his problem, then he proceeded to fail again in a pressure-packed game.
Head coach Andy Reid spoke to the media on Monday and said Humphrey simply needs to "get the snaps up," yet it appears to be much easier said than done at this point. Until the former second-round pick strings together a few good showings in a row, it's hard to be confident that he'll put this confusing trend behind him.
When the Chiefs announced that L'Jarius Sneed was going on the injured reserve list and rookie Mansoor Delane would sit out Week 8 , they knew they'd be shorthanded at the cornerback spot. Not many folks doubted the ability of someone like Nohl Williams to get the job done on the outside or someone — anyone — to at least match Sneed's production in the slot, but the jury remained out on Kristian Fulton.
A whopping 60 snaps later, it's virtually impossible to feel much better about Fulton being a viable replacement for anything more than brief stints.
The veteran defensive back committed defensive pass interference on the Broncos' opening drive and later had an illegal block in the back on special teams. In the second quarter, he also totally whiffed on an attempted jam on wideout Courtland Sutton and got burned because of it.
Fulton remains someone who's a valuable depth piece and maybe even a trade chip , but don't confuse him for a starter on the same level of Williams or Delane.
Yes, we're cheating here and including a coach instead of a player. I think it's entirely justified, though, considering how much Reid melted down over the course of Sunday's contest. Penalties and on-field execution by the players were deserving of blame, sure, but Reid's baffling game management is still at or near the top of the list.
When the Chiefs opted to kick to try to go up 6 (never great!) our model had it as a toss-up between go...and punt. It saw field goal attempt as clearly the worst option. pic.twitter.com/Z7ugriKYkj
From botching a fourth-and-short to trotting out placekicker Harrison Butker for a boot he was bound to face an uphill battle to make, Reid fell flat against a bitter rival. He also still isn't explaining what's going on with benching left guard Kingsley Suamataia ; backup Mike Caliendo predictably struggled in relief.
Reid doesn't owe anyone answers, and his track record speaks for itself, but part of that includes decision-making concerns that crept back up at the worst time in Week 8. He needs to bounce back as badly as any of his players do.

title: The Good News and Bad News About the 2026 Kansas City Chiefs
full_text:
After back-to-back losses in the last two weeks , the Kansas City Chiefs are no longer the No. 1 seed in the AFC. They no longer hold the top spot in the AFC West . They've split with the Denver Broncos, meaning that the head-to-head tiebreaker they earned in Week 1 was one of many things wasted in their Week 8 meltdown.
Still, there is good news and bad news about where the Chiefs stand, particularly in the AFC. Do you want the good news first or the bad news?
The illusion of choice strikes again. It's all the same news.
Until further notice, the Chiefs are just another flawed contender in the AFC. How that makes you feel is a matter of perspective.
The AFC has somewhere between six and 10 teams that I could genuinely see making a playoff push that lands them in the AFC Championship Game. I could also see any of those teams being ousted in the wild card round. Sure, the Buffalo Bills seem like the worthy favorite, but who could be surprised by a mistake-filled opening-round loss to a barely-qualifying Houston Texans team that forces a few turnovers in January? No, I don't really believe in the Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) or Cleveland Browns (5-3), but at least one of those teams seems likely to be playing in the postseason, even if the Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) end up winning the AFC North.
Meanwhile, those heating-up Bengals just needed overtime to squeak past the lowly Tennessee Titans. Before that, they handled the Lamar Jackson-less Baltimore Ravens. Before that, they beat the then-winless Miami Dolphins by just seven points.
Look around the AFC and you'll see a wave of competent but unspectacular teams who do some things well and some things poorly. The good news is that the Chiefs still exist firmly within that class. The bad news is that they have been better than that for the majority of the Patrick Mahomes era.
The Chiefs, quarterbacked by Mahomes and with the AFC's only Super Bowl rings since Tom Brady's New England Patriots, are essentially neck-and-neck with Bo Nix's Broncos. Right there with the AFC North contenders who leave me uninspired. Tied in the standings with the Jacksonville Jaguars. The Bills are the only AFC squad with just one loss through eight weeks.
Kansas City isn't standing above their competition, reclaiming their boogeyman status for the rest of the AFC. They aren't sitting in the basement with other squads focusing on their 2027 NFL Draft boards. They're just sharing "flawed contender" status with the rest of the conference that has high hopes and measured expectations.
The Chiefs' path to the top should still be more climbable than others—Mahomes alone changes the math of what Kansas City can accomplish—but the Chiefs have enough flaws and have suffered enough self-inflicted wounds now that it's no longer reasonable to expect the best at every turn. Could they still represent the AFC in the Super Bowl? Absolutely. Could they be bounced weeks prior? Sure could. Just like everybody else.
