title: Raiders Confidence Meter: How I'm Feeling Ahead of 49ers Bout
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers is their next opportunity to prove they can beat good teams this season. Based on several close losses, it is fair to believe the Raiders have a chance to pull off an upset.
On the other hand, Las Vegas' four losses make it fair to wonder which Raiders team will show up against the 49ers. This has been one of the biggest questions facing this year's Raiders every Sunday.
Should the Raiders that nearly beat the Kansas City Chiefs show up, they will have a chance. If the Raiders that slept walked through their game against the New England Patriots show up in Week 9, it will be a long, long Sunday.
Las Vegas has struggled to run the ball for most of this season. Sunday against the 49ers will give Las Vegas' offense all it can handle. The Raiders must find a way to get their ground game going, no matter which back gets the job done. Last week, that was rookie Mike Washington.
"I thought overall, outside of Mike [Washington Jr.], the offensive line did a really good job. Tight ends blocking well. Mike ran well, so gave us a spark in the run game. But I don’t think it was a one-man show. It was a group effort, and I think we were able to stay more balanced [against the Jets]," Kubiak said earlier this week.
“I think it’s always a moving target. See where your team’s at, and who’s playing the best ball at the time. And it’s a 17-game regular season where things change every week. And they’ve been changing at guard. They’ve changed up front defensively. Changed at corner, and that’s the NFL. We have a young roster, and we’re going to give guys opportunities and see what fits us best."
Kubiak elaborated, noting that he aims to stick to the plan he outlined in the offseason. That plan was to use all three running backs as much as possible, with Jeanty accounting for most of those carries. Jeanty's health and the lack of a dependable offensive line have impacted things.
“I stand by what I said, that we’re going to need Mike [Washington Jr.], we’re going to need Ashton [Jeanty], we’re going to need Dylan [Laube],” Kubiak said.
“They’re all part of our success, run and pass, and Ashton made huge plays for us in the game yesterday in the pass game, in protection. Phenomenal in protection like he’s always been, and just the way the game went yesterday, Mike got more carries, and going forward, we’re going to be counting on all three of those guys.”
Rookie offensive lineman Trey Zuhn has also become a critical, but moving, part for Las Vegas. This is after spending weeks largely in a reserve role as he continued to develop in practice. Last week against the New York Jets, Las Vegas' coaching staff started Zuhn at right guard.
This could continue for the foreseeable future, as Las Vegas continues to look for answers along its interior offensive line. Overall, Zuhn played well last week, but that was against a Jets defense missing players. San Francisco will pose a much greater test.
Still, the Raiders' plan at running back and offensive guard will remain unclear until they take the field on Sunday.
Based on what Las Vegas has shown over the season's first eight games , I believe Sunday will be more of the same. The Raiders' four wins have come against teams with losing records. Las Vegas' losses have come against teams with losing records.
San Francisco has a winning record and a coaching staff and roster that are superior to the Raiders' at the moment. The Raiders have a shot at beating the 49ers, but their four losses have made it clear in my mind that, as constructed and as used, the Raiders are highly unlikely to beat an elite team.
The Raiders are set for another challenging game on Sunday. Good teams can pick apart what their opponents do well and where they struggle. San Francisco has much more information on Las Vegas' strengths and weaknesses than the Raiders have on the 49ers.
Confidence Meter: Not confident.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: How Kirk Cousins Rebound Year Fueling Raiders Hopes
full_text:
Last year, the Las Vegas Raiders had a quarterback problem.
The trade for Geno Smith did not pay dividends, and the team moved on after a season. For a team that has struggled to find consistency at that position since Derek Carr's departure, fans were left wondering where the next franchise quarterback would come from.
The long-term answer came quickly during the college football season, as with every Raiders loss came another Las Vegas native-turned-Hoosier fan. Raider Nation tuned in every Saturday to watch their expected future signal-caller, Fernando Mendoza , who seemed on a collision course with the franchise.
However, minority owner Tom Brady spoke out about playing quarterbacks before they're ready and ruining their development, which raised questions about adding a veteran and allowing Mendoza to sit and learn until he was fully prepared to take the reins. The Raiders were going to add a vet to the locker room.
But where would that come from?
Kirk Cousins' tenure in Atlanta did not go well. The Falcons signed him to a massive contract with loads of guaranteed money, but he did not lead them to the playoffs and dealt with turnover issues.
However, he was injured for much of his time there, and the Falcons drafted a QB to eventually replace him, turning to Michael Penix Jr. when their playoff hopes were desperate. He took over when Penix got injured in 2025, but it wasn't enough to get Atlanta to the postseason.
The Falcons cut ties, and a month later, the Raiders added him. A low-risk move for a player who seemed like his best days were behind him.
However, Cousins got healthy and has proven to be more than a bridge quarterback who's over the hill. He has played like one of the better QBs in the league, ranking second in the NFL in passing touchdowns and sitting at third in passing yards.
At 38 years old, Cousins has the Raiders at 4-4 and still playing competitive football in November, a place this team hasn't been in years. Mendoza is still the long-term answer, but fans have to enjoy the way Cousins is slinging it right now.
The Raiders continue to shatter expectations, fighting for a Wild Card spot because of how they're moving the ball through the air. It seemed like his career was done just a year ago, but he's not only back in a starting role; he's thriving in it.
And the Raiders are reaping the benefits.
Carter Landis studied journalism at Michigan State University where I graduated in May of 2022. He currently is a sports reporter for a local television station, and is a writer covering the Las Vegas Raiders

title: Raiders Arrive in California for Old-School Rivalry Showdown
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) will take on the San Francisco 49ers (6-1) on Sunday, and the once neighbors in the Bay Area will renew an old rivalry.
The 49ers have ruled out three wide receivers, including future Hall of Fame star Mike Evans, and have a fourth listed as questionable.
That said, big things are swirling around the Silver and Black franchise with the NFL trade deadline looming this Tuesday at 1 PM PT, and for the first time in years, it isn’t drama or controversy.
Under the steady hand of GM John Spytek, the Raiders are being run professionally from top to bottom, and this storied franchise is now being talked about for all the right reasons.
One of the many advantages that the Raiders have with a 15-year veteran like Kirk Cousins leading the way for the 2026 NFL Draft No. 1 overall pick, and the man NFL executives ranked as the best QB prospect in the last four drafts, Fernando Mendoza, is that he isn’t just showing the Nandolorian the on-field complexities of the game, but the off-field.
Cousins leads from the front, and it is why his teammates love and trust him.
A lot has been made of Klint Kubiak facing his brother, Klay, the 49ers' offensive coordinator, on Sunday, but Cousins has ties there as well.
But for Cousins, it is about leading this team from the front into what could be the biggest win of Kubiak's early career, and perhaps projecting them from playoff hopeful to playoff-bound.
Kyle Shanahan, like his father Mike, is a gifted offensive mind, and his team deserves the respect they get on offense, but as Cousins pointed out, that defense is elite.
“Another top five defense in the league. Feels like I’m saying that every week the last several weeks. I don’t know who the bottom five defenses are, but we’re not playing them. So, maybe someday. But what a challenge. Great opportunity, great football team, well coached, great players. So, it’ll be a great challenge for us, and we’ve got to be at our best, but going to their place, great environment, great fan base there, and it’ll be a good test for us. So, take any questions you have.”
KIRKO CHAINS IS BACK 🥶 pic.twitter.com/zPhBjtxAkc
Cousins' alter ego, Kirko Chainz, came back in force this week on the plane ride back from New Jersey after the win over the Jets. Cousins explained why it may have returned.
“I don’t know. It’s been a while. I think probably the longer the flight, the more likely the chains, and it was a long one coming back, and it was a great win, and so we had fun with it. But a lot of football up ahead.”
Raiders RB Dylan Laube is the Silver and Black's unexpected dog, and one area he is contributing is helping his QB with his TD celebrations, such as Cousins' recent “Wellness” appreciation to the training staff.
Kirk Cousins just hit the most UNC celebration possible pic.twitter.com/XbrXyVWwD6
“Oh yeah, that was all Dylan [Laube]. So, I’m famous for – shout out to my college teammate, specifically Todd Anderson – I don’t get my own jokes, I steal them from other people, and then I’m just a better megaphone. So, Dylan came up with it, and then I was like, ‘I’m going to use that.’ So, he gets all the credit for coming up with it. I get all the credit for spreading the joy.“
Cousins then got sentimental for his days at Michigan State.
“But in college, I was known for hearing a good joke in the locker room in one corner, and then I would go run over to the other corner and tell the same joke as if it was my joke. So, it got to a point where guys are like, ‘You’re a joke stealer. You can’t do that.’ So, anyways, I guess I kind of stole that one, but I did my part.”
Kubiak asked his veteran QB to talk to the team about how he prepares, and the 38-year-old Cousins sounded like a 120-year-old sage, bringing his teammates' attention back to the joy of the game of football.
“Klint [Kubiak] had asked me maybe 20 minutes before the team meeting, ‘Can you share a thought about your preparation today?’ And I said, ‘Okay.’ So, I kind of was thinking quickly through some thoughts that I thought would resonate, and I just find in this league that comparison is a big part of what this league is all about.”
Cousins elaborated, “You’re third in this or seventh in that, whatever it may be. And comparison is the thief of joy. And so, this league and the way this league works can steal your joy really quick if you let it. And it’s done it to me many times."
"And so, I was just challenging myself. What I was trying to communicate to the team is, ‘Guys, it’s a daily battle for me to come in here and have joy because of the way that this league beats you up in the comparison factor.’ And so, I said, ‘Don’t let this league steal your joy, and let’s help each other and how we do that.' And it’s a daily battle.”
After the win over the Jets, Cousins and several teammates went to his favorite place to eat, and it has become a victory cry after a Raiders win.
“Yeah, I mean, we lost four in a row, so it’s been a while. But man, as the weeks grew and the losses mounted, the In-N-Out started sounding better and better. So, we knew, ‘Hey, if we win this game, let’s all land and let’s all go to In-N-Out.’”
Kirk Cousin’s In-N-Out winning meal crew got bigger after snapping a 4-game skid on Sunday vs. the Jets. #vegas #raiders #raidernation pic.twitter.com/Zx6GX73VhD
Cousins, since he was a freshman at Michigan State, has always been known as generous. So when asked about picking up the tab, I already knew the answer.
“In-N-Out’s not that expensive, so I think, yeah, the last time, there weren’t that many of us, maybe 15 guys or whatever it was, but yeah, you put your card down; it doesn’t go too far, which is nice.”
The Raiders have had their troubles coming out of the locker room at halftime. Kubiak hasn’t hidden from that, and the team was significantly better against the Jets, and Cousins explained why that is so vital in the NFL.
“Yeah, I think it was. I think the first play of the second half might have been the throw to Brock [Bowers], and I thought that was a key play in the game and a great call by our coaches, and that whole drive, to finish that drive, it got us right back in the game, which we needed, very important. If you punt and they go down and score, it could be a whole different story."
"So, it’s very important, and we’ve got to be really strong in the third quarter the rest of the way. And I felt we have continued, last week in the fourth quarter, continuing to play well in the fourth quarter. But it’s a four-quarter game. You’ve got to do it, all four of them.”
The grounded Cousins broke down the fact that he talks about joy and comparison, but he also brings up the second-half slow starts and how he balances the two in telling detail.
“Well, I think I talk about it out two sides of my mouth because on one hand, it’s, ‘Comparison is the thief of joy,’ but welcome to the NFL. You’re also being evaluated, and this is a big boy business, and you’ve got to deliver, so it’s both.”
He added, “And my message to myself and to our team is, ‘Hey guys, we’ve got to hold ourselves to a very high standard, but we can’t let that cause us to come in here with our heads down or without joy because we’ll be at our best when we’re able to do both.’ And that’s what you’re looking to do, is to find that balance in the middle."
"But there’s no doubt that when I’m looking every week, saying, ‘Where are we ranked in the bottom of the league, where do we have to be better, where are we getting beat, or what will get us beat?’ And you have to be on those things and working to improve them at all times.”
The reality about the NFL, whether you are a fan or a player, is that you always want more. The Raiders improved against the blitz last week and in man coverage, but for Cousins, it was only a start—not a milestone—the mark of a good leader.
“Yeah, I mean, it’s week to week, but I was very impressed with the effort and the way guys were separating and making plays versus man. And it’s…

title: Raiders vs. 49ers: Key Players To Watch in Bay Rivalry
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders return to the Bay Area for the first time since relocating from Oakland, facing one of the NFL's best teams thus far, the San Francisco 49ers.
Las Vegas is 4-4 and could find itself back in the playoff sweepstakes with an upset in Santa Clara. The Raiders need to thrive in a few key matchups while head coach Klint Kubiak looks to establish more balance in his offense, which is a top-five passing unit in the NFL. Here are five players to watch on Sunday against San Francisco.
The Raiders may have found their starting right guard for the foreseeable future. Zuhn looked impressive against the New York Jets in his first career start, and it is no surprise that a technical player with good functional athleticism was able to have some success this early.
Against a 49ers defensive front with DeForest Buckner and Osa Odighizuwa, it will be one of the biggest challenges of his young career and a potential "Welcome to the NFL" moment.
With Darien Porter questionable to play, there is still uncertainty about whether he'll have significant reps against the 49ers if he does.
Either way, Raiders fans should be keeping an eye out for rookie Jermod McCoy, who had a rough go against the Jets and is still getting his feet under him after missing football for nearly two years. Look for McCoy to be in the cornerback rotation whether Porter plays or not.
Nailor has been the best route runner on the team thus far and was getting open before last week, when he caught four passes for 38 yards and a touchdown.
The free agent signee from Minnesota has not been productive this season, but it seems like the Raiders are finally getting him the ball, and the offense is beginning to produce and become more efficient in the passing game than it was. Look for Nailor to continue to get looks against the 49ers.
Arguably the most consistent cornerback on the roster, Johnson has been a steady presence at nickel this season, and I think that will continue this week against the 49ers.
Johnson is likely to match up against a mixture of George Kittle, Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing, or even Christian McCaffrey. He'll play a key role in the secondary and run support, which has been lacking on the defensive front lately.
Jared Feinberg, a native of western North Carolina, has written about NFL football for nearly a decade. He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. title: Raiders NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: Potential Fits With One Week Left
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders' first eight games of the season went about as expected. Las Vegas had the most productive offseason of any team in the league. This was the perfect response to finishing last season with the No. 1 overall pick and arguably the league's worst roster.
A team can only make so much progress in one offseason. Surpassing last season's win total in less than half a season confirmed that they made as much progress as reasonably possible. Yet the first eight games also confirmed they need more if they hope to compete with the league's best.
Las Vegas has several holes on its roster that it can address at the trade deadline, should its front office feel inclined to make a move. However, with the Raiders off to their best start in years, any potential trade would need to make a lot of sense for the Silver and Black.
The trade deadline is less than a week away. Although the Raiders need help at several positions, their offseason moves have both eliminated many needs and left little room for additional quality moves. With so little room left, Las Vegas should avoid unnecessary moves.
Given the resources it would take to complete a trade, it seems the Raiders likely won't do so this time around. They have little to gain and a lot to lose; swinging a trade would be risky.
Below are a few options that fit their needs, as they cross the halfway point of the season.
By other teams' standards, Payne's play appears to have dipped over the past few seasons. However, it seems inevitable that he would make an immediate impact on the interior of Las Vegas' defensive line. Whether rushing the passer or helping stop the run, Payne would be an upgrade along the interior.
The compensation to the Washington Commanders and Payne would be obvious contractual hurdles to work out. At first glance, I'd guess Las Vegas would probably rather not trade future assets for an interior defensive lineman nearing 30 years old.
Still, Payne would unquestionably help the Raiders against the run, which would help the unit improve against the pass as well.
The Raiders' receivers could use another capable option. Each of their current receivers is talented enough to fit Las Vegas' goal of addressing the position group by committee. Still, an injury to any one of their receivers is more significant than it is for other teams.
As with any midseason addition, Downs will need some time to fully gel with Las Vegas' offense, but Klint Kubiak's staff has shown it can develop players on offense. Downs is not an elite receiver by any means, but he would be another solid addition to Las Vegas' wide receiver committee.
Although the Raiders could use additional help at receiver, it is worth noting that veteran receivers Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor have been open a decent amount this season on plays where they did not get the ball. Many of those plays would have gone for a significant gain or even a touchdown.
“You’re always trying to find your playmakers and put them in the best position possible to have success. And last week, while the ball didn’t find him as much, he was doing things away from the ball that were really good stuff that helped us be successful,” Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said earlier this week.
“That guy, I’ve never seen somebody so happy for his teammates to have success. So, that’s really the mark of somebody you’re looking for to be on your offense. But you know anytime his number is called, he’s going to be ready to go, and it’s something that we try to get him in the best position possible to be successful.”
There are a lot of ways the Raiders could improve overall, but a trade, let alone a significant one, seems unlikely with the deadline just a few days out. Still, the Raiders' front office will keep their options open, as improving the roster is always top of their mind.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: 2 Players Raiders Should Call About Before Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders brought in a load of talent on both sides of the ball this offseason. The Raiders' front office left nearly no stone unturned to quickly revamp its roster. That led to Las Vegas' 3-0 start, which has now leveled out at .500 heading into Week 9.
The strides Las Vegas made this offseason have produced instant, tangible results for the Raiders' front office and coaching staff. Yet that progress lets them move on to the next areas that need improvement.
Las Vegas made so much progress on its roster this offseason that the positions it needs help at most are glaring. Those roster weaknesses showed up during their four-game losing streak. That losing streak confirmed that coaching can only do so much; Las Vegas' roster needs more.
The Raiders may ultimately not be serious players at the deadline, but there are undoubtedly players on the trade block that could help Las Vegas win games this season. Below are two players that the Las Vegas Raiders should kick the tires on, with the trade deadline only days away.
Thomas has too much talent for Las Vegas not to at least reach out to the Jacksonville Jaguars to see what they would want in return for the young receiver. The Raiders' and Jaguars' current front offices worked together last season to complete a trade for wide receiver Jakobi Meyers.
Las Vegas will keep building out its receivers over the next few seasons and may need even more after the season, depending on what happens with Tre Tucker. Thomas would be a solid addition to the position group, helping open up the offense even more.
The interesting thing about both players listed here is that Las Vegas' current front office got an up-close and personal look at both players last season. Thomas had the best game of his career against Las Vegas last season. Payne also made his presence felt against the Raiders last season.
At the very least, Las Vegas' front office should do its due diligence on any proven interior defensive lineman who may be on the trade block. The Raiders owe it to their roster to at least see what the Washington Commanders' asking price for Payne would be.
Payne would not solve all of Las Vegas' defensive issues. However, he would be just as good as, if not better than, what Las Vegas currently has on its interior defensive line. After moving on from Jonah Laulu and injuries to Tonka Hemingway and Thomas Booker, the unit is thinning.
The Raiders' difficulty stopping the run stems from their interior defensive line. Las Vegas has been unable to find multiple interior defensive linemen who are both durable and dependable, which has quietly impacted the unit's ability to stop the run.
As the trade deadline approaches, head coach Klint Kubiak gave insight into how his coaching staff handled their defense's struggles against the run. Las Vegas' defense allowed the New York Jets to run for 140 yards in the first half before holding them to 26 in the second half.
“That’s something as a coaching staff and as players and as coaches that we’re working together to fix. It’s not going to happen overnight. Something that is going to take practices, it’s going to take experience, it’s going to take us putting our heads together and having a better product so that we’re not giving up those many yards on the ground,” Kubiak said earlier this week.
“But the people that we have doing it together, our players and coaches, I believe in, and that’s a really important piece of it. We have each other’s back, and the thing I love about our defense is that when things didn’t go well, we kept playing."
“We got key stops. Made a huge play at the end with [Jeremy] Chinn, and in the NFL, it’s not always going to be pretty. It’s not always going to be how you wanted it to happen. But at the end of the game, it’s who won the game, and I think as a team we found a way to win.”
The Raiders face a talented 49ers team tomorrow.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Kubiak Leads Raiders to Cali, Eyes Upset Win vs. His Brother
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev.—The Las Vegas Raiders (4-4) headed to California this afternoon to take on the San Francisco 49ers (6-1), and they are going with the mindset of a win.
Under Klint Kubiak's leadership, the Raiders have won every game they were supposed to, an incredible indicator of how far the first-year head coach has taken the storied franchise.
This Raiders rebuild is ahead of schedule, and the praise goes to Kubiak, the organization, Tom Brady, John Spytek, and the players and coaches who have bought in.
The Raiders are renewing a rivalry with their former Bay Area neighbor, the 49ers, and while the rivalry has changed with both teams moving away, the respect and contention remain the same.
The Raiders injury report was interesting today, offering more positives than negatives. Klint Kubiak said today that starting CB Darien Porter is questionable for the game, but he seemed optimistic while praising his efforts to get back.
“Very intentional. He’s working really hard to get back. He’s made improvements every day.”
Kubiak is very familiar with the 49ers, as we discussed before , but Kubiak was asked whether that familiarity with him and some players is helping as he reviews the film.
“Yeah, they’re top offense in the league, top defense in the league. Extremely well coached, great talent everywhere. That experience was very meaningful for me. But a couple years removed from that, and on Sunday it’s a players’ game.”
Fred Warner, the 49ers linebacker, is a bona fide superstar, and his presence in the 49ers' defense is going to force the Silver and Black to know where he is at all times, something Kubiak is very aware of.
“He’s the best in the league. He’s the most physical, smartest, most athletic guy that you’ll see. So, we have a great challenge with him.”
The 49ers added another elite defender by trading with the Indianapolis Colts for DeForest Buckner. Kubiak was asked how to prepare for a guy he knows well, but you don’t have much film on him in this new scheme.
“Go back and watch what he’s done at other places. But I think it’s very well known number 99 [DeForest Buckner] is a heck of a player. Excellent, one of the best in the league at his position and upgraded their defensive line quite a bit.”
The Raiders' running game improved against the Jets, and it needed to. Kubiak broke down what he saw as the reasons for that.
"Well, you saw improvements in the production, so the production’s got to continue to improve, and that’s a group effort.”
Darrell Luter Jr. earned a captain spot this week, and Kubiak was quick to explain why.
“Yeah, he’s been just a guy that has worked very hard since he’s been here. We’re really happy to get him when we did, and he’s been a great addition to our team as a corner, as a special teams player, as a teammate, and obviously he’s going back to play his old team. So, excited for him to be a captain.”
Dylan Laube has become an unexpected dog for the Silver and Black, and Kubiak discussed what he brings to the franchise.
“I think just an overall professionalism. The way that he goes about his work. When you are professional the way that he is and you’re intelligent, then people start following his lead and want to have the same success. And how do you do it? Well, look at his example. Look at Maxx [Crosby]’s example. Look at Kirk [Cousins]’s example."
"The way they work and the way they prepare and the way they take care of their bodies. Those are great examples of guys that have played a long time. So, Dylan [Laube] goes after them, and then he starts making plays.”
One key ingredient in this restoration is how the franchise, from top to bottom, interacts and the quality of its leaders. Kubiak’s key, and the bigger key for the organization, is trust.
The entire organization is on the same page, and trust is the key. Kubiak talked about trust and how Laube earned it.
“Yeah, it’s simple. It’s his silent tape. So, he’s been producing and deserves the opportunities.”
Kubiak didn’t want to get into details, and you can’t blame him, about how the rushes will be distributed on Sunday between Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr. Instead, he talked about the situation in generic terms.
“I just know both guys are going to play, and Dylan [Laube].”
The aforementioned trust the Raiders have in him is demonstrated in a myriad of ways. One of those is the competitive fire, and the team sees what guys do in practice. Players’ performance in practices doesn’t lie. Kubiak emphasized the daily competition, and he wants players to earn more reps and a bigger role.
“Yeah, well, it’s a long season, and you’ve got to make sure your practices continue to have that competitive edge. Going good-on-good in the competitive period situationally. You just got to make sure in November you’re climbing and you’re getting better as a team.”
The 49ers' home atmosphere is not easy, and Kubiak understands the importance of preparation and getting his young team ready for it.
“With any great road environment, the crowd noise is a big part of it. But yes, there’s things that we talk about in our team meetings. This is why you coach in the NFL. This is why you play for games like this and for environments like this.”

title: Raiders Latest Injury Report Presents More Positives Than Negatives
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders are all but set to travel back to California to continue their long-running rivalry against the San Francisco 49ers.
Starting with their Week 8 trip to the East Coast, Las Vegas will play four road games in five weeks. During that span, they will again play some of the league's best teams. Sunday will be their next challenge , against a deep, talented 49ers team.
As they continue through one of the league's toughest schedules, the Raiders' offense aims to stay hot in the second half, specifically in the third quarter. Last Sunday against the Jets, Las Vegas exploded for its best third quarter of the season.
What Las Vegas' offense did in the third quarter has made the difference between winning and losing. In the Raiders' four losses , their offense scored three points in the third quarter. In their four wins, Las Vegas has scored 37 points in the third quarter. It is that simple.
In their four losses, Las Vegas' offense scored 13, 10, 13, and six points through three quarters. In their four wins, Las Vegas' offense scored 27, 17, 22, and 28 points through three quarters, respectively. Scoring points on offense can negate a "bad" defense.
More importantly, an offense that can score points without the defense or special teams setting it up for success, in theory, would be able to sustain drives and eat time off the clock, helping protect their defense. The Raiders did this in their four wins. In each of those games, the defense made big plays.
When the Raiders' offense provides the points, their defense has generally played better.
As bad as Las Vegas' defense played against the Jets, the Raiders' offense scored enough points to give their defense enough time to make game-changing plays down the stretch. Las Vegas' front office invested heavily in the offense this offseason. The unit must produce weekly, for four quarters.
The unit must score points, not stats.
The unit delivered an impressive second half, led by veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins. Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko praised Cousins and the unit for a productive second half in Week 8 and hopes they'll be just as productive in the second half against San Francisco.
“That’s really something that, as the head coach sets a vision for something, it’s on all of us as an organization to get that done. So, when he sets a goal for the week, or he sets something that he’s talked about, that he makes a priority, it’s something that we take to heart,” Janocko said earlier this week.
“We implement it in practice. We implement it in things that we’re trying to do, how we’re going about our business, our planning, and then when it comes to fruition, we’re really carrying out his vision, and that’s what it takes to be successful.”
Thomas Booker, Folorunso Fatukasi, and tight end Ian Thomas were limited in practice early in the week. Fatukasi and Thomas have gradually gotten healthier. Both participated in Friday's practice. Booker missed practice on Friday. It was the second practice in a row that he has missed.
Kubiak declared Booker out for Sunday's game. That is another blow to an already vulnerable interior defensive line. Las Vegas has struggled to stop the run this season, largely because of its interior defensive line. The Raiders will need more from Tonka Hemingway, Adam Butler, and Tim Keenan.
Darien Porter missed Wednesday's practice with a groin injury he suffered against the Jets. After missing Wednesday's practice, Porter returned on Thursday on a limited basis. Porter was a full participant on Friday. Fatukasi, Thomas, and Dont'e Thornton were full participants.
Kubiak announced Friday that Porter will officially be listed as questionable heading into Sunday's game. His absence against the Jets was obvious, forcing the Raiders to adjust much faster than they expected.
Thomas was a limited participant on Wednesday, but fully participated in practice on Thursday and Friday.
Although he was not listed on Wednesday, Thornton was listed as a limited participant in Thursday's practice with a back issue. He returned to practice on a full basis on Friday. It remains to be seen if Kubiak is comfortable enough with Thornton to put him on the field.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: Raiders vs. 49ers: 4 Crucial Matchups To Watch
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders return to the Bay Area for the first time since leaving in 2019, facing the San Francisco 49ers in a battle between two of the NFL's better offenses.
Head coach Klint Kubiak helped his team end a four-game losing skid dating back to the beginning of October. As the Raiders look to right the ship and get back into gear for a potential run down the stretch, the 49ers stand in their way as one of the top teams in the NFL. Something will have to give as we take a look at the key matchups for Sunday at Levi's Stadium.
The Raiders' run defense has gone down the toilet in the last month and is currently 31st in rushing yards allowed per game (146.4). Defensive end Maxx Crosby is seemingly doing the heavy lifting again for a defensive front that is getting blown off the ball far too often. Someone must step up at defensive tackle or opposite Crosby, or it could be a long day against the 49ers' run game.
Kyle Shanahan is one of the great offensive minds of the last two decades, deploying some of the most explosive offenses throughout his tenure. This year, we're seeing Christian McCaffrey and rookie Kaelon Black split carries and remain highly effective. However, it is unclear if we'll see McCaffrey, who didn't practice on Wednesday with a hamstring injury.
McCaffrey will clearly provide the most headaches for opposing defenses, including the Raiders. However, Black is a great player, too, and fits the wide-zone scheme with proficiency. Leonard must be aggressive against the run this week, utilizing his linebackers downhill consistently. Maybe we'll see more of Tim Keenan III, who helped Las Vegas limit big plays on the ground in the second half against the New York Jets.
Another aspect that falters for the Raiders' defense is their pass rush. Again, it seems Maxx Crosby continues to do the heavy lifting, with 35 pressures and three sacks this season, according to Next Gen Stats. He is due for a monster day, but other aspects of the Raiders' pass rush must step up.
The Raiders rank among the bottom 12 in total pressures and pressure rate, and their time-to-pressure average time to pressure is the fourth-worst in the NFL (2.85 seconds), per NGS. San Francisco's offense has an average time to throw of 3.00 seconds, the fourth-best in the NFL, and has allowed seven sacks all year, by far the fewest in football.
There's a whole Raiders offense that should be covered here, as they bolster one of the best passing units in the league and face a 49ers defense ranked top-five in yards allowed, sixth in points allowed, and 11th in passing yards allowed per game.
However, the story will be tight end Brock Bowers, one of the great offensive weapons in the sport. The Raiders don't align him as an in-line player often, as Kubiak has done a great job using his skill set as a receiver to dominate opposing defenses. The 49ers are a heavy single-high safety team that loves to deploy Cover 3 and Cover 1, and I expect them to play a little bit more man this week against Bowers, but that may not even matter.
The Raiders have won games without Bowers, but I'm not sure this current version could survive. This is the league's best tight end, and the Raiders must deploy him as such. Look for another productive outing in the Bay Area.
This is a dream game for many X's & O's gurus in the online football communities. Shanahan, as I mentioned, is one of the great offensive minds we have seen and is a big reason we see so many successful and efficient offenses. He runs 21 personnel at a 34.5 percent clip, per SumerSports, but he uses his running backs, fullback, and tight ends as receivers in this regard.
Kubiak comes from the Shanahan tree and is doing similar things in Las Vegas with his backs and tight ends, especially as both teams continue to have consistency or injury issues at wide receiver. Both utilize wide-zone systems and are passing-game savants. However, Kubiak seems to be the one who struggles with how best to deploy his running backs, a conversation I've seen brought up in recent days in the wake of Mike Washington and Ashton Jeanty's usage.
Both coaches will be attempting to out-scheme one another's defenses, and both defensive coordinators, Rob Leonard and Raheem Morris, are likely sweating this game. Basically, this game could come down to who has the better day offensively. Get ready for a lot of points.

He has contributed to several national outlets and is now part of our On SI team as an NFL team reporter. title: Raiders' Primary Focus Clear Heading Into Week 9 Against 49ers
full_text:
The Las Vegas Raiders defense came up big when it mattered most in Week 8 against the New York Jets. However, almost everything else about last Sunday's game raised red flags for a Raiders defense that is still in transition in its first year under Rob Leonard.
The Raiders are only in the first season of their actual rebuild. Las Vegas' front office addressed multiple positions as much as it reasonably could, with what they hoped would be serviceable options. This was especially the case in the defensive backfield.
Las Vegas drafted several young defensive backs and planned to develop them throughout this season and beyond. The Raiders' defensive backfield is filled with several first- and second-year players they expect to contribute early in their careers.
However, few positions go through the rites of passage that young cornerbacks and safeties do, which is where the Raiders find themselves halfway through their first season under Klint Kubiak, and second under general manager John Spytek.
Week 8 proved that rebuilds take time, and that a team can win and walk away with some of the same feelings as a loss. Still, the Raiders didn't lose, which is both a win in the record books and a moral victory for Las Vegas' defense and defensive backfield, which made enough stops to seal the win.
“It was tough sledding. We need to be better, and we talked about some things. It’s hard to comment on what their mindset was, but we tried to fix some things and adjust," Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard said following practice on Thursday.
“ It wasn’t pretty. There’s a lot we have to fix, but I’ve been here a couple years, and not many times we come out finding a way to win. I was proud of the resilience of getting hit in the mouth the first three plays, and we have a red-area stop on the three-yard line. So, there’s a lot of points on the little things that helped us win that game and how they rallied in the fourth quarter. It was really fun to see.”
The 49ers are tough to play. Their 6-0 start to the season firmly established them as one of the league's best teams. This season, Las Vegas has struggled against teams that are considered such. Leonard knows his unit, specifically, the defensive backfield, will have their work cut out.
“They’re fundamentally sound, man. They’re a clean operation, and they got some good players. Quarterback’s playing at a high level, good tight end, running backs, and the offensive line is really good. So, that’s what jumps out to me, how fundamentally sound they are, and they’re able to put a lot of pressure on you,” Leonard said.
San Francisco presents Las Vegas with no shortage of issues, as the 49ers excel at many of the things the Raiders do not. This is true on both sides of the ball. Few teams on the Raiders' schedule will pose as many problems specific to Las Vegas' remaining roster issues as the 49ers will.
Given how injured the New England Patriots were when Las Vegas faced them earlier this season, Week 9 is arguably the toughest test to date for Klint Kubiak's Raiders. The game itself will be enough. It will be the first taste many of the 2026 Raiders get of a long-running rivalry, which will only add to it.
“If you respect the game and understand how this thing really went down and what it was when they were there, it means a lot to a lot of people. I think it’s awesome to be a part of. It’s very humbling, and we want to go and put on a performance that everybody’s proud of as a team,” Leonard said.
At 4-4, Sunday is a chance for Las Vegas to gain ground in the playoff hunt. It is also the start of another brutal three-game stretch for a Raiders team still processing the last five games, four of which they lost. The Raiders must take things one game at a time.
As they do, they must improve significantly upon the past month. The Raiders have a chance at a statement victory.
Ezekiel is a former Sports Editor from the Western Herald and former Atlanta Falcons beat writer.

title: The Dolphins Will Pull Off a Major Upset This Season, But When?
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins will face another difficult challenge in Week 9 when they play host to the Detroit Lions, who will bring to Hard Rock Stadium the top-ranked offense in the NFL.
It will be Lions head coach Dan Campbell's first game in Miami since he served as Dolphins interim head coach for the final 12 games of the 2015 season.
Detroit will go into the game as a 6.5-point favorite, according to the Fan Duel Sportsbook, while the Dolphins will be looking for their most significant victory of the season.
Not surprisingly, the national opinion from media members is the Dolphins are going to lose for the seventh time in eight games, and all logic suggest it's a reasonable prediction because Miami simply doesn't appear to have the firepower to stay with the Lions.
But we all know the saying about any given Sunday, and there will be a time this season when the Dolphins win a game nobody expects them to win.
Just think back to that 2019 season we always bring up as a comparison point. After starting 0-7, the Dolphins defeated not one but two eventual playoff teams down the stretch, including the gigantic upset at Gillette Stadium in the season finale.
The Dolphins will have plenty of opportunities in the remainder of the season for a big upset with a schedule that includes games against the Buffalo Bills (twice), Denver Broncos, Chicago Bears, Green Bay Packers and a rematch against the Patriots.
Book it, the Dolphins will record a major upset this season.
And it will defy logic after we really break down the game and the matchups, just like this game against Detroit where it's just really difficult to see how Miami can slow down the best offense in the NFL.
But the games aren't played on paper or computer screens, and there will be a Sunday where Malik Willis has a big game throwing the ball or the defense forces a couple of turnovers.
We just probably won't see it coming.
If you look around the national media, nobody is seeing it happening Sunday against the Lions.
Quite frankly, we don't either. But we'll be wrong one of these Sunday. That, you can count on.

title: Examining the Looming Dolphins Roster Moves After the Week 9 Final Injury Report
full_text:
The good news for the Miami Dolphins with their final injury report for Week 9 is they didn't rule out any players for the matchup against the Detroit Lions at Hard Rock Stadium.
The team did list three players as questionable and it might require some roster juggling Saturday. In fact, it probably will require it.
The three players listed as questionable were running backs Jaylen Wright and Kaytron Allen, both of whom are dealing with a quad injury, and defensive end Malik Herring, who has a neck issue after sustaining a stinger in the Week 8 loss against the New England Patriots.
Wright and Allen are the two backups at running back behind new starter Ollie Gordon II (with De'Von Achane on IR) and it would seem almost a given that the Dolphins will be elevating Carlos Washington Jr. as insurance.
The Dolphins also need a kicker and the only one they have also is on the practice squad, that being veteran Zane Gonzalez.
And lastly, the Dolphins have operated with five edge defenders every game and if Herring can't play, that would leave them with four — Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Rodney McGraw and newcomer Jamree Kromah.
Max Llewellyn was elevated from the practice squad for the game against New England, but that was his third elevation. That means the Dolphins can't use him again this season unless they sign him to the 53-man roster, which certainly appears to be a possibility since they've kept him on the practice squad.
Other practice squad options if Herring can't play would be elevating either Amari Gaither or Eric Watts from the practice squad.
Signing Gonzalez to the 53 is another option, even though he did have a bad field goal miss against New England. He's already been elevated twice, meaning being brought up for the Detroit game would end his elevation eligibility.
Any roster adjustments, including practice squad elevations, have to be made by 4 p.m. ET on Saturday.
It's also possible the Dolphins don't have to do anything beyond elevating Gonzalez if the three players listed as questionable are deemed fit and ready to go against Detroit before the deadline.
As expected, Kadyn Proctor has gotten out of the concussion protocol and will be back in the lineup against the Lions.
Along with the three questionable players, the only other one who was limited in practice Friday was long-snapper Tucker Addington with his ongoing shoulder issue.
The others who popped up on the injury report this week — Chop Robinson, Malik Washington and Zach Sieler — all are good to go.
For Detroit, the big news was safety Brian Branch being cleared out of the concussion protocol and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown
The one update for them involved backup running back Sione Vaki, who popped up on the injury report and did not practice Friday. He was listed as questionable.
Detroit ruled out five players, including safety Kerby Joseph, who's on IR, and obviously linebacker Jack Campbell, who sustained a serious neck injury against the Minnesota Vikings last Sunday. The others were center Cade Mays, cornerback D.J. Reed and edge DJ Wonnum.

title: Dolphins Tuesday Mailbag: How Should We Evaluate the Rookie Class?
full_text:
Part 1 of the post-Patriots game Miami Dolphins on SI mailbag:
Why hasn’t any reporter asked either the head coach or the special teams coach what is up with the kickoff/punt coverage? Or maybe they have and I’ve missed it. But can’t we do better than simply just kicking out of the end zone and giving up the 35-yard line? Thank you!
Hey Rob, yes, Jeff Hafley and Chris Tabor have been asked and you make a valid point because ideally you’d like to pin the opponent inside, say, their own 25 and that can happen easily with a penalty on the return, for example. The flip side, though, is giving the ball at the 35 with the touchback eliminates the possibility of a big return, and there’s value in that as well. Another factor is the idea of providing the special teams game reps in kickoff coverage, which is not happening with the touchbacks. So, yeah, maybe covering kickoffs again might be the play here.
Was it due to the lousy weather conditions against the Pats, or are we going to continue to see a short game passing attack by the Dolphins?
Hey Ed, the Dolphins utilized a short passing game against the Jets and it worked great. Against New England, there were a couple of shots downfield, including the late touchdown pass to Kevin Coleman Jr. I don’t think we want as many shots downfield as we saw in the early weeks and the New England was good in that sense. There just has to be better execution along with better production from the run game.
Hi Alain, from your perspective in the locker room, how are team morale and confidence changing each week as the losses accrue? Is it noticeably different to what you have seen since the 2019 season?
Hey Matt, it’s all about expectations and the make-up of the team, and in 2019 as in 2026 it’s mostly a young group that fully understood the challenges ahead. Nobody likes losing and there’s always frustration after a loss, but we haven’t seen any effect on team morale or confidence to this point, and I suspect we won’t at any time during the season.
From Jorge Francisco boyd:
Hi Alain, with the way we played against the Patriots, do the Dolphins have any chance to win against Detroit and, if so, why? Is Chop Robinson coming into his own?
Hey Jorge, last question first, and the answer depends what you mean by “coming into his own.” If you’re asking whether Robinson has improved from last year, then the answer is yes. If the question is whether Robinson has arrived as an impact player, the answer is there’s still more to be done, and it starts with consistency. Robinson has been a major topic of discussion lately because his pass-rushing metrics are really, really good, except that some (like me) just don’t see that on film and we also have to remember he’s pretty much a pass rusher still at this time. As for the Detroit game, sure, the Dolphins can win, but I suspect it would take a gigantic effort from the offense because I don’t see how the defense will slow down the Lions.
I know it’s early, but what do you see as the positions of need for next year’s draft?
Hey Charles, it might be quicker to point out the positions where there’s no need. But I’d say the ones that stand out, assuming the main players are back in 2027, would be edge defender, cornerback, tight end, safety, defensive tackle and guard. Quarterback comes into the picture if the Dolphins decide that Malik Willis simply isn’t the answer and I personally am not ready to do that.
I’m a big fan of both of our 3rd round WRs. I’m waiting for the Chris Bell awakening. When is it coming? Also, shoulder issue? Omar hinted at something on the collective. Appreciate the answer and your work!
Not aware of a Chris Bell shoulder issue, so can’t speak to that, though we’ll get an injury report Wednesday and might see if there’s something there. I’ve been saying for a bit that I think it’ll be toward later in the season, if not next year, that we see a Bell awakening, as you call it. As this time, he looks like a solid possession receiver and nothing more, but I think there’s more to his game.
Alain, I know there is a lot of hype on the Dolphins rookie draft class; I’m optimistic as well. Is this class possibly overrated because so many get to play as rookies? If on veteran teams many would only play special teams, opportunities abound this season. Thoughts?
Hey Jeff, can’t disagree with anything you said there. I also think that every time a rookie makes one play, it seems to be portrayed later on as having had a great game, even with some breakdowns later on. As you said, there’s every reason to be optimistic about what the Dolphins have in their 2026 draft class, but I think we would do well to wait a bit before we start anointing too many players based on highlight plays here and there.

title: Dolphins Week 8 Report Card: Front Seven Earns Highest Marks
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins have gone right back to leaving one on the table.
Miami led New England 13-3 at halftime at Hard Rock Stadium before giving up 21 unanswered points in a 24-19 loss.
There were encouraging individual performances, particularly from some of the Dolphins expected to eventually beome foundational pieces.
But there were also penalties, stalled possessions and coverage breakdowns
Malik Willis finished 21-of-32 for 211 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. He didn’t offer much as a runner this time, rushing for just 2 yards on one carry.
He looked encouraging in the first half while completing 12 of 15 passes for 112 yards and helped Miami finish the half with a touchdown after zipping a pass to Malik Washington in the goal line.
The second half wasn’t as smooth however, with 73 of his 99 second-half passing yards coming on the final touchdown drive.
His interception came after an unfortunate ricochet off a defensive lineman’s helmet, but he threw another one that was erased by an offside penalty. The passing game needed more consistency before the deficit reached 11.
The next step in Willis’ development may require a few more uncomfortable seconds in the pocket. Offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik’s slower-developing play-action concepts, particularly those sending only two receivers downfield, require patience. The defensive backs need to show their hand, and at times that means open routes won’t show up until the last second.
Ollie Gordon II finished with 69 yards on 19 carries, averaging 3.6 yards per attempt. Jaylen Wright added 5 yards on two carries, and Miami managed just 74 rushing yards overall.
Bobby Slowik keeps trying to find small ways to change the picture for opposing defenses, like offsetting Gordon farther to the right in the backfield instead of just stacking him behind the quarterback. This time, his creativity wasn't rewarded.
The bigger problem was Gordon’s third-quarter unsportsmanlike conduct penalty, which turned a manageable third-and-5 into third-and-20. Miami punted, and Gordon’s frustration spilled onto the sideline.
Willis later said he told Gordon he was “dead ass wrong.”
Kevin Coleman Jr. continues developing and showcasing the route-running ability that can make him a reliable fixture in the receiver rotation
On his 35-yard touchdown, Coleman sold the out before turning upfield, giving Charles Woods a taste of the turf.
He caught all three of his targets for 46 yards and a touchdown.
Malik Washington continues to produce at a steady clip, with Miami putting his skills to use near the goal line on a short motion that created a matchup against safety Kevin Byard III, and Washington stopped on a dime before sprinting to the flats and catching a 1-yard touchdown.
Washington finished with five catches for 40 yards. Caleb Douglas added four for 43, while Chris Bell caught four for 31.
Greg Dulcich followed his season-high performance against the Jets with four catches for 43 yards.
His 19-yard reception on third-and-8 helped keep Miami’s touchdown drive alive before halftime.
The blocking looked rough, though.
New England kept generating pressure through matchups against Miami’s tight ends, primarily Will Kacmarek, who had difficulty holding up against Gabe Jacas and Elijah Ponder, most notably on a failed cutblock midway through the first quarter.
The first two sacks weren’t necessarily examples of terrible blocking. They were longer-developing plays where nobody was open before somebody eventually got free.
Jonah Savaiinaea, however, had a couple of reps that didn’t require much explaining.
With 7:45 left in the first quarter, he reached with his hands, leaned too far forward and absolutely whiffed as Christian Barmore knocked his punch away. Barmore and Gabe Jacas finished the sack.
At 5:05, Savaiinaea was driven backward by Cory Durden, who helped blow up Gordon’s run for a 3-yard loss. Savaiinaea also committed a holding penalty before halftime.
Miami was without Kadyn Proctor, with Jarrett Kingston starting at left guard. Still, five first-half sacks and 74 rushing yards make it difficult to be generous with this grade
Josh Uche has pretty much defined serviceable this season.
He might not be keeping offensive tackles awake at night, but he generally does his job.
On a misdirection run, much of the defense followed Corey Kiner’s jet motion. Uche stayed home and was able to corral Rhamondre Stevenson. He also finished with four tackles and a third-down sack that dropped Maye for a 10-yard loss.
Chop Robinson added two sacks and showed some versatility beyond rushing the passer. On third-and-5 with 9:22 left in the first quarter, he bluffed a rush before dropping into the middle of the field, helping take away an option as Maye threw incomplete.
Robinson also had a chance to bring Maye down before DeMario Douglas’ 48-yard touchdown and couldn’t finish it.
The tackle totals are impressive, but watching Jordyn Brooks and Jacob Rodriguez help each other is becoming almost an art form.
One will step up and stonewall a blocker to clear space for the other. They’re willing to do the dirty work even when somebody else gets to finish the play.
Brooks finished with 11 tackles, while Rodriguez added eight and punched the ball out of Efton Chism III’s hands. JuJu Brents recovered, giving Miami the short field that produced its first field goal.
Willie Gay Jr. continues to live a life of extremes, and this time it ended badly. He bit on Drake Maye’s fake pitch near the goal line, allowing the quarterback to keep it for the go-ahead touchdown.
Michael Taaffe is naturally the type of player you want to root for. A former walk-on, willing tackler, always ready to throw himself into somebody.
But, man, he keeps getting beaten in coverage.
Kyle Williams jetted across his face on the deep post for a 43-yard touchdown. New England used motion to create that matchup within Miami’s Cover 3, and Williams said afterward that he knew it would be a touchdown when the play was called.
At this point, it’s worth wondering how much Miami can hide those weaknesses by walking Taaffe closer to the line and giving him more work against the run.
JuJu Brents also gave up Douglas’ 48-yard touchdown. Maye finished 16-of-20 for 199 yards and two passing touchdowns, completing 9 of 10 for 146 yards after halftime.
Wright continues to do more damage returning kicks than carrying the ball on offense
He returned five kickoffs for 142 yards, including gains of 43 and 36 yards. He did, however, failed to make the simple play of stepping out of bounds while fielding a kickoff near the sideline in the fourth quarter, which would have resulted in a New England penalty and Miami getting the ball at its 40. Instead, there was a holding penalty on the play and Miami began that drive at its 12.
Zane Gonzalez connected from 31 and 52 yards, but missed a 43-yard attempt with 6:41 remaining that would have cut Miami’s deficit to eight.
Bradley Pinion averaged 45.8 yards on four punts, with a 37.0-yard net, while Miami allowed Marcus Jones a 26-yard punt return.
There was some improvement in the return game, but another missed opportunity when Miami needed points.
Miami built a 13-3 halftime lead, then went right back to getting in its own way.
This team plays hard for Jeff Hafley, and while it may sound like a consolation prize, it should be the most encouraging sign of this entire process so far.
Tyler M. Carmona is a Miami native whose work has appeared in the Miami Herald and Associated Press. He previously worked as a local television news reporter. He recently graduated from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and played college football at Savannah State University and the University of St. Francis

title: Examining the Mistakes that Cost the Dolphins in Week 8 ... And How to Fix Them
full_text:
The Miami Dolphins gave themselves a chance to pull off an upset against the New England Patriots in Week 8, but ultimately came up short at Hard Rock Stadium.
Maybe the simplest explanation is that New England is a better team that rose to the occasion in the second half when the Dolphins failed to do so, with a dubious replay overturn clearly not helping matters, but Miami also did it to itself.
As young teams are prone to doing, the Dolphins hurt themselves with mistakes that had little to do with the Patriots.
They are the type of mistakes the team will have to eliminate to continue the progress they've already shown in the early stages of this massive rebuilding project.
This is the one that stands out as the biggest self-inflicted wound because it was so unnecessary, and it turned a third-and-5 situation into a third-and-20 on the Dolphins' second drive of the third quarter after New England had scored to cut their lead to 13-3.
The Dolphins needed to at least get a first down or two to stop the Patriots momentum, but Gordon gave them no shot.
Gordon got an earful from quarterback Malik Willis on the sideline after the drive after head coach Jeff Hafley also talked to him, but beyond Gordon having to hear it from his teammates, this is one mistake with no easy fix beyond Gordon learning how to control his emotions.
And that's the tricky part, right? Because we want Dolphins players to play hard and with passion, but also control their emotions once they reach a certain point.
The fix here isn't benching Gordon because he's become so important to the offense with De'Von Achane on injured reserve.
Of course, if this happens a couple more times this season, then there'll be a major problem, but for now let's just hope he's learned his lesson.
Look, missed field goals happen, it's just that Zane Gonzalez badly going wide left on a 43-yard attempt down 24-13 midway through the fourth quarter basically sealed the Dolphins' fate.
It's not like the Dolphins are operating with a great margin for error, so they basically need their kicker to be near-perfect — like Riley Patterson was in 2025 when he went 27-for-29.
Gonzalez missing (again, badly) on his third attempt during his second practice squad elevation should make the Dolphins think long and hard about devoting a roster spot to him after he's elevated for a third time next Sunday against Detroit.
Sure, Drake Maye deserves maybe a small degree of credit for shaking off Johnson's tackle attempt when he came in free from the blind side on a fourth-down blitz, but that was way more about Johnson and what he did wrong.
The day after the game, why Johnson dove at Maye's legs instead of running through his back remains a mystery. Even more so because Johnson has been a good tackler — maybe ever a great tackler for a cornerback — so far in his rookie season.
Maybe he got too excited about the possibility of a big play, maybe he was going too fast and lost some body control. Regardless, this is a teaching moment for the Dolphins' defensive coaches because, again, it's not like Johnson isn't physical or a good tackler.
The Dolphins should have started their drive after New England took the lead at 17-13 at their own 40, but instead began at their 12 after Jaylen Wright fielded the kickoff near the sideline and Julius Wood was flagged for holding.
All Wright had to do was put himself out of bounds before touching the ball — it wasn't difficult — and that would have resulted in a penalty on the Patriots.
Yes, that drive ended with the Malik Willis interception off the helmet of a Patriots defensive lineman, but the yardage difference off the kickoff based on the same sequence of events would have given them the ball after the pick at their own 19-yard line instead of their 47. Maybe they call plays differently from back there and don't score the touchdown that made it 24-13.
In any event, this should be Kick Returning 101 and we've seen player after player in the NFL do that move and invariably earn praise from TV analysts for their great awareness.
Here's the thing, though: This is something special teams coordinator Chris Tabor already should have drilled into every one of his kickoff returners, whether it be Wright, Malik Washington or anybody else who's gotten practice reps back there.
And now he should remind his returners before every kickoff about the rule.

title: Four Losers And Four Winners From Miami's Week 8 Loss
full_text:
Some things are too good to be true, including the Miami Dolphins winning two games in a row, as they fall to New England by a painfully close score of 24-19.
To many fans, the idea of "tanking" and not messing up their draft stock went out the window as soon as they saw that a win over the Patriots was possible, and it certainly looked that way at halftime. However, the offense, defense, and special teams all seemed to regress in the second half.
In the end, the Dolphins lost their third straight game by a touchdown or less. A competitive game for sure against the defending AFC champions, but it's the Patriots. Any loss against them is guaranteed to sting.
To see Savaiinaea on this list is frustrating because this performance came out of nowhere. He's been having a stellar resurgence for the Dolphins this season, but if everyone is guaranteed at least one stinker per season, this was certainly it for him.
The first half was especially difficult for Savaiinaea. Mainly matched up against Christian Barmore and Corey Durden, he struggled to give Malik Willis time in the pocket and was a non-factor in blocking for Ollie Gordon and Miami's run game.
Barmore breezed by Savaiinaea for a sack on Willis on their second drive of the game on third down, forcing a punt despite being near midfield. And while it didn't end up mattering because Miami scored four plays later, he was called for a holding penalty that wiped a 15-yard touchdown for Gordon off the board.
This performance by Savaiinaea really came out of left field. He hadn't allowed a sack or committed a penalty through the first seven weeks of the season. The o-line obviously took a hit with Kadyn Proctor not playing, but the Dolphins will hope this was a one-time slip-up and nothing more.
The jokes about Robinson appearing on milk cartons should thankfully be over after his performance against the Patriots. After the shaky start to the season he had, he's only gotten better, and he blew up against the Patriots with three solo tackles and two sacks.
In the first half, the Dolphins sent the house on Drake Maye play after play, usually to resounding success. His second sack came after getting past a trio of New England linemen, literally brute-forcing his way to the quarterback and forcing a punt.
That said, New England eventually cracked the code in the second half, and Miami's pass rush began to sputter. But for Chop specifically, this was the game he needed to start proving to Miami that he deserves to stay a member of the Dolphins. Consistency is key, however, and it won't get any easier against Jared Goff and Detroit's offense.
OK, there's really not much that Johnson did wrong in this game. He actually provided much-needed durability to the secondary, being one of four players to play all 60 defensive snaps alongside Jacob Rodriguez, Jordyn Brooks and Michael Taaffe.
Really, there's only one major thing he did wrong, but he likely won't hear the end of it for a while. On fourth-and-2 with five minutes to go in the second quarter, Johnson had Maye dead to rights, breezing by Eli Raridon and facing the back of Maye, who never saw him coming. It looked like a surefire sack.
Instead, Johnson dove low and to the left of Maye, who then completed a 12-yard pass to extend the drive. Thankfully for Johnson, New England would go on to miss an ensuing field goal, but it's an awful look for the rookie. If he's given 100 chances to tackle Maye in the same situation, he would likely take him down 99 times, but unfortunately not 100.
How do you, as an underdog, wish to upset a team that has aspirations of making it back to the Super Bowl? You need a spark, and Rodriguez delivered that in the second drive of the game.
Down by three, Rodriguez performed his signature peanut punch on Efton Chism III, knocking the ball free. It was ultimately recovered by JuJu Brents and led to the Dolphins tying the game with a field goal of their own. That fumble proved to both Miami and New England that the Dolphins' defense could hang with the Patriots.
The list of winners and losers for Week 8 is filled with players who earned their spots mainly based on a single play. But every play matters more in a game that was won or lost by seven points or less.
That said, this was a disappointing game for Gordon, who was held to 69 yards on 19 carries. Is it too surprising? Not really, as the Patriots have one of the best run defenses in the NFL. As we mentioned earlier, his best run of the day was wiped off the board due to a holding penalty.
But in Miami's second drive out of halftime, Gordon committed an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty that resulted in a third-and-20. Not surprisingly, it forced a Dolphins punt, and the Patriots drove 73 yards in 13 plays to score a touchdown and take their first lead since early in the first quarter.
Gordon was irate on the sidelines, having to be cooled down by his quarterback. His emotions have been tested multiple times this season, including their loss to Cincinnati, but at least that tantrum was limited to the sidelines and, to some, justified given their struggles. But costing the team 15 yards and indirectly leading to a Patriots' lead that they wouldn't give up is unacceptable in a game like this.
Coleman was only targeted three times in this game, but he was a guaranteed target in all three of them, recording 46 yards. However, his final reception is an early highlight for the fifth-round pick.
It's not just that he scored a 35-yard touchdown that gave the Dolphins a sliver of hope with just about two minutes to go. It was the way he did it, absolutely shredding Charles Woods' ankles. His draft profile, which highlighted his speed and effectiveness after the catch, checks out.
Between Coleman, Douglas, and Bell, the group of rookies contributed almost equally in this game in terms of receptions and yards. It's a nice sight to see, but if anyone had doubts about what Coleman can contribute from the trio, he shut them down with that touchdown.
Miami's offense looked promising in the first half, taking a 13-3 lead to the break. But everything unraveled for the unit after halftime, and the play-calling on offense was a major contributor.
Even looking away from the back-to-back punts in the third quarter, the tempo of the offense in the fourth was off. They were at a deficit but handled the situation like they were ahead, draining 10 minutes and 23 seconds off the clock in their final three drives. Had they picked up the pace, there may not have been a need to go for an onside kick after the Coleman touchdown.
It didn't feel like there was a sense of urgency you would expect for an offense down by double digits with not much time remaining.
Pinion was asked to punt four times in this game - an unfortunate number, but he was at least consistent - with his kicks going 50, 40, 45, and 48 yards, respectively. His best work was his second attempt, pinning the Patriots deep at their 15-yard line.
Was it anything too special? Not really, but factoring in the not-so-optimal weather conditions and how sloppy the field can get, it was refreshing to see a mistake-free game for him. Pinion also handled a pair of kickoffs, resulting in a touchback on both occasions.
Jake Gibson is a writer for the Miami Dolphins on SI. title: Miami Dolphins 2026 Week 8 Snap Counts Stories: Rookie Revelations, Top Guys Emerge
full_text:
What stood out regarding play counts in the Miami Dolphins' 24-19 loss against the New England Patriots on Sunday:
We'll start with the list of inactives, which was highlighted by guard Kadyn Proctor missing the game because of a concussion.
The only Dolphins players who were active but did not play were backup quarterback Kyle McCord and offensive lineman Andrew Meyer.
Since we've been keeping track every game, the starting lineup was back to six rookies with Proctor being out. The six starters were fullback DJ Herman, Will Kacmarek at tight end, wide receiver Caleb Douglas, linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe.
-- There two things that stand out about the offensive snap counts, both of them involving rookies.
-- While Malik Washington missed a few plays after taking a big hit to the head on a play that resulted in a personal foul flag against New England, Caleb Douglas still looked like he emerged as the No. 1 wide receiver in this game. He played 56 of the 65 offensive snaps, compared to 48 for Washington and Chris Bell also got an elevated role with 45 snaps. That was a big jump from Bell's 31 snaps against the New York Jets in Week 7.
-- Then there was rookie tight end Will Kacmarek, who played only 20 snaps on offense, his lowest total since the season opener after he had dealt with injury issues in training camp. Kacmarek has been on the injury report in recent weeks with a hamstring problem, and if that's the reason his snap count was limited, then maybe the Dolphins need to sit him for a game to get him completely healed. If not, we'd question using him so little when the running game could have used extra blocking help against the Patriots.
-- Kacmarek's usage on offense ended up being the same as Herman, and we just don't understand that — again, barring injury complications.
-- It again was the Ollie Gordon II show at running back, as he played 53 snaps (82 percent) and Jaylen Wright got only eight offensive snaps. Given Wright's lack of production — he's averaging 1.9 yards per rushing attempt this season — it's difficult to argue against the snap distribution here, though the Dolphins might eventually want to take a look at recent waiver wire pick-up Kaytron Allen.
-- Veteran Jalen Tolbert was active but got only six offensive snaps, by far the fewest of any of the wide receivers.
-- Four players were on the field for all the team's 60 defensive snaps — LB Jordyn Brooks, LB Jacob Rodriguez, S Michael Taaffe and CB Chris Johnson. Those were the same four with 100 percent participation against the Jets in Week 7.
-- Josh Uche again led all edge defenders with 48 snaps, with Chop Robinson second with 33. Rookie seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn got only two defensive snaps and didn't play on special teams, and one can't help but wonder why the Dolphins wasted his third and final practice squad elevation for that amount of work. The Dolphins now won't be able to use in another game this season unless they sign him to the 53-man roster.
-- Also note that Llewellyn's low snap count happened even though fellow edge Malik Herring missed some game time because of an injury before returning.
-- The Dolphins went big on about a third of their defensive snaps with at least three of their interior defensive linemen. The snap counts behind Zach Sieler were pretty even between Jordan Phillips, Zeek Biggers and Kenneth Grant, with all of them getting between 27 and 37 snaps.
-- In his second game back after being on IR with a knee injury, rookie Kyle Louis played a season-high 11 snaps on defense in a nickel role.
-- Linebacker Willie Gay Jr., back after missing the Jets game because of illness, played 27 defensive snaps alongside Rodriguez and Brooks.
-- Tackle Chukwuebuka Godrick, who the Dolphins claimed off waivers from the Kansas City Chiefs after the cuts to 53, made his season debut and it consisted of four snaps on special teams.
-- Godrick and Kaytron Allen were among the six non-specialists who saw action only on special teams, along with LB Shaka Heyward, LB Jackson Woodard, CB Reese Taylor and G/T Caedan Wallace.
-- Finally with special teams, rookie Seydou Traore again led the way with 22 snaps, followed by 17 for Julius Wood, followed by 16 each for Louis, Heyward, Woodard and Allen.
