title: Making A Case for Rob Gronkowski as the Greatest Tight End in Patriots, NFL History
full_text:
On Saturday, the "Gronk Spike" will officially be immortalized as star tight end Rob Gronkowski is inducted into the New England Patriots Hall of Fame.
Gronkowski will become the 38th member of the Patriots organization to be inducted into the team's Hall of Fame , and the latest second dynasty player (following Vince Wilfork, Julian Edelman and Tom Brady) to wear the red jacket.
Gronkowski has more receiving touchdowns than any other Patriots player (79), and ranks second in receiving yards (7,861) and fifth in receptions (521). The dominant tight end played nine seasons in New England, and joined Brady in Tampa Bay for two more, acheiving a total of four Super Bowl victories in his career (XLIX, LI, LIII, LV).
The words " greatest tight end of all time " often describe the menacing 6-foot-6, 265-pound force, but people continue debate the accolades of Gronkowski with recent successes like Travis Kelce and previous players like Tony Gonzalez who made the tight end position unique.
However, when comparing Gronkowski, or "Robby G," or "Gronk" with other tight ends, it's clear that no one played the game like New England's No. 87.
Gronk has some of the clutchest plays of any tight end for any organization ever. He's a defining point of the 2010's Patriots dynasty, serving as one of the three figureheads with Brady and Edelman, who each carried a load in winning three Super Bowls in five years.
In Super Bowl XLIX, the tight end made an empowering catch over the Seahawks' K.J. Wright for a touchdown to give New England the lead before halftime in what would be their first title in a decade.
Brady also relied on Gronk for big third and fourth down conversions, in the 2015 AFC Championship, Gronkowski kept the Patriots in the game, catching a 40-yard reception and following it with a four-yard touchdown (New England would go on to lose to that year's Super Bowl champion Denver Broncos).
Perhaps one of his most notorious plays as a Patriot came in his final reception with a flying Elvis sticker attached to his helmet, as the veteran tight end hauled in a 29-yard seam route reception to put the Patriots within scoring position, and open up Super Bowl LIII in an effort to beat the Los Angeles Rams.
Even in Tampa Bay, Gronk still showed flashes of dominance, especially in his sixth Super Bowl appearance against the Kansas City Chiefs, where he was the Buccaneers leading receiver and acquired two touchdowns of his own.
Watching Kelce nowadays reminds me of how impressive it was that when Gronk was done physically he still made the biggest catch to win a Super Bowl. pic.twitter.com/iZlq7NK1LZ https://t.co/fC4SVladlg
The remarkability of Gronkowski's tenure is brought into higher status when considering the injuries he suffered during his 11-season career. He missed half of the 2016 season, including Super Bowl LI, where the Patriots overcame a 28-3 defecit to defeat the Atlanta Falcons.
Early in his career, Gronk sustained multiple back injuries, including a herniated disc that occured during his time at the University of Arizona. In 2013, he tore his ACL and MCL in his right knee, and also suffered a broken arm, playing with an implant in his forearm for most of his career.
He also sustained multiple rib and lung injuries, often taking big hits to the chest in an effort to bring down the towering pass catcher. Worse than the hits to his chest, were the hits to his head, which resulted in an unknown number of concussions that Gronkowski has openly estimated to be in double digits range.
Though he wasn't the most available tight end of all time, there's a case to be made that he was the toughest. Remarkably, his play never faltered from injury, despite the toll football put on his body.
There's no encapsulation of Robby G's NFL career without summarizing his escentric personality and the entertainment value he brought to football.
Picked in the second round of the 2010 NFL Draft, Gronkowski famously huddled with his family before walking on stage to shake the commissioner's hand, and put a Patriots helmet on as soon as he exited the stage.
His irresistable and humorous identity as a not-so intelligent figure and a party lunatic allowed him to coin the phrase, "Yo soy fiesta," which translates from Spanish with plenty of grammatical errors to ,"I am party." After his NFL career he held parties during the Super Bowl titled, "Gronk Beach," and awkwardly, yet hilariously, made Robert Kraft and Bill Belichick take shots on stage during the Roast of Tom Brady, just four months after Belichick's tenure as New England's head coach ended.
Draft Day. 2010. Gronk! #NFLDraft #tbt pic.twitter.com/GBx3nOVGRj
More so than his off the field antics, Gronkowski brought his rambunctious behavior to the grid iron, too. His "Gronk Spike" was a generational touchdown celebration replicated by football fans and players across the world, each one more powerful and just as demeaning to New England's opponents.
When asked on Thursday about one moment in his career that stood out to him, Gronkowski couldn't define a singular play, but rather a trend.
"The 'Gronk Spike!' [It] was lethal, it was legendary," he exclaimed. "[The Gronk Spike] kind of defines my career, as well — powerful."
So many TDs, so many Gronk spikes 💪 Celebrating #NationalTightEndsDay with some of the best @RobGronkowski touchdowns. pic.twitter.com/qzeBnLPvD3
He laughed in the faces of defenders who failed to prevent him from scoring, used his massive arms to drive tacklers into the ground, and finished blocks by creating pancakes into the field, and at times, the stands (just ask the former Colt Sergio Brown who was on the receiving end of a block).
His competitive attitude was most evidently seen in his playstyle. While his receiving accolades were some of the best ever at his position, he was well-known for being one of the best run-blocking tight ends to ever play football. This allowed him to dominate in a Patriots offense that ran almost more play-action than any other team.
"That's why I love blocking" said Gronkowski. "That's what got my foot into the door with the Patriots. That's what got my respect from my teammates. I was a blocker first."
While Gronkowski's statistics aren't exactly better than any other players at his position, he still ranks top-six in yards, top-three in touchdowns, and had a much shorter career than the other players ahead of him (such as Gonzalez, Jason Witten, Antonio Gates, Kelce, and others).
The argument surrounding Gronkowski as the greatest tight end to ever play football comes from how transformational he was at the position, his two-way ability as a blocker and receiever, and his ball carrying skills to extend plays.
What Gronkowski did that other tight ends hadn't yet, was line up as both a receiver and a true tight end/extra offensive linemen. He excelled in a two-tight end offense — the first of its kind — and had the ability to be on the field for every offensive snap, unless he was dealing with injuries.
His four Super Bowls are more than any other player at his position, and to do it with two different teams and the same quarterback adds to how impressive that feat is.
"I know I gave it my all, I really really did," exclaimed Gronkowski. "I held on the last couple of years, I basically would've been carried off the field if I played one more year."
"To be recognized with [Patriots legends] is an absolute honor, an absolute thrill, it means everything."
Rob Gronkowski once played through a regular season game with a herniated disc and a punctured lung that was causing him to spit up blood… There will never be another Gronk. The #Patriots Hall of Fame just got a one-of-a-kind addition! (🎥 @Patriots ) pic.twitter.com/BssPWHE3CC
For New England fans, Gronkowski is a centerpiece of what it means to be a Patriot. He still resides in Foxboro and is a major advocate of the new era Patriots. On Saturday, Gronkowski will add to his abundant resume of accomplishments that make him…

title: Patriots QB Drake Maye Named October's AFC Offensive Player of the Month
full_text:
For the first time in his young NFL career, New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye has been named the AFC's Offensive Player of the Month.
Maye wins the award for October after leading the Patriots to a 3-1 record over four weeks of play, and turning around a slow start, following last year's Super Bowl LX appearance.
From Oct. 1 to Nov. 1, Maye threw for 1,398 passing yards, had 17 total touchdowns, and an average passer rating of 122.2. His 67.4% completion rate contributes to his nomination as player of the month.
October belongs to @DrakeMaye2 🤩 pic.twitter.com/VDlWFOadC0
Maye earns the nod as AFC Offensive Player of the Month in a competitive decision that saw the likes of Josh Allen, Jaylen Warren, and Kenneth Walker IV — September's AFC Offensive Player of the Month.
Maye turned around his season after putting up a 1-2 record in September , which saw the third-year player turn the ball over seven times and throw just one touchdown.
After a remarkable month of October, Maye becomes the first Patriot to win AFC Offensive Player of the Month since Tom Brady did so in November of 2017.
In the last 5 weeks… Drake Maye is #1 among all QBs in: 🏅 Total yards 🏅 Total TDs 🏅 EPA 🏅 Passer Rating Despite the following… ⚠️ Injuries to his WR1, WR2, WR3, TE1, RB2, LG and RG ⚠️ Pressured at the 4th highest rate in the NFL ⚠️ Playing with one of the league's… pic.twitter.com/xAeJX1jkP4
Over the course of the past five weeks, Maye has led the NFL in total yards, passing touchdowns, EPA (expected points added), and passer rating.
Maye is currently sixth in passing yards on the season (1,983) and tied for fifth in touchdown passes (15). Over the past two seasons, Maye holds the lead for touchdown passes of 30-plus yards, including two that he threw to Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas in Week 8's win against the Miami Dolphins.
What makes Maye's recent success even more impressive is his ability to dominate with a weakened supporting cast. Maye has had his top-three receivers miss a combined six games due to injury, leaving last year's MVP runner-up to spread the ball around to other skill position players.
Earlier in October, Maye was asked if he's had to intentionally spread the ball around to build the confidence of his teammates.
"I try not to have that in the back of my mind," Maye said. "I was like that a little bit in high school, to be honest with you, of wanting – especially when we would run it up on teams in high school – to try to spread it around and get guys touches."
He's also used his legs to give the Patriots an advantage, running for 129 yards and two touchdowns throughout the October window of play.
On Thursday, Maye appeared on Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman's show on Fox, Gronk and Jules. He reflected on the turnaround this season, saying,"you got to realize that turning over the football is not going to help us win games."
"Realizing that the work you put in week-in and week-out is going to end up paying off, and not losing sight of trying to change things up."
Maye's October success has paid off for the Patriots, who now hold a 5-3 record as the calendar turns to November. Now they have the AFC Offensive Player of the Month leading their team.

title: Saints vs. Browns: 3 Things to Know About Cleveland's Defense
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints will look to get their offense back on track Sunday when they face a Cleveland Browns defense that has experienced its share of ups and downs this season.
Despite losing superstar defensive end Myles Garrett , Cleveland has remained a formidable defensive opponent, especially at generating pressure and creating turnovers.
However, the Browns have also struggled to stop the run, giving the New Orleans offense an opportunity to exploit that weakness.
For quarterback Tyler Shough and the Saints, exploiting Cleveland's weaknesses while limiting costly mistakes could be the difference between another frustrating offensive performance and a much-needed bounce-back win.
With New Orleans preparing for its first game following the bye week, here are three things to know about the Browns' defense heading into Sunday's matchup.
Cleveland made significant offseason changes, but none were bigger than trading superstar defensive end Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams.
Garrett was coming off a historic 2025 season in which he established an NFL record with 23 sacks and recorded 33 tackles for loss.
His departure, combined with defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz's resignation, raised questions about whether Cleveland could maintain its defensive identity.
However, the Browns have remained competitive defensively under first-year coach Todd Monken .
Cleveland has recorded 21 sacks through eight games, ranking ninth in the NFL, while collecting six interceptions.
Several young defensive players have also contributed, including defensive end Jared Vers e, who arrived from Los Angeles as part of the Garrett trade.
The Browns are allowing 126.9 rushing yards per game and 4.7 yards per carry, ranking among the league's bottom 10 in both categories.
Those struggles were especially apparent against Pittsburgh, which rushed for 200 yards in Sunday's victory.
That's an encouraging matchup for New Orleans, which has struggled to establish a consistent rushing attack throughout the season.
The Saints managed just 18 rushing yards in their 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh before entering their bye week.
If New Orleans can exploit Cleveland's defensive weaknesses on the ground, it could take considerable pressure off quarterback Tyler Shough and create more opportunities through the passing game.
Although Cleveland has struggled against the run, its secondary remains one of the defense's more dependable units.
The Browns are allowing 214.6 passing yards per game and have surrendered 11 passing touchdowns through eight games.
However, they have also intercepted six passes and held opposing quarterbacks to a relatively modest 6.6 yards per pass attempt.
Much of Cleveland's success in coverage begins with veteran cornerback Denzel Ward .
Ward has continued to establish himself as one of the NFL's premier coverage defenders, earning a 91.6 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, the highest among qualified cornerbacks entering Week 9.

title: Saints Get Major Injury Boost as Browns Face Quarterback Uncertainty
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints received encouraging injury updates Wednesday as left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. and rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson returned to practice ahead of Sunday's matchup against the Cleveland Browns .
Meanwhile, Cleveland could be without starting quarterback Deshaun Watson , who entered the NFL's concussion protocol Wednesday after reporting symptoms following Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers .
Watson initially passed concussion evaluations and finished the game but reported symptoms Monday night, putting his availability against New Orleans in question.
If Watson cannot play, second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders is expected to make his first start of the season.
Sanders started seven games as a rookie in 2025, throwing for 1,400 yards, seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions. However, he has seen limited action this season, completing just three passes for 2 yards.
Watson has started all eight games for Cleveland this season, completing 65.5% of his passes for 1,806 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions.
Despite his efficiency, the Browns have struggled offensively, ranking 29th in the NFL with just 17.4 points per game.
For New Orleans, Wednesday's biggest development was the return of Banks, who practiced for the first time since undergoing ankle surgery in September .
The second-year left tackle has progressed considerably faster than initially expected, returning more than a month ahead of schedule.
The Saints now have a two-week window to activate Banks from injured reserve, potentially providing a significant boost to an offensive line that has struggled in his absence.
Backup left tackle Asim Richards has experienced difficulties adjusting to coach Kellen Moore's offensive scheme while filling in for Banks.
Initially expected to return in mid-December, Banks could reclaim his starting role once medically cleared, giving the Saints additional protection up front.
New Orleans also welcomed back Tyson, the No. 8 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft out of Arizona State.
The rookie wide receiver participated on a limited basis Wednesday after missing the entire season to this point with a hamstring injury suffered during training camp .
Although his availability for Sunday's matchup remains uncertain, Tyson's return represents another encouraging development for a Saints offense looking to improve its passing attack.
With Banks and Tyson progressing toward their respective returns and Cleveland potentially facing a quarterback change, Sunday's matchup could feature a considerably different outlook for both teams than initially anticipated.

title: Saints Make Coaching Staff Changes, but Mickey Loomis Shouldn't Escape Blame
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints have fired run game coordinator T.J. Paganetti following their Week 8 bye, according to Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football.
The decision comes as head coach Kellen Moore attempts to fix one of the NFL's least productive rushing attacks, with New Orleans sitting at 2-5 through seven games.
The Saints have parted ways with run game coordinator TJ Paganetti, according to sources. Paganetti came from Philadelphia, where he helped architect the run game and was part of developing one of the league’s best offensive lines
The Saints are averaging just 86 rushing yards per game and 3.5 yards per carry, with their struggles reaching a low point in a 16-10 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris on Oct. 25.
New Orleans had one of the most embarrassing rushing performances in franchise history, managing only 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts and averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Paganetti joined Moore's staff in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles , where he helped develop one of the NFL's most dominant rushing attacks.
During Philadelphia's Super Bowl-winning 2024 season, the Eagles rushed for a franchise-record 3,048 yards and averaged 179.3 yards per game, ranking second in the NFL.
However, that success never consistently translated to New Orleans.
While Paganetti deserves some responsibility, the Saints' problems extend beyond coaching.
While Moore is getting heat for the Saints’ offensive struggles, ultimately the biggest issue with the New Orleans Saints is the person who hired him: general manager Mickey Loomis .
Loomis is responsible for building the roster, including the backfield and the offensive line, the two weakest links on the Saints.
The running back room, featuring Alvin Kamara , Travis Etienne , Kendre Miller and CJ Donaldson , hasn't delivered consistent production.
Etienne's placement on injured reserve has further complicated matters, especially when the Saints signed him on a four-year, $52 million deal.  Kamara, by contrast, hasn't shown the same explosiveness that made him one of the NFL's most dynamic playmakers.
The offensive line also remains a concern despite significant investments, including first-round selections Kelvin Banks Jr. , Taliese Fuaga and Cesar Ruiz along with the free agent signing of David Edwards for $76 million
New Orleans has struggled to consistently create running lanes, particularly along the interior, leaving its running backs with limited opportunities.
Paganetti arrived in 2025 after spending 10 seasons with Philadelphia, where he helped develop one of the NFL's most productive rushing attacks. However, the Eagles also had considerably better offensive line personnel.
Moore and Loomis must now share responsibility for determining whether the Saints' struggles stem from their offensive philosophy, player development or questionable roster construction.
Firing Paganetti sends a message that the current production is unacceptable, but changing coordinators won't automatically solve personnel deficiencies.

title: Saints Midseason Stock Report: 4 Bright Spots Amid a Disappointing Start
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints enter their bye week with a disappointing 2-5 record despite the hype around the Saints being contenders to possibly win the NFC South.
While the season has been anything but positive, the team still has bright spots on both offense and defense.
Here's a look at four players who have performed above and beyond as we reach the midseason point.
Tyler Shough hasn't been perfect, but the second-year quarterback continues to show encouraging signs of development under coach Kellen Moore .
Through seven games, Shough has completed 67% of his passes for 1,721 yards, 13 touchdowns and six interceptions. He's also contributed 111 rushing yards and two touchdowns.
His pass yardage and touchdown totals are both in the top 10 as he is tied for seventh in passing touchdowns and ninth in passing yards, but for a majority of the season he was either No. 1 or No. 2 in passing yards.
Those numbers are impressive considering New Orleans' struggles establishing a consistent rushing attack and protecting its quarterback.
Despite occasional mistakes, Shough has demonstrated improved accuracy, pocket presence and command of Moore's offense.
If he continues developing and limits turnovers, the Saints should feel increasingly confident about their quarterback situation.
Wide receiver Chris Olave has shown why the Saints gave him a 4-year, $132 million extension.
Through seven games, the former first-round pick has caught 49 passes (fourth in the NFL) for 636 yards (third in the NFL) and two touchdowns, averaging 90.9 receiving yards per game.
He opened the season with four 100-yard performances in his first four games, including a dominant 182-yard outing against Detroit .
Chase Young has arguably been New Orleans' most impressive player on defense through seven games.
The former No. 2 overall pick has recorded seven sacks, establishing himself as one of the NFL's most productive pass rushers.
Out of 50 edge rushers with at least 125 pass rushes, Young ranked second with a 90.0 Pro Football Focus pass-rush grade.
Young is on pace to record over 15 sacks, potentially putting him in the conversation for Pro Bowl recognition.
Though Young draws much of the spotlight, Carl Granderson is quietly putting together a standout year as well.
Across seven contests, the experienced defensive end has registered 25 tackles alongside 5.5 sacks, highlighted by a 1.5-sack effort versus Pittsburgh .
Granderson's current trajectory puts him on track for roughly 13 sacks, setting up a potential career mark.
Combined, Granderson and Young have racked up 12.5 sacks, forming one of the few reliable highlights for New Orleans' defense.
Even with the unit's broader difficulties, his growth paired with Young gives the Saints a high-caliber pass-rush duo for the future.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: Four 2027 NFL Draft Prospects the Giants Should Watch This Weekend
full_text:
As the New York Giants (4-2-1) prepare for a Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles (2-6) at Lincoln Financial Field, several Big Blue scouts will be watching closely as college football’s Week 10 slate unfolds.
After a much-needed Week 8 bye, this could be a good time to scout potential targets as they make their cases for selection in the 2027 NFL Draft.
While the rumor mill continues to churn for running back, the team’s biggest need remains along the defensive line. Coach John Harbaugh and his staff may also want to add a player to bolster their tight end depth chart.
Here are four players the Giants may keep an eye on this weekend.
Fresh off the Tigers’ bye week, Green has declared himself “ready to go” while showing few signs of lingering effects from a knee injury that sidelined him two weeks ago. He is expected to play a major role in LSU’s offensive game plan against Alabama this weekend.
In four appearances this season, Green has caught 19 passes for 272 yards and two touchdowns. At 6-foot-7 and 242 pounds, the Jackson, LA native has the length and sure hands to be an effective weapon in contested-catch situations. Green can split out wide, line up in the slot, or control the perimeter when matched up against linebackers or safeties.
With New York’s depth at the position uncertain beyond starter Isaiah Likely , Green could be a highly productive fit within offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense. A strong showing against the Crimson Tide in Week 10 would go a long way toward bolstering his draft stock.
Given the Giants’ need for an imposing presence on the interior of their defensive line, Scott could be an intriguing fit.
The 6-foot-4, 300-pound lineman moves well for his size, especially sideline to sideline. In seven games this season, he has collected 25 total tackles, two fumble recoveries, and 0.5 sacks.
Most importantly, Scott could strengthen the Giants’ run defense. The Chicago native anchors well thanks to his wide base. He is at his best absorbing double teams while stacking and shedding blocks.
Combined with his explosive first step, Scott should contribute to an NFL team right away. As such, expect the Giants to keep the Hurricanes’ tackle in their sights against Notre Dame on Saturday.
If New York wants a dedicated run-stopper, Jackson should be on their list of potential targets. The 6-foot-2, 310-pound tackle has logged 29 total tackles, 1.5 tackles for loss, and 0.5 sacks this season. In 2025, PFF gave him a 70.5 run defense grade and credited him with 11 pressures.
At the pro level, Jackson projects as a true nose tackle who contributes on early-down run responsibilities.
Given New York’s difficulty in consistently stopping the run, Jackson could be an enticing mid-to-late-round option, especially if he helps to contain the Florida Gators’ star running back Jadan Baugh during this weekend’s prime-time showdown in Gainesville.
Following a standout season at Michigan in 2025, Haynes has used his second trip through the transfer portal to become a significant force in the Yellow Jackets’ running game.
In his first season with Georgia Tech, the 5-foot-11, 210-pounder has compiled 548 yards on 112 carries and four touchdowns. He has also caught 13 passes for 71 yards and two touchdowns.
While much of the Giants fan base remains intently focused on established pros such as Jonathan Taylor and Derrick Henry to provide an immediate upgrade to New York’s running game, a player with Haynes’ versatility is always worth watching as a draft prospect.
His breakaway speed and ability to read the box would complement Cam Skattebo’s strength-based style.

title: Giants Reportedly Eye Ravens’ RB Justice Hill While Jonathan Taylor Talks Linger
full_text:
The New York Giants seem to want to add a running back, not only to reinforce depth in their depleted backfield, but also to add a potential bell cow who can carry the bulk of the load.
To that end, ESPN insider Adam Schefter reported that the Giants reached out to the Baltimore Ravens , head coach John Harbaugh’s former team, to inquire about a running back, but not Derrick Henry, whom Schefter said the Ravens have not considered trading before Tuesday’s deadline.
Instead, the Giants have reportedly inquired about obtaining running back/kickoff returner Justice Hill from the Ravens.
Hill, 5-foot-10 and 195 pounds, was selected by Harbaugh and the Ravens in the fourth round of the 2019 draft following a strong career at Oklahoma State, where he earned two first-team All-Big 12 honors and was named the Big 12 Offensive Freshman of the Year in 2016.
The 28-year-old Hill has appeared in 93 games for the Ravens with five starts. He has 301 regular-season rushing attempts for 1,495 yards and nine touchdowns, and has caught 136 of 177 pass targets for 1,017 yards and five scores.
Hill also has kickoff return experience, having recorded 1,009 yards on 39 kickoff returns (25.9 yards per return).
Hill is currently in the final year of a two-year extension, which pays him $2.75 million in base salary and $14,705 per game he’s active.
Harbaugh and the Giants are believed to want a running back not just for the short term but for the long term.
While they could easily seek to extend the expiring contract of a player they acquire, such as Hill, it might make more sense in this case for the Giants to try to sign him in free agency so they don’t have to give up any draft assets (assuming they don’t land their other reported option, Colts running back Jonathan Taylor).
Speaking of Taylor, there may be some gamesmanship at play if the Giants’ reported interest in Hill is accurate. The Colts are thought to be holding out for the best possible deal for Taylor, which means any trade is likely to go down to the wire.
The Giants currently have a thinned-out running back room. They released Najee Harris a few weeks ago, and Tyrone Tracy Jr. is on IR with a hamstring strain. In addition, their de facto RB1, Cam Skattebo, is dealing with a hamstring strain of his own and is listed as “doubtful” on this week’s injury report.
The Giants have two critical divisional games, against the Eagles and the Commanders, sandwiched around the Nov. 10 trade deadline. New York is also thought to be exploring options at defensive tackle, but it’s unclear whether it can satisfy both reported needs or will have to prioritize one over the other.

title: Giants Mailbag:  Trade Winds, Deonte Banks, Game Stuff and More
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
How do you compare Thomas Fidone’s skillset to Theo Johnson? Any chance he pushes him for playing time once Johnson is healthy?
Truth be told, I am not sure a fair comparison can be made given the small sample size of Fidone's snaps in this offense.
That said, Johnson has more explosive straight-line speed, while Fidone, with a leaner frame, is more agile and more effective in short-area lateral explosion.
Hi Patti, Has the compensatory pick we'll be receiving in 2027 moving up from a 5th to a possible 4th Rd. pick satisfied the requisite number of snaps that C Austin Schlottmann has played? Or, does it appear that Schlottmann will reach that threshhold? Please check Thanks, Lyle
Lyle, per Over the Cap's Nick Korte , who does a great job at tracking and calculating these things, the projected comp pick is NOT for Schlottmann but rather for Wan'Dale Robinson, and it's a projected fourth-round pick.
Let's wait until the season draws to a close though before counting our chickens on this so as to not end up disappointed if something throws a monkey wrench into the plans.
Can you explain why a “virtual measurement” takes five times as long as two guys with chains? Is the NFL using dial-up? A slide rule?
I do not know what parameters they have been given. If you want a conspiracy theory, maybe it's to allow another commercial break and, hence, more money for the network?
Are there plains to use Hyatt more?
Possibly. He has two more practice squad elevations to go, and with receiver Charlie Jones ailing due to a hand injury, I could certainly see Hyatt getting the call-up from the practice squad.
What's the consensus feel about Jj
By "consensus," do you mean the locker room? Fans? Another group? (All of whom I'm not the appointed spoeksperson by the way.) But if you want my opinion, I'm encouraged based on what I've seen on the small sample size so far.
most likely giants acquisition at this point?
I mean, right now all signs point to Jonathan Taylor, right? Personally, I still think they should try to land a defensive lineman—I'm just not sure there is one out there worth trading for after the Buckner and Simmons deals.
That John Harbaugh got involved with the Titans to try to get Jeffery Simmons after reportedly hitting a stonewall with Titans' GM Mike Borgonzi tells me they agree that they need and desperately want a defensive lineman in the worst way. The fact that they were aiming for Simmons tells me they're not messing around.
Fans have seen the on field difference John Harbaugh has made.  Are there other subtle things you see day to day that have made a difference that aren’t as noticeable to the fans?
Not really, Kris. Harbaugh has great attention to detail, and he has shown that he can handle adversity when it pops up, better than some of the previous head coaches who preceded him and followed Tom Coughlin.
I suppose that's the biggest thing I've noticed: in tough times, players want a leader who doesn't let the world see him sweat. But I'm sure Giants fans have probably drawn that conclusion as well so I'm not sure the answer fits your question.
how likely is JT to become a giant
I’m not one to assign a percentage to what should be a “yes or no” response question, but what I will tell you is that unless the Colts come down off their reported asking price, which, depending on what report you believe, either includes a first-round pick or a Christian McCaffrey type of haul (second, third, fourth, and fifth), I’d say zero chance if either of those is true.
The Giants don't have a fourth- or fifth-round pick in next year’s draft, so unless the Colts are willing to take their 2028 picks, I don’t think a deal gets done unless, again, the Colts become more reasonable with their asking price.
What  do you attribute Deonte Banks’ turnaround to this season? Is it more about the defensive scheme putting him in better positions to succeed, or has there been a significant shift in his confidence and mental approach to the game?
I think it's a combination of scheme and coaching. The scheme being run is a better fit for what Banks does well.
The Giants, under Shane Bowen, played a lot of soft zone coverage, which forced the cornerback to play about eight yards off the receiver and often led to disaster because Banks had to second-guess what was unfolding in front of him.
Dennard Wilson has deployed tighter press-man and man-match coverages for Banks, bringing him closer to the receiver so he can use his physical toolbox to disrupt receivers as they look to get off the line of scrimmage and make breaks. Banks has the speed to keep up with the league's better receivers, and Wilson's approach has proven that.
Then, in defensive backs coach Addison Lynch, you have a coach who has clearly made a connection with Banks, in which he's helped to build up the cornerback's confidence and also get it through to Banks that one bad play shouldn't be the catalyst for giving up, thinking he's not good enough or that he'll be pulled from the lineup.
From Gary W. (via e-mail): Can someone please tell me why the league insists on the ridiculous 35-second rule? A stupid penalty or a forced timeout should decide no game. It certainly doesn't add anything or improve the game.
Gary, did you mean the 25-second clock, which is used after specific administrative stoppages?

title: Giants RB Cam Skattebo Doubtful for Eagles Game After Missing a Third Straight Practice
full_text:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) missed his third day of practice since the team returned from its bye, raising doubt about his availability for Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles.
Skattebo worked with a trainer during the last three days of the media viewing periods. While head coach John Harbaugh said that they’re going to keep the door open for Skattebo to play on Sunday, things do not appear to be heading in the right direction for Skattebo.
Even if Skattebo, who received a "doubtful" game status, were to play, he’d likely be significantly limited in terms of his snaps. That means the Giants are probably planning to add a running back from their practice squad, either via a signing or a standard elevation.
“I'm not making any announcements at this meeting, this particular press conference,” Harbaugh said in response to a question about the roster spot the team opened by waiving quarterback Jake Haener. “We have certain roster moves we need to make with our various situations.”
Skattebo, who usually takes to the podium on Fridays, did not do so this week, another sign that he likely won’t play on Sunday.
The Giants are all but certain to tap into the practice squad for a running back to fill the empty roster spot.
A best guess would be that Eric Gray, signed to the practice squad this week, gets the spot that opened following the waiving of Haener, as Gray, who not only knows the system but can also contribute as a return specialist with receiver Charlie Jones (hand) ailing and listed as questionable for Sunday's game, would make the most sense.
Harbaugh and Malk Nabers (knee) both confirmed that the receiver practiced fully after sitting out Thursday’s session.
It’s unknown if the knee issue that Nabers has been listed with is the same one that he suffered the torn ACL in last year or something else. Regardless, Harbaugh said Nabers’ issue was “an in-season type thing,” without elaborating, adding. “It's not an issue. He'll be full-go for the game.”
All other Giants on the injury report are good to go, with tackles Andrew Thomas (groing) andJermaine Eluemunor (calf) both having practiced in full on Friday.

title: Isaiah Likely: Giants Goal vs. Philly is Simple
full_text:
New York Giants tight end Isaiah Likely is no stranger to heated rivalries.
After spending his first four NFL seasons with the Baltimore Ravens, Likely has certainly faced his share of battles with Baltimore’s hated rivals, the Pittsburgh Steelers.
Now a member of the Giants, the 26-year-old is about to get his first taste of Big Blue’s longstanding divisional feud with the Philadelphia Eagles when the clubs face off on Sunday at Lincoln Financial Field. It will mark the 183rd regular-season meeting between the two NFC East franchises.
Though he may have great respect for gridiron history between New York and Philadelphia, Likely is entering this weekend’s matchup with only one goal in mind.
“We’re just always trying to have the mindset of leaving 1-0,” Likely said.
Likely signed a three-year, $40 million contract with the Giants this offseason, joining head coach John Harbaugh in Baltimore.
Through the first seven games of the season, the five-year veteran has caught 41 passes for 395 yards and five touchdowns. In the process, he has established himself as New York’s top tight end option.
Still, Likely’s quick assimilation into the Giants’ offense has not only endeared him to his coaches, but also made him a favorite target for quarterbacks Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy.
In fact, the Cambridge, MA native has played a major role in New York’s ascent to the top of the division with a 4-2-1 record.
Heading into the season’s home stretch, the Giants not only have the chance to earn their fifth win of the season (which would eclipse their 2025 total) but also to exorcise a decade-plus road losing streak to the Eagles. New York has lost 13 straight road games at Philadelphia since its 15-7 victory on Oct. 27, 2013.
As the Giants try to take a major step forward in the NFC East standings, Likely knows he and his teammates must focus solely on the task at hand.
“I feel like every win should be the team's mindset, whether you haven't won in Philly in 13 years, whether we beat the opponent earlier this year and you got to play them again,” Likely said.
“I mean, every mindset, every week should be trying to finish 1-0, whatever the record was in the past. I mean, I wasn't here 13 years ago. So, my mentality is winning the game at hand.”
In the end, I understand that the Giants will need their best effort to defeat their bitter rivals in a hostile environment on Sunday.
Though the Eagles may be weakened by injuries (especially the season-ending loss of quarterback Jalen Hurts to blood clots), they are still more than capable of beating New York.
Although they are the current favorites to win their first division title since 2011, Likely and the Giants may be best served by maintaining their “underdog” identity.
“In my mind, I feel like every time we play, we should be the favorite,” he said.
“And that's just the mentality I have cause I feel like the mindset should be winning your one-eleventh, snap in, snap out. Whether you're an underdog or whether they got you winning, it doesn’t really matter.”

title: Eagles Offense in Flux: What the Giants Will Face After the Bye
full_text:
After a Week 8 bye, the New York Giants face a very different Philadelphia Eagles team than they expected at the start of the year. Most of that difference is on the offensive side, where major changes have occurred over the first eight weeks due to injuries, trades, and retirements.
The biggest loss is quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is out for the season with blood clots. Losing their offensive leader and his cool, calm demeanor changes the temperature of this team.
Still, the Giants would be foolish to walk into this game and underestimate a team that has nothing to lose.
Let’s take a look at this current Philadelphia Eagles offense.
Like so many NFL offenses today, the Eagles’ primary personnel grouping is 11 personnel. They will supplement heavily with 12 personnel, using longtime tight end Dallas Goedert along with guys like Johnny Mundt.
Their three receivers have been reshuffled this year, with the trade of A.J. Brown before the season, the signing of Dontayvion Wicks, and the drafting of Makai Lemon with the first-round pick.
The major changes have come through injuries, as Lemon missed the start of the season and the Eagles have been without the services of DeVonta Smith for most of the year.
The once mighty Eagles’ rushing attack has been limited this season, primarily due to a lack of continuity on the offensive line and in the backfield.
The rushing attack ranks near the bottom of the league, 29th in total rushing at 88.1 yards per game. Their 3.8 yards per carry is well below their standard.
All-Pro caliber running back Saquon Barkley has dealt with injuries throughout the season that have kept him in and out of the lineup.
More concerning, every backup running back they’ve had this year has also suffered an injury. They have had to sign multiple backs off waivers or the practice squad to supplement their backfield.
They primarily run an inside zone and duo rushing attack, using split zone and counters out of the shotgun.
With the offensive line losing continuity, they have tried to use more downhill A- and B-gap attacks, rather than the wide zone stretches they used in the past.
Obviously, without your starting quarterback, the passing attack is going to suffer. Since Jalen Hurts’ injury, they have had Tanner McKee on the field, and his performance has been substandard.
They are turning their attention to Joe Milton, whom they acquired from the Cowboys’ practice squad a few weeks ago.
He brings a unique skill set as a strong-armed quarterback who is big and athletic, but he has very little experience playing in meaningful games. It will be interesting to see how the passing attack fits his skill set.
This season, they rank 27th in passing yards per game at a paltry 177 and 30th in yards per attempt at 5.27.
Dallas Goedert is their most reliable target, given his availability and red-zone prowess. Makai Lemon, since returning from injury, has emerged as the team’s high-volume target on underneath and intermediate routes.
Darius Cooper has found the end zone four times this year as a red-zone contested-catch receiver. But the injuries to Wicks and Smith have really hurt the continuity of the passing attack.
The Eagles have felt the effect of right tackle Lane Johnson’s retirement and center Cam Juergens leaving in a trade to the Ravens.
Jordan Mailata and Landon Dickerson still provide an effective left side of the offensive line. Still, everything else seems up in the air regarding the offense’s continuity.
We have already discussed Hurts, Smith, and Wicks being out, and Saquon Barkley’s limited availability this season.
Currently, the Eagles have three other running backs on the IR: Dameon Pierce is out with an undisclosed injury. Tank Bigsby had core muscle surgery. Will Shipley had plantar fascia surgery that has him out for the season.
The first thing the Giants’ defense needs to do is take away any confidence the Eagles’ offense might have in the running game. Force this to be a Joe Milton game where he tries to run around and make plays.
Don’t let him throw in rhythm, take away his quick reads, and turn him into a backyard football player improvising out of structure. That is where he feels he can make the most plays, but it is also where he makes critical mistakes.
That’s the opportunity for the Giants to turn the Eagles over, get the game into a positive script where they can control it with the rushing attack, and dominate the time of possession.

title: Giants’ OC Matt Nagy Explains Why He Has Confidence in Devin Singletary to Carry the Rock
full_text:
New York Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy remains confident in his running game despite an onslaught of injuries.
With second-year back Cam Skattebo dealing with a hamstring injury and veteran Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve (also with a hamstring), New York faces the prospect of entering its Week 9 showdown with the Philadelphia Eagles with a significantly depleted depth chart.
Still, the Giants' offensive coordinator has faith in Big Blue’s next men up.
“For us, the confidence there, it’s been a point of emphasis all year,” Nagy said. “We talked about the run game to the actual players. We want to be able to lock in on whoever those guys are, make sure that we give them a great opportunity to succeed in the scheme, and to put them in a spot where we can use their strengths.”
Despite facing an Eagles run defense that ranks 28th in the NFL (allowing 131.9 yards per game and 10 touchdowns), the Giants have only two healthy running backs on their 53-man roster.
If Skattebo can’t play, veteran Devin Singletary is expected to start as New York’s lead back. In four games this season, the 29-year-old has carried the ball 18 times for 80 yards and a 30-yard, game-winning touchdown in the Giants’ 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans in Week 7.
Given Singletary’s seven-plus years of experience, Nagy is optimistic that his running back is up to the challenge.
“The story I’ll give you with Motor Singletary is this is a kid that’s been in this game for a long time,” Nagy recounted. “He’s a savvy vet. He’s been here from day one, from OTAs, and through training camp, through the season, wasn’t playing, wasn’t active.
“He’d sit back in practice when he wasn’t playing and not say a word, but just be completely professional,” he continued.
“And we talked, and we talked about how ‘great things happen to great people,’ and I think back to that Texans game when he scored that touchdown at the end. I remembered the discussions we had in practice when he wasn’t playing; he never became negative, and he never made it about him.
“He was as great a professional player as there was, and look what happened,” Nagy concluded. “I think it’s a story for young kids; it’s a story for vets to be patient, to understand things happen for a reason.”
Greg Desrosiers, who was recently signed from the Los Angeles Chargers’ practice squad, would be the top reserve.
The Giants also have Phil Mafah and Eric Gray (signed earlier this week) available for game-day elevation from the practice squad, and one of them is expected to be called up for Sunday’s game.
While having both Tracy and Skattebo healthy would be the ideal scenario, Nagy believes the Giants can keep building momentum with their current lineup.
“It’s going to be of the utmost importance to keep the run game going,” Nagy said. “We talked about that in Houston. You can’t be one dimensional and just be dropping back, throwing.
"You’ve got to keep that run game going. So, no matter who’s back there with the carries, we’ve got to be efficient with the run game.”
New York’s running backs have experienced their share of ups and downs through the first seven games this season. As a group, they have run for 652 yards and five touchdowns, but they have not been a consistent complement to the passing game.
Despite the injury woes, Nagy’s faith may pay off for the Giants in Week 9 against the Eagles. Kickoff is set for 1 p.m. ET at Lincoln Financial Field.

title: How the Giants Plan to Slow Eagles QB Joe Milton
full_text:
New York Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson will face a familiar challenge as he prepares his unit for a Week 9 showdown against the Philadelphia Eagles.
While Philadelphia (2-6) has been reeling since placing incumbent starter Jalen Hurts on season-ending injured reserve because of blood clots in his lungs, the Eagles will play this weekend with added mobility and arm strength at quarterback.
Third-year quarterback Joe Milton III, recently signed off the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad, will make his first NFL start against Big Blue, taking the job from backup Tanner McKee.
Though many coordinators would be intrigued by the prospect of game-planning for a novice starter, Wilson expects the Eagles to deploy some recognizable looks Sunday at Lincoln Financial Field.
“They’re going to do certain things they want to do with him because he’s an athletic guy,” Wilson said.
“We understand that. Some of the stuff that they did with (Eagles quarterback) Jalen (Hurts) probably resurfaced that they haven’t done.”
Known for his strong arm and playmaking speed, Milton was a sixth-round pick by the New England Patriots in 2024. He spent most of his rookie season as the Patriots’ third-string quarterback behind Drake Maye and Jacoby Brissett.
However, he saw extensive action in his in-game debut in Week 18. In a 23-16 victory over the Buffalo Bills, Milton completed 22 of 29 passes for 241 yards and one touchdown. He also carried the ball 10 times for 16 yards and one rushing score after relieving Maye in the first quarter.
In April 2025, Milton was traded to the Cowboys in exchange for a fifth-round draft pick, as New England committed to Maye full time.
Despite not yet making an NFL start, he has completed 69.8 percent of his passes for 424 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions, while adding 66 yards and a score on 15 carries in five games.
For Wilson, the sample size on Milton is enough to devise an effective strategy to neutralize the Tennessee product as he tries to resurrect a struggling Eagles offense.
“He has some tape. There hasn’t been ‘starting’ tape in the National Football League, but you’ve seen him play in the preseason,” Wilson said.
“He’s a big man. He can run. He’s elusive in the pocket, and he can throw the ball 100 yards. So we have to be aware of that. He’s going to bring a different dynamic to the offense, and we’re really aware of it. It’s not going to change what we do. We’re going to play attack-defense, and that’s what we pride ourselves on.”
The Giants’ “attack-defense” has served them well through their first seven games this season. New York’s unit ranks 15th in the NFL in scoring defense, allowing 23.0 points per game, and has helped the club compile an NFC East-leading 4-2-1 record.
Wilson will undoubtedly rely on his linebackers’ athleticism, along with a blitz-heavy scheme, to contain Milton’s mobility.
With rookie linebacker Arvell Reese deployed as a sideline-to-sideline spy, New York’s secondary will be called upon to keep the Eagles’ new starter from showcasing his cannon-like arm in the deep passing game.
As they return from a much-needed bye, Wilson’s aggressive defense will be needed to snap Big Blue’s 13-game road losing streak against Philadelphia at Lincoln Financial Field.
Kickoff between the Giants and Eagles is set for Sunday at 1 p.m. ET.

title: Why Giants Special Teams Coach Still Believes in Kicker Dominic Zvada
full_text:
New York Giants assistant head coach/special teams coordinator Chris Horton still believes in kicker Dominic Zvada.
Despite the rookie’s recent struggles, Horton remains confident that Zvada has the physical talent and mental fortitude to be New York’s long-term investment at the position. To ensure that happens, one of his most important post-bye duties will be keeping the kicker’s confidence high.
“I’ve said this before: Just continue to believe in the kid,” Horton said. “Just help him understand some of those misses; a lot of those things are fundamental things that I know we can get fixed, we can take care of.
“We spend a lot of time on the bye week, just diving into it and just thinking about what we can do on these kicks,” he added.
“We just watch those kicks over and over and over again, and he will be consistent, and those are the things that we are expecting of him, and he’s expecting of himself.”
After starting his rookie season a perfect 9-for-9 on field goals, including three makes from 50-plus yards, Zvada’s fortunes have reversed sharply in recent weeks.
The undrafted rookie out of Michigan missed three field-goal attempts in New York’s Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders, followed by 44- and 56-yard misses in Week 7 against the Texans.
In total, Zvada has connected on 13 of 18 field-goal attempts while going 12-for-12 on extra points.
Though some have begun to question whether Zvada’s difficulties may be a harbinger of things to come, Horton made it clear that the Giants are not yet ready to declare them a worrisome problem.
“I don’t think that’s something that we think about,” Horton said. “I think we think about the process of now, where are we now? And so far, you think about the kicks that he has missed, the five kicks that he’s missed, again, to me, those are all fundamental things that we can work on. I don’t think you go into it and say, ‘hey, alright, we need to be worried about this, we need to be worried about that.’”
Head coach John Harbaugh has also said the Giants have no current plans to make a change at kicker. After all, Zvada is still in the midst of an impressive season.
His 51 points not only put him on track to lead all rookies in scoring in 2026 (Ali Haji-Sheikh had 127 in 1983), but also put him just two points behind Washington Commanders kicker Drew Stevens.
Therefore, they remain hopeful that helping Zvada with his plant-foot placement and other fixable mechanics will be enough to get him back on track. While the talent is clearly there, New York cannot afford for its kicking game to become a liability in a postseason bid, a point Horton knows all too well.
“We just let him go out there, and we perform, and we believe in him, let him know we believe in him, and then, yes, we expect kicks to go in,” Horton said. “That’s a requirement. Those are the things that we are asking of him, and he’s asking of himself, and we put him out there, and he’ll go get it done.”
Zvada and the Giants will return from their bye with a Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field. Kickoff is set for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Giants Injury Report: Skattebo Out Again, Nabers Added With Knee Issue
full_text:
New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo missed his second straight day of practice with a hamstring strain, further putting his status for Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles in doubt.
Skattebo was seen on the sideline with a trainer during the media viewing portion of practice. It’s probably safe to say that if he doesn’t get at least some practice in on Friday, he’s likely to be scratched for Sunday, with the team instead eyeing the second-year running back for its Thursday night game against the Washington Commanders four days later.
Devin Singletary and Greg Desrosiers are the healthy running backs on the roster, with Tyrone Tracy on injured reserve. The team also has Eric Gray and Phil Mafah on the practice squad.
Receiver Malik Nabers, the newly minted NFC Offensive Player of the Month for October 2026, is now on the team’s injury report after missing Thursday’s practice.
Nabers, who appears to have put the ACL injury that ended his 2025 season firmly in the rearview mirror, was listed with a knee injury and did not participate Thursday.
Nabers last appeared on the injury report in Week 5 with a knee ailment, missing Wednesday’s practice, being limited Thursday and returning to full participation Friday.
Nabers assured reporters that he’d “be good” for Sunday’s game against the Eagles.
In other injury developments, receiver/return specialist Charlie Jones (hand), wearing a red non-contact jersey, was seen with a cast on his hand while trying, unsuccessfully, to field punts during the media portion of Thursday’s practice.
Jones also participated in a limited capacity Wednesday.
The Giants’ unofficial depth chart lists safety Jevon Holland as the backup punt returner, but it’s unlikely they would go in that direction since Holland is a starter.
On kickoff returns, assistant head coach/special teams coordinator Chris Horton didn’t rule out using starting cornerback Deonte Banks alongside Singletary, who is expected to have a bigger role on offense if Skattebo can’t play.
“I don’t think anything’s off the shelf,” Horton said. “We talk about trying to win football games. And if that gives us the best opportunity to win a football game. We’re talking about one rep. We’re talking about one rep where we can go out there and have the most success. So I don’t think anything’s off the table in that regard.”
The most likely scenario is that running back Eric Gray gets the call-up from the practice squad, since he has experience on punt and kickoff returns. Gray would also give the Giants additional depth at running back if Skattebo can’t play Sunday.
Outside linebacker Abdul Carter (illness) returned to practice on a limited basis after being sent home Wednesday to rest.
In addition to Nabers, four other Giants were added to the injury report: defensive lineman Darius Alexander (foot), tight end Thomas Fidone II (thumb), outside linebacker Trace Ford (knee) and inside linebacker Micah McFadden (foot). All four were full participants.
As anticipated, quarterback Jake Haener was waived from the 53-man roster. The Giants will look to add him back to the practice squad, but they will need an extra roster spot to accommodate the injury-related additions.
The Giants had four players in for a tryout Thursday: receivers Maurice Alexander, River Cracraft and Steven Sims, and punter Wes Pahl.

title: Taking Braelon Allen Out of RB1 Role Would Be a Huge Mistake as Breece Hall Returns
full_text:
Coming off a second-half collapse against the Raiders last Sunday, the Jets hit the road to face the Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium with a 2-6 record and their season all but lost at this point.
Injuries have been an issue all season for the Jets, which have kept them from being at full strength and forced them to test their depth chart each week.
While that's not an excuse for the poor coaching and lackluster defensive play so far, it has been a prevailing theme since the season began and has continued this week with some key players finding themselves on the injury report once again .
Wide receiver Garrett Wilson has been ruled out of Sunday's game against the Chiefs due to a concussion. But running back Breece Hall appears set to return from a five-game absence due to a quad injury after ESPN's Rich Cimini noted in Thursday's injury report that Hall "practices fully for the first time since his injury and later said he will play Sunday."
Jets injury report: Breece Hall practices fully for the first time since his injury and later says he will play Sunday. Not looking good for Garrett Wilson. #Jets pic.twitter.com/KwpP20EOGf
While head coach Aaron Glenn has insisted that both Hall and Braelon Allen will play in Sunday's game, it remains to be seen how much of a workload Hall will have as he returns to the field amid what has been a breakout season for Allen.
Offensive coordinator Frank Reich seemingly made it clear that the Jets plan to use both RBs instead of exploring a trade for their RB1, but his return from injury should not take away from what Allen has accomplished in his absence.
With back-to-back 100-yard rushing games and three of the five games Hall has missed, it could prove costly for Gang Green if Allen is not the lead back amid Hall's return, at least for another week as the latter gets back up to speed.
Before the 2025 season, Allen only had three rushing touchdowns and had never rushed for more than 55 yards in a single game. While he has two rushing TDs in the five games without Hall, Allen has equaled his previous number of scores on the ground in eight games this season and has had at least 14 carries in each of the last five games.
Even more impressive, Allen's 5.0 yards per carry are considerably better than Hall's (3.2), albeit in five more games. Pro Football Focus paints an even bigger picture, giving Allen the eighth-best overall grade (82.4) and sixth-best rushing grade (85.6) out of 45 qualified RBs in the league.
Something else to keep an eye on is Wilson's absence from the WR room and the impact it could have on the depth at that position. While Reich's inability to consistently get his WR1 touches has been a recurring issue, the recent returns from rookie Omar Cooper Jr. and Adonai Mitchell should still give quarterback Geno Smith some trusty options downfield. We also shouldn't rule out Hall's potential usage in that area.
Allen and RB3 Isaiah Davis have a combined 149 yards on 22 receptions this season. Hall has had a much greater impact in the pass game with 198 catches, 1,744 yards, and nine TDs in 59 career games, including 10 catches on as many targets for 102 yards this season. Hall already faces more pressure to perform after the Wilson news , but this could be the ideal way to ease him back into things in an area he has excelled in more than Allen.
It is hard to ignore the explosiveness Allen has shown in Hall's absence and how impactful his physical downhill style of play between the tackles has given this offense a nice balance that has proven to be hard to contain at times. Look no further than the fact that they scored on each of their first six drives in the Week 8 loss to Las Vegas, which was a huge improvement from the slow starts they have gotten off to earlier this season.
It seems like Hall is likely to stay around in Gotham as the trade deadline looms on Tuesday, especially with $14.5 million and $15.5 million cap hits in 2026 and 2027 , respectively, but regardless of how everything plays out between now and then, it would be a huge mistake if the Jets pivot away from Allen in favor of Hall, considering how productive he has been.
If anything, this could be a case of workload management as Hall returns to full strength and potentially splits carries with Allen while being a solid contributor in the passing game. Hall has not forgotten how to play, but Allen's emergence should be enough to keep him as the lead back for at least another week as Hall makes his long-awaited return.

title: 3 Matchups That Will Decide Jets’ Week 9 Game Against Chiefs
full_text:
After dropping two winnable games at home, the Jets will look to end their three-game losing streak when they head to Arrowhead Stadium to take on the Chiefs in Week 9.
Kansas City is also on a losing streak of its own, falling to the Seahawks and Broncos in the last two games. Despite this, the Chiefs are widely viewed as heavy favorites to win, given how poorly New York has played the past few weeks.
With head coach Aaron Glenn’s job on the ropes, he’ll need an upset victory over the Chiefs to have any chance of saving his job. Otherwise, the Jets could be compelled to make some deals ahead of the trade deadline.
For New York to come away victorious, it will need to win these three key matchups.
Kenneth Walker has picked up right where he left off in the 2025 playoffs and has been a dominant force on the ground with the Chiefs. Head coach Andy Reid has made the reigning Super Bowl MVP the offense’s engine, unlocking a new dimension with his high-impact production that Kansas City hasn’t had in years.
Through seven games, Walker ranks third in the league in rushing yards (770) and second in rushing yards per attempt (5.5). He’s been one of the key ingredients to the Chiefs' 5-2 start, with his success on the ground playing a significant role in determining the outcome of their games.
Kansas City is 5-0 when Walker rushes for over 70 yards, whereas it's 0-2 when he rushes for fewer than 70. Those losses came in the past two weeks to the Broncos and Seahawks, who prioritized neutralizing Walker, limiting him to a combined 105 yards.
Seattle played nickel or dime personnel on all 50 defensive snaps, stacking the box on just 7% of its plays. As a result, Walker rushed for just 36 yards and had zero explosive runs.
Although Seattle’s approach was effective, the Jets shouldn’t necessarily follow the same blueprint. The Seahawks have one of the best defenses in the league, with elite defenders at each level who can fly to Walker without committing additional players to the box.
New York doesn’t have that luxury, nor has it been effective at containing the run. Through eight games, the unit ranks 21st in rushing yards allowed per game (123.6). To limit Walker’s impact, head coach Aaron Glenn should emphasize clogging the interior lanes and preventing him from reaching the second level with room to operate.
Walker’s patience, elusiveness and tackle-breaking ability make him one of the best runners in the league. If New York is to beat Kansas City, the defense has to win at the point of attack and make the offensive line work to create running lanes.
Linebackers Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood will need to play a critical role in that effort. The pair have struggled with missed tackles this season, combining for 17, and must clean this up to contain Walker. Giving him extra opportunities to break tackles could quickly turn a stop into a big gain.
If New York can limit Walker’s impact and hold him to minimal gains, it will force the Chiefs to become more dependent on Patrick Mahomes and the passing game.
Through seven games, Geno Smith has been sacked 23 times, which is tied for the second-most. While the blame will be placed on the offensive line, it’s not entirely their fault. Smith shares responsibility for this.
The 14-year veteran has played too conservatively this season. At times, he’s held onto the ball too long, waiting for deep or developing routes instead of throwing it away or checking down.
Things changed dramatically last week against the Raiders. Smith made quicker decisions and attempted more downfield passes, recording a 31.3% deep rate, per Next Gen Stats. The offensive line played a key role, limiting Max Crosby and Las Vegas’ pass rush to just two sacks and seven pressures.
Although the Raiders didn’t have the best pass rush heading into this matchup, New York’s line did a terrific job of limiting its impact. They’ll hope to replicate that success against the Chiefs' pass rush, which has also struggled to generate consistent pressure.
Through seven games, Kansas City is tied for last in sacks (9) and ranks 29th in pressure rate (19.3%). A major reason is that star defensive tackle Chris Jones’ production has dropped significantly this season, with just half a sack and just 16 pressures.
This has put immense pressure on edge rusher George Karlaftis, who leads the team in sacks (2) and pressures (34). Even though Kansas City hasn’t done well generating pressure, it’s been among the best teams against the run, ranking eighth in rushing yards allowed per game (96.3).
Even with star receiver Garrett Wilson sidelined , the Jets can exploit the Chiefs' lack of a pass rush. New York needs to take advantage of the Chiefs' inability to create pressure by giving Smith enough time to sling the ball around and attack downfield.
Even though Jones has been quiet, the emphasis should be on not giving him one-on-one opportunities. The Jets will need to slide protection and use chip blocks to limit his impact.
While this creates more opportunities for Karlaftis, New York should be encouraged by Olu Fashanu and Armand Membou’s recent play, as the two have allowed just seven pressures and zero sacks over the past two games.
Pre-snap communication will also be critical against defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, as he’ll try to test the line with simulated pressure and timely blitzes. And with Arrowhead Stadium being one of the loudest stadiums, having everyone on the same page will be crucial.
If the offensive line can give Smith enough time to work through his progressions and find open receivers, the Jets should find success through the air.
Although New York won’t have Wilson on Sunday, rookie edge rusher David Bailey should be returning to the lineup after missing Week 8 against the Raiders with a groin injury. Without their No. 2 overall pick, the defense wasn’t nearly as productive generating pressure without him, posting just 12 pressures and one sack.
Despite missing the game, Bailey still leads the team in pressures (26), quarterback hits (5), and sacks (5.5). If New York is going to have any chance of upsetting the Chiefs, they’ll need Bailey to apply consistent pressure against Mahomes.
Getting to Mahomes won’t be easy, as he’s been sacked just nine times this season. However, with Bailey primarily lining up on the left side, he’ll have a favorable matchup against right tackle Jaylon Moore, who’s struggled in pass protection.
According to Next Gen Stats , the 2021 fifth-round selection has allowed a 12.6% pressure rate, which ranks fourth-highest among right tackles with at least 100 pass-blocking snaps. Moore has also had his share of penalty issues, most notably last week against the Broncos, where he committed a false start that nullified a potential game-winning touchdown.
With Bailey generating the fifth-highest pressure rate this season (20%), per Next Gen Stats, the Texas Tech alum must have a big day against Moore.
The top priority for Bailey will be getting to Mahomes quickly. With his elite burst and speed, he can make life difficult for the heavier Moore, who has had difficulty against explosive edge rushers.
If Bailey can wear down Moore with his relentless motor, it could force him into making similar mental mistakes as he did last week and potentially force the Chiefs to double-team him. With more eyes on Bailey, it could create more opportunities for Joseph Ossai or Will McDonald IV to get to Mahomes or force him to make a quick decision.

title: Breece Hall Returns to Jets With Clear Message About Trade Rumors & Starting Job
full_text:
Just two months ago, New York Jets running back Breece Hall was considered one of the top running backs in the game. His ability as both a runner and pass catcher comes in rare form across the NFL.
But as former coach Jerry Glanville once said, the NFL's best acronym is "Not For Long."
A quad injury cost the Jets' running back the last five weeks. In his absence, Braelon Allen has turned into one of the more productive runners in team history. The former Wisconsin product is the first Jets running back to record three straight 100-yard rushing games since Curtis Martin in 2004.
Heading into Week 9, Hall is back. And with it, questions about his future with the team, where the depth chart stands, and how things will look for the offense going forward.
Speaking to reporters this week, Hall made it clear: he remains the team's starter regardless of what Allen has done over the course of the last month.
"I'm still a starter, still a very good running back in this league," Hall said. "Obviously, Braelon's been playing good. I think him and the offense have caught their stride after the first three, four games. So it's going to be good to just get in there, just play some ball."
In a modern offense, both Hall and Allen can coexist in a way that is great for the Jets. New York can scheme open Hall in the passing game while using Allen up the middle and between the tackles. The more the two play on the field together, the harder it will be for opposing teams to stop Gang Green.
That task, though, will be based on the creativity of offensive play-caller Frank Reich .
"We have some plays that are tagged for one or the other, but it's a great problem to have," Reich said. "You've got two No. 1 backs. Breece is, obviously ... our guy, but it'll be a mix."
Reich's comments also pour cool water on the heated rumors of a potential trade of Hall. New York is refusing to open trade dialogues at this time for their running back, but with Allen's breakout, the team may simply want to keep Allen as the starter going forward.
Hall, though, believes any trade rumor is based on the fanbase's point of view. Not with what the team wants.
"It's like if I have 100 yards, they love me," he said. "If I don't, everybody's like, 'Get him out of here.'"
The former second-round pick out of Iowa only further increased awareness of his standing with the Jets after seemingly deleting his social media this week. In the modern age of professional athletics coupled with social media, it's common to see outspoken individuals make cryptic posts or delete pages altogether to convey deeper meaning.
That doesn't appear to be the case either, though.
"I've had people threatening me and my family on social media," Hall said. "So that's not something that's good for your mental health that you should be looking at. So I'm just like, all right, if people think it's that serious, if you're willing to go that low, then it's like nothing that I need to look at."
There will always be a good and bad side to NFL fandom. Passion and loyalty are rare throughout modern society, but with that passion comes an overzealous attitude toward trolling their own athletes. Hall should never have to go through threats made on social media simply because he was injured over the last month.
That doesn't mean he wants out of New York, or the Jets want to move on from him either. Since arriving at the team last year, head coach Aaron Glenn has shared his intention to run a "by committee" approach to their running back room.
In short, it doesn't seem like Hall is going anywhere, but his role as the feature back in New York's offense has fundamentally changed—for better or worse.
