title: 49ers WR Brandon Aiyuk's Reinstatement Reveals His Costly Mistakes
full_text:
After a Summer of nonstop weird social media posting, Brandon Aiyuk has finally decided to file for reinstatement.
He's expected to show up at the 49ers' facility on Friday, setting up an extremely awkward situation. No one on the 49ers is thrilled with his return, and you can't blame them.
Aiyuk burned his bridges with the 49ers in the Summer. Had he remained quiet, there would have been a realm where he plays for the 49ers this season. They certainly could use him right now .
In any case, Aiyuk has taken steps towards reawakening his NFL career. However, by filing for reinstatement now, he's revealing his costly mistakes.
Aiyuk is essentially admitting that he messed up by not doing all of this before the season. That his entire approach in the Summer until now has been a mistake.
Otherwise, why file for reinstatement now?
He seemed dead set on not playing this season since he refused to file before the regular season. He literally admitted that in a social media post.
His filing for reinstatement now is his way of throwing his hands up and admitting he gaffed everything. He could've easily done this in July.
The 49ers would've been forced to cut him. Aiyuk could've joined a team months ago to embed himself in an offense and build rapport with ample time.
Instead, he's either going to be traded or cut next week and sign with another team, where he will be rushed into a playbook with zero connection to anyone.
What a foolish route he's taken. All he's done is set himself up for a struggle. Had he forced the 49ers' hands months ago, which he easily could've, he would be in a perfect spot to maximize his value.
How's he going to do that with less than half of a season left?
There's still a way to raise his stock, but it wouldn't be as significant had he started for a team in Week 1. Now, he needs to hit the ground running.
He better hope he's close to the same player that he was before he tore his ACL. The hurdles of adapting to a new playbook and a new quarterback are more than enough of a challenge.
If he's struggling to return to the high-level player he once was, then he'll have done nothing to help his stock. All of this could've been avoided had he not acted like a teenager this Summer.

title: One Buccaneers Weakness Could Be Exposed Against Bears
full_text:
After a dreadful start to the 2026 NFL season, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers have finally found some positive momentum to build off.
Not only have the Buccaneers secured back-to-back victories for the first time in over a year, but following their decisive victories over the Panthers and Falcons these past two weeks, the Buccaneers are 2-0 against NFC South teams and just half a game behind Carolina for first place in the division.
After dislocating his thumb in Week 3, Mayfield managed to return just in time for those crucial NFC South games — at which time the Bucs really began to lean into a new look, run-first approach on offense under Zac Robinson.
Since then, the Bucs have limited turnovers, controlled the time-of-possession battle and dominated opponents by running the football with incredible efficiency on offense. At the same time, Todd Bowles' defense has been surging due to a combination of consistent pressure on the quarterback, good tackling, sticky coverage on the back end while generating turnovers from all three levels.
Despite their success playing complementary over the past few weeks, the Buccaneers will face an entirely different type of challenge this weekend when they travel to Chicago to take on the impressive 6-2 Bears on Sunday Night Football.
Although the Buccaneers have found success playing old school, smash mouth offensive football the past two weeks, that is not an approach that is necessarily sustainable in the modern NFL.
Not to mention, it's not like the Buccaneers opted for this run-heavy approach purely by choice. The team's inability to pass the football consistently throughout this entire season gave Robinson little choice. So even though he deserves some credit for adjusting his offensive scheme, it was a result of necessity more than it was ingenuity.
Regardless, the fact remains that the Buccaneers' passing offense is not a threat to any opposing defense, let alone the Bears, who have an explosive offense in addition to a really solid group on the defensive side of the ball.
Heading into Week 9, the Bears are eighth in points allowed and seventh in total yards allowed. Like the Bucs, they're also one of the top run defenses in the NFL, ranking fourth in rushing yards allowed as they give up just 86.8 rushing yards per game.
Even more impressive is the fact that Dennis Allen's defense is best in the league on third downs, allowing conversions on third down just 23.75% of the time.
So how does this impact the Buccaneers?
First and foremost, the Bears are simply too well-rounded of a defense for the Bucs to expect to win this game with a one-dimensional offense like they did against both the Panthers and Falcons. Chicago is very stout against the run, and if the Buccaneers are going to put up points against this them, they will need to balance the run with the pass. It's that simple.
As much as Mayfield's thumb (or even the weather during last week's game against Atlanta) could be used as potential excuses for the Buccaneers' lack of production through the air, that ship has sailed. This upcoming game against the Bears marks Mayfield's third game back from injury. If Mayfield isn't healthy enough to make quality throws to all levels of the football field? He should not be in the game.
This Sunday night provides a golden opportunity for the Buccaneers to re-establish themselves as a quality NFL team on a national stage. If they can knock off the Bears in Chicago on national television, it will not only be a huge boost to their chances of eventually finishing the season atop the NFC South Division, but it will prove they are a team capable of competing with the league's best.
But if the Buccaneers' passing game continues to struggle, that simply won't happen.

title: Buccaneers Reveal Much-Needed Injury News Before Bears Matchup
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers will need the cavalry to beat the Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football. After Friday's practice, it looks like they'll have it.
The only player that the Buccaneers were expecting to miss some time was outside linebacker Yaya Diaby, who sprained his MCL and could be out for a little bit. But the team was hopeful that wideout Emeka Egbuka could return on Sunday night after missing the last two games, and his practice on Thursday trended in that direction.
Another name to watch was left tackle Tristan Wirfs, who appeared on Thursday's injury report as a non-participant with a toe injury. If he weren't able to go, the Bucs would be at a significant disadvantage.
The good news? The Bucs will have both players at their disposal on Sunday night.
Both Egbuka and Wirfs practiced on Friday — Egbuka was there from the start, while Wirfs came out shortly after warmups. Head coach Todd Bowles did not rule them out during his media session on Friday, which paves the way for both of them to go on Sunday night.
Todd Bowles confirms that the only player he’s ruling out is Yaya Diaby — he says Emeka Egbuka is questionable and Tristan Wirfs “should be okay.” pic.twitter.com/V0GMW1nWQr
Egbuka should be a help for Tampa Bay's absent passing game, even if he hasn't played to the standard Tampa Bay has expected of him. The Bucs will have to pass the ball against the Bears to win the game, and quarterback Baker Mayfield can lean on him as a receiving option alongside players like Chris Godwin, Ted Hurst and Tez Johnson.
Wirfs' impact cannot be overstated — he's arguably the best pass protector in football, so the Bucs missing him would be crucial. Tampa Bay will need him against a stout Chicago defensive line that now includes All-Pro Jeffery Simmons, and while Wirfs won't square off with Simmons himself, he'll likely face some added pressure from the edge with so many resources devoted to stopping him.
Tampa Bay still will have Diaby out and will not have the services of wideout Jalen McMillan, who remains on injured reserve with a knee injury. But other than that, the Bucs appear very healthy heading into what could be one of their biggest games of the year.
The Bucs play the Bears at 8:20 p.m. in Chicago. It will be the last game they play before their bye week in Week 10.

title: Bears Have One Advantage Buccaneers Haven't Faced in Recent Weeks
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are set to face a very difficult challenge on Sunday night when they play the Chicago Bears. The Bears are one of the best teams in football, and their offense is piloted by a deadly tandem of head coach Ben Johnson and quarterback Caleb Williams.
Their defense is a force to be reckoned with too, though, and that's especially true after a blockbuster trade involving one of the NFL's elite defensive players. The Buccaneers have played some tough defenses this season so far, but they haven't faced a dimension like this since the first game of the year.
Here's why the Bears' defensive line will be a big problem for the Bucs on Sunday night:
The Chicago Bears acquired defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons in a blockbuster trade from the Tennessee Titans that included two first-round picks in Week 6. Simmons, a First Team All-Pro last season and one of the NFL's best interior defensive linemen, is a force to be reckoned with — and the Bucs haven't played an interior defender like him in a while.
Offensive coordinator Zac Robinson spoke at length about the challenges Simmons will bring to the team and explained that he'll likely be even better against the Bucs than he was against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 8.
"Yeah, he's one of the better just players in the league, regardless – offense, defense," Robinson said. "He's disruptive [in the] run game, pass game. When you see him in person, the physical presence alone, you see it. Obviously, there's really nothing he can't do to disrupt the game. So, you've got to account for him at all times.
"I know now he had the first week there, just kind of getting his feet wet with the system and getting around his players that he's playing around. So, I'm sure they've [had] another week to kind of install some new things and kind of sprinkle him in in some different ways that didn't present themselves last week."
The last time the Bucs faced a dominant, game-wrecking defensive tackle was in Week 1. The Bucs played the Bengals, who traded their first-round pick for Dexter Lawrence in the offseason, and Lawrence made his presence known — he had three pressures, two hurries and one quarterback hit, per SumerSports, and the Bengals had a 40.9% pressure rate with Lawrence on the field against a 28.6% pressure rate with him off of it.
Quarterback Baker Mayfield knows a game-wrecker when he sees one. And he made it very clear on Wednesday that the Bucs will have to keep tabs on Simmons the whole game.
"Obviously, he's a game wrecker. No matter what team he's on, even when he was in Tennessee, all eyes are [on him], you're figuring out where he is," Mayfield said. "We [have to] change some protection things and make sure you know where he's at at all times and take care of that."
Running the football up the middle will be exceedingly difficult with an elite defensive tackle like Simmons in the mix. Additionally, guards Ben Bredeson and Cody Mauch will have their work cut out for them — Seattle Seahawks right guard Grey Zabel was tasked with guarding Simmons in Week 8, and it didn't go to plan.
The Buccaneers face the Bears at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night. They can win the game if they keep tabs on Simmons, but he presents a unique challenge this team hasn't faced in some time.

title: Emeka Egbuka Update: Was He At Buccaneers' Thursday Practice?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are set to play a tough Chicago Bears team that may be among the NFL's best. They've won their last two games off the rushing attack and only passed 14 times, but that almost certainly won't be good enough to get the win over Chicago.
If the Bucs are going to pass, they're going to want as many weapons in the passing game as possible. One of those players is Emeka Egbuka, who has missed his last two games with a foot injury.
Egbuka didn't practice on Wednesday. The Bucs held their Thursday practice at 11:30 — here's the latest update on Egbuka's status:

The Buccaneers could certainly use Egbuka. title: Buccaneers-Bears Matchup: Biggest Advantage, Biggest Fear
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are now in line to face one of the toughest teams in the NFL in the Chicago Bears. Throughout the 2026 season, the Bears have taken on all challengers and, more often than not, come out ahead with a combination of offensive innovation by head coach Ben Johnson and solid defensive play from coordinator Dennis Allen.
However, this team is not immortal, and there are things the Buccaneers can take advantage of and do well. One good example is what's been working for them the past two weeks offensively in the rushing attack.
Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell have looked like one of the best back combinations in the past two weeks, with some massive help from the offensive line and tight end rooms with their blocking ability.
Yes, the Bears did add former Titans great Jeffery Simmons to help shore up their defensive line, but the Bucs will continue to lean on their top strength offensively going forward in this matchup, and it could give the Bears problems in this upcoming game.
Also, look for Graham Barton, Ben Bredeson and Cody Mauch try to rise to the occasion in this contest against Simmons. This interior group started the season very slowly but has gotten much better in recent weeks, especially when it comes to the ground game and how well they've been blocking up front.
One thing the Bucs do have to worry about is the offensive mind of Ben Johnson. Yes, the Bucs' defense has been stellar the past two weeks, but a monsoon is not coming this game as it was against the Falcons. Johnson is also a much better offensive play-caller than either Brad Idzik of the Panthers or Tommy Rees of the Falcons.
Kudos to Todd Bowles for getting this defense in shape and really guiding a turnaround in the past two weeks of football, as it has been a treat to watch. However, this should be the toughest coaching test he's faced yet this season, and it will be one of the best tests the team could hope for to find out how legitimate their defense really is.
We will see if the Bucs can prove that they are here to stick around in the NFC South race and make another run at the playoffs or if the team falls back down to earth in a tough matchup.

title: Buccaneers’ Vita Vea Addresses NFL Trade Rumors
full_text:
We are less than a week away from the NFL trade deadline, and the phones are starting to ring.
Just a few weeks ago, we were discussing whether the Tampa Bay Buccaneers would be sellers at the deadline given their disastrous start to the season, but they have since won back-to-back divisional games to put them right back in the hunt for the NFC South crown.
Even though the Bucs might not see themselves as sellers now that they are just a half-game back of the Carolina Panthers in the NFC South, it doesn't mean that they aren't willing to make moves.
In fact, a recent report suggested that the New York Giants are possibly interested in obtaining the services of Vita Vea after striking out on Jeffrey Simmons.
However, Vea was quick to shut things down when asked how he felt about being linked to a potential trade.
“I didn't know until you brought it up, honestly. Shoot, I just come in here to do my job," Vea said during player availability following Wednesday's practice.
The 31-year-old Vea has served as the Buccaneers' run stopper up the middle for nine years, and despite his lack of stats, he constantly impacts the game thanks to being double-teamed for the majority of snaps he plays.
Through eight games, he has 16 total tackles, including a tackle for loss, a sack and two passes defended.
It's an interesting quote from Vea, given that he publicly requested a trade this offseason with the hopes of getting the Bucs to budge on a contract extension that would pay him like one of the elite interior defensive linemen in the league.
Vea ultimately got what he wanted, signing a one-year, $30 million extension that locks him in with the Bucs through the 2027 season.
While it doesn't seem as though general manager Jason Licht and the front office have any intention of trading him, they could decide to do so given his slow start to the season, capitalizing on his peak trade value as he continues to age as well as saving them some headaches when it comes to salary cap impact.
Even though it would make sense to try and get some high draft capital for Vea, it's highly unlikely that Tampa Bay makes that trade — or any trade at all.

title: 3 Ways the Buccaneers Upset the Bears on Sunday Night Football
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have a tough, tough task on Sunday Night Football. They're set to duel against the Chicago Bears, who just defeated the defending Super Bowl champions and are looking like Super Bowl contenders themselves this year.
The Bucs haven't been slouches themselves in recent weeks either, though. They've won three of their last four games, and they currently boast one of the best running offenses and one of the best overall defenses in football.
The Bears will be favored to win this one on home turf against a Bucs team that has struggled this year, and they definitely should be. But the Bucs will try their hardest to get the upset done on the road to move to 4-5 and, potentially, the NFC South lead.
Here's how the Bucs can defeat the Bears on Sunday:
This one shouldn't be too hard for the Bucs — they're really, really good at it, and Chicago is middling at running the football.
Chicago's rushing success rate is 40.6% and their EPA/play on the ground is -0.096. The Bucs have been excellent against the run, allowing a rush EPA/play of -0.208, and they allow just a 35.3% success rate. The Bucs allow the second-fewest yards per game on the ground (80).
Despite their overall lack of advanced metrics in their favor, the Bears still tend to produce on the ground in raw numbers. They're second in the NFL in rushing yards per game behind Tampa Bay's offense (150.8) and they run the ball quite often, the fourth-highest rate in the league (48.87%).
If the Bucs are going to stop the Bears, it starts right here. The Bears have high production but run inefficiently, so limiting explosive plays from running backs like D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai (if he plays) will be key.
Tampa Bay has done a good job of that so far this season, but they can't just be tough against the run in Chicago — they have to bury it.
The Buccaneers are going to have to throw the football sometime. This would be a great game to start.
The Bucs have thrown just 14 passes in their last two games for 64 yards. The Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons were almost entirely unable to handle Tampa Bay's run game, and as a result, the Bucs had no need to throw as they ran for hundreds of yards and easily won both matchups.
That will not be the same environment that Tampa Bay walks into on Sunday. New defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons will ensure that the middle is sufficiently blocked, so Tampa Bay simply must be able to pass with a passing game that has been largely ineffective under Zac Robinson.
Robinson will have to dial up some strong concepts to combat Dennis Allen's defense in Chicago. Additionally, quarterback Baker Mayfield must play well as he recovers from his injured thumb and the receiving corps — potentially without Emeka Egbuka — has to get some separation.
Caleb Williams may very well be the most talented quarterback in football. He's had some consistency issues, but ever since returning from a hamstring injury, he's been simply excellent.
Williams thrives off-platform and is very comfortable outside the pocket. Recently, however, he's been very good at standing and delivering the football inside the pocket, too, and there isn't a throw he cannot make. The key for Tampa Bay will be to get pressure on Williams from the interior and get him down quickly with Calijah Kancey and A'Shawn Robinson — they're in for a long night if they don't.
The Bucs could also utilize some man coverage against Williams, too. He has a +0.048 dropback EPA/play against man coverage and a +0.294 dropback EPA/play against zone, so getting Tampa Bay's excellent secondary a little closer to the football may help them.
Williams will get his. The Bucs just have to make sure it isn't often.

title: Emeka Egbuka Injury Update: Latest on Bucs WR After Missing Another Practice
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have a tough task ahead of them. They're set to face off against one of the best teams in the NFC, the Chicago Bears, on the road in prime time on Sunday Night Football in Week 9.
Tampa Bay hasn't thrown the ball all that much the last two weeks — just 14 times — but it'll probably need to if it wants to beat the Bears. Quarterback Baker Mayfield is recovering from a thumb injury, and while he'll need to throw the football well, his receiving corps will need to step up, too.

"I don't know. He was kinda 50-50 last week," Bowles said Monday. "We'll see how he progresses."
So far this season, Egbuka has netted 28 receptions for 240 yards and two touchdowns. He also has a rushing touchdown on the ground.
In Egbuka's stead — and without Jalen McMillan — wideouts Tez Johnson and Ted Hurst have taken on some work. The Bucs also just got wideout David Sills back from injured reserve, so he's another receiver who could step up in Egbuka's absence, should he not be able to go.
There is still a chance that he could, however. And if he does, Tampa Bay will need to use him against a Bears defense that has only gotten more formidable in recent weeks with the addition of star defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons. title: Buccaneers Star Vita Vea on NFC East Team's 'Radar' Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is approaching very fast. There's one week of NFL play left before it hits on Nov. 10, and naturally, teams are calling all around the league to try to make their squads better before that time.
There was a time when the Tampa Bay Buccaneers could have become sellers at that trade deadline had things not gone according to plan. It was sure looking that way — the Bucs lost their first four games of the season and were 2-5 heading into Week 8 — but now, the Bucs are 3-5, half a game out of the NFC South lead and very much in the mix.
That would seem to indicate the Bucs aren't really going to be sellers anymore. But if they got the right offer, anything could be appealing — and according to an NFL insider, one NFC East team could be looking to trade for one of Tampa Bay's star players on defense.
ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler reported that the New York Giants are keeping tabs on Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea ahead of the deadline, but that the Bucs don't plan to trade him at the moment.
"Another player on the Giants' radar is Tampa Bay's Vita Vea. (The Bucs are not expected to move him.) It would be a mild surprise if New York doesn't walk away with some help up front," Fowler wrote .
Vea's case is an interesting one. Vea held out of training camp for a significant portion of the year and even requested a trade for a new deal, and the Bucs gave it to him by giving him a one-year contract extension worth $30 million. He hasn't lit up the stat sheet since signing that contract and has clearly declined, so the Bucs may be wise to move on from him this season.
That being said, his ability as a space eater is still very valuable, and he remains a stalwart of a defensive unit that is currently top-three in the NFL by most advanced metrics. If head coach Todd Bowles still wants Vea in that unit, the Bucs will keep him around.
Tampa Bay plays a very tough Chicago Bears team on Sunday night. If the Bucs win, trading Vea feels out of the question — they'd be 4-5 with a shot to lead the NFC South entirely.
If the Bucs lose, though? Perhaps general manager Jason Licht picks up the phone, and perhaps the New York Giants can get some help on the defensive interior.

title: Buccaneers Not Worried About Lack of Passing Game
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have won their last two games against NFC South opponents. They've done so in quite an unusual way.
The Bucs have thrown just 14 passes in their last two games for 64 yards — quarterback Baker Mayfield didn't complete a pass at all in a 16-0 win against the Atlanta Falcons. Mayfield is recovering from a thumb injury, but over the past two weeks, he hasn't had to test it at all.
Now, the Bucs are facing off against the 6-2 Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football. The Bears just traded for one of the best defensive tackles in football in Jeffrey Simmons and knocked off the defending Super Bowl champions the Seattle Seahawks. It's probably safe to say that the Bucs won't be able to win on the run game alone for the third week in a row.
So, are the Bucs confident that their quarterback can throw the ball if needed? Head coach Todd Bowles certainly seems to be.
Bowles spoke to the media on Monday, and during his time, he stressed that the conditions are mainly what caused the Bucs to abandon the pass entirely.
"I've seen it in practice. Like you said, the conditions [didn’t require it]," Bowles said. "Carolina just got away in the second quarter, and we kind of got ahead. Yesterday, it was kind of impossible to throw, especially early on. In the last part of the ballgame, we had the lead and we really didn't have to throw the ball. You saw what happened when they threw the football."
Despite that, though, Bowles is confident that the Bucs can pass the ball if they need to. Mayfield may be recovering from a thumb injury, but Bowles believes his recent practices have shown he can accurately throw the ball when it's necessary.
"But we see it every day in practice, [I am] very confident. I thought Baker [Mayfield] had a great week of practice throwing the football, but we knew what the conditions were going to be," Bowles said. "Obviously, as they turned out, it was pretty much a monsoon most of the ballgame, so we didn't have to throw it. We kind of [grinded] it out, but [I'm] very confident our passing game will be fine."
The Bucs will likely have to throw against the Bears, who are looking more like a Super Bowl contender every week. It will be cold, but conditions will be much more favorable to throwing the football on Sunday night.
The Bucs play the Bears at 8:20 on Nov. 8. When they do, it might be time for Mayfield to put his thumb to the test.

title: Titans Trending in Best Possible Direction With Trade Outlook for Tony Pollard, Calvin Ridley
full_text:
Hours after the Titans On SI staff put out our trade deadline predictions this morning, the NFL's never-ending churn of news had to go and throw a wrench in it. This thing won't stop until the November 10 deadline hits. We've got new notes on the Tennessee Titans today.
Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport have freshly reported that the Titans "are not interested in trading running back Tony Pollard," but are "listening" on Calvin Ridley, who "could be had for a late-round pick." This news comes just one day after prices had seemingly been set for both players.
Pollard's previous fourth-round tag appears less important in the light of this news, but Ridley's sixth-round ask appears even more important. Beyond players being tabbed as available or unavailable, names coming up consistently on the trade market can hint at a team's attitude toward them.
Tennessee being timid about moving Pollard has been reflected in how volatile his market appeared to be prior to today. It was hard to get a clean price, and even then, Albert Breer used the term "pry" to describe a team potentially plucking the RB out of Nashville.
"Pry" and "could be had" are worlds apart. Pollard may not be going anywhere, but Ridley could pop any day now.
The Titans' trade plans are clearer than ever before; that's speaking with a built-in skepticism given how often these things change, but you can take Ridley's state specifically with more than a grain of salt.
Schefter added that the Kansas City Chiefs, Pittsburgh Steelers, and San Francisco 49ers have been making calls in an effort to add a pass-catcher by the deadline. The closer that day gets without any moves, the better Titans fans should feel about Ridley potentially being moved.
He's unlikely to be the first option anywhere, but interest hasn't completely waned on Ridley due to no WRs being moved up to this point. If there are multiple teams searching for help at the position, Ridley's lower price tag bodes well for his tradability.
The veteran and third-year Titan just hasn't worked things out in Nashville. But with a year remaining on his restructured deal and his general good health, a sixth-round selection (or even a seventh) might be a sensible sacrifice for a contending team trying to add last-minute talent.
Just as potential suitors for Ridley can't be picky at this point, Tennessee can't either. If a remotely fair offer comes across the table, general manager Mike Borgonzi should jump on it.

title: Staff Predictions for Titans' Trade Deadline: Who Goes, Who Stays, and Why
full_text:
The trade deadline is now just three days away, on November 10. That means speculation and "he said, she said" is at an all-time high in the NFL, and the Tennessee Titans are very much involved in the noise.
The Titans On SI staff have all thrown hats into the ring on trade talk to some degree, but now, it's time we put down some official predictions to stand on.
Here are a round of staff predictions - expected and bold alike - ahead of the Titans' trade deadline, guessing who goes and who stays. It's shaping up to be an important date for a 1-7 Tennessee team facing another busy offseason. Let's jump in.
By next Tuesday, the only Titans player that I expect the team will find a way to actually move is WR Calvin Ridley. The veteran pass-catcher has faded out of this offense to a near-irreversible degree, and the team's reported sixth-round asking price seems to suggest that they agree.
It feels likely that Tennessee will try and move on from Ridley to clear out space in the WR room for the likes of Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike to compete. Elsewhere, though, I'm not sure I see the Titans hurrying up to move anybody.
Amani Hooker and Jacob Martin appear safe as two hyper-active defensive pieces in the secondary and on the defensive line, respectively. RB Tony Pollard could go at the right price, but at this point, it seems safer that Tennessee would hold on there too for Cam Ward's sake.
Who does that leave? DE Jermaine Johnson and LB Cody Barton, perhaps, both of whom have either been quiet or completely absent in recent trade talks. I'd be surprised if the Titans didn't make a single move, but the only one that looks "likely" is Ridley to me.
Over the last two weeks, Pollard has played the best football of his Tennessee Titans tenure, racking up nearly 300 yards from scrimmage and five touchdowns. Offensive coordinator Brian Daboll has been gung-ho on Pollard being the led running back in Nashville, leaving younger backups Tyjae Spears and rookie Nick Singleton with a handful of healthy scratches.
There appears to be no working backup plan if Pollard is dealt at the deadline. Therefore, I see Pollard finishing out his age 29 season with the Titans, especially when more decorated options are available at the deadline, like backs Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley.
On the flip side, the Tennessee Titans are reportedly seeking a sixth-round pick in exchange for WR Calvin Ridley, which has been made known for roughly a week now. In my opinion, there’s no surprise why he hasn’t been moved yet... the Titans are asking too much. Ridley turns 32 years old next month, and he’s two years removed from his last 1,000-yard season.
There’s a stronger possibility Ridley is moved for a seventh-round pick to a team like the Las Vegas Raiders looking to harvest the final snaps of an aging receiver.
Onto a bolder take. For reasons beyond comprehension, Tyjae Spears has been ghosted from significant playing time for the majority of this season. In Week 5, Spears led the offense with a team-high nine receptions in a blowout loss to the Texans, since he’s only been handed one carry and caught one pass. Spears hasn’t played in the last two games.
At 25 years old, I could see a team taking a flyer on Spears, especially if the asking price for players like the aforementioned Taylor and Barkley is too high.
I think the Titans will ultimately stand pat at the deadline, especially when it comes to Pollard. Cam Ward needs the balanced attack that Pollard provides in order for him to start reaching his full potential.
Making an already inconsistent offense one-dimensional could end up being a critical blow for Ward’s development, which is why outside of landing a top-100 pick, I think they’ll choose to keep Pollard to help Ward develop over the final nine games of the season.
If they do make a trade, I believe it will be something that won’t yield a large return, such as trading Calvin Ridley for a late-draft pick. The Los Angeles Rams could be a possibility given their current depth at the position, but we’ll see if anybody is willing to give up anything for an older receiver who has yet to eclipse 100 yards on the year.
In short: I'm not expecting fireworks.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: How Titans' Trade Deadline Could Impact 2027 Draft: 2 Names to Watch Plus Potential Replacements
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are in the midst of their much-needed bye week. The team currently sits at 1-7, with five of those seven losses coming by one score. The Titans know their chances of a playoff run are somewhere between slim and none, but they still have a lot to figure out before the end of the season.
The next hurdle to cross is the upcoming trade deadline. The Titans have already traded away superstar DT Jeffery Simmons, so anything is possible at this point. The Titans have a handful of possible trade candidates , including: S Amani Hooker, WR Calvin Ridley, and LB Cody Barton.
The NFL's leader interception leader, Hooker, would undoubtedly bring the biggest return, but reports are the Titans aren't interested in trading away another captain , but as we saw with Simmons, everyone has a price, so that possibility can't be discarded completely
But here, we're going to take a look at arguably the Titans’ two most notable trade candidates, what it would take to move off them, and which potential prospects could eventually replace them down the line.
Having said that, let’s dive right into it.
This is one that could go a few different ways. The Titans are either gonna trade Pollard before Tuesday’s deadline, re-sign him at the end of the year, or let him walk once free agency rolls around. But for the first time, the possibility of trading Pollard feels at least somewhat realistic.
Sitting at 1-7, the Titans could obviously use as much draft capital as possible, and getting something in return for a player likely to leave in the offseason makes a lot of sense. However, Pollard’s stability and consistency in the backfield is something that QB Cam Ward needs right now, and you could argue that’s more valuable than having an extra mid-round pick.
But should someone desperate enough to secure Pollard’s services offer a top-100 pick in exchange for the Titans’ running back, then they would be crazy not to at least strongly consider it. Regardless of how this situation plays out, Tennessee will likely need a plan to replace the veteran ball carrier at some point in the near future.
The draft could have plenty of intriguing options, including Ole Miss RB Kewan Lacy and Florida RB Jadan Baugh should they decide to take one early, while BYU RB LJ Martin and Louisville RB Isaac Brown could be options somewhere in the middle rounds.
Only time will tell how this plays out, but this is easily the most intriguing one to keep an eye on.
The Titans desperately need to address the edge of their defensive line this offseason. But with the recent emergence of Martin, would trading him just create another unnecessary hole, or should they take advantage of his value while it's at its highest?
When the Titans signed Martin to a two-year deal back in March, I don’t think even the most optimistic fan could’ve predicted how impactful he would be through eight games. Martin currently has 6.5 sacks on the year (T-5th most), and he’s making a real case for himself to have a starting job on this team beyond this season.
On the flip side, there’s also a strong possibility that the 30-year-old pass rusher is going to want more money after the numbers he’s produced. So, rather than deal with that future headache, the Titans could get ahead of it by flipping him for an extra draft pick instead.
If the Titans do end up with a top-five pick, Texas EDGE Colin Simmons and South Carolina EDGE Dylan Stewart will undoubtedly be on the shortlist of realistic possibilities. There are also a handful of guys they could target later on in the draft, but if the Titans want a day one instant impact player along the edge, those are the two to get.
Other intriguing options include: Yhonzae Pierre (Alabama), Devan Tompkins (Alabama), Will Heldt (Clemson), Jordan Ross (LSU), Princewill Umanmielen (LSU), Kenyatta Jackson Jr. (Ohio State).
Whatever the case may be, the Titans have until Tuesday to decide whether Martin will be in their future plans. Martin would likely fetch a mid-round pick in return, so it’ll be interesting to see if Tennessee ends up getting something worth moving off the productive pass rusher.
I believe a fifth-round pick is probably fair for Martin, but I would try to do everything possible to get a fourth-round pick instead, even if that means kicking back a late-round pick in return.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Titans Don't Have to Rush Their Rebuild — But Robert Saleh's Post-Bye Goals Say Otherwise
full_text:
Earlier this week, the Tennessee Titans interrupted a typically quiet bye week on social media with a clip from head coach Robert Saleh. At 1-7 and having just traded their franchise star, in Jeffery Simmons, the Titans looked primed to sell at the trade deadline and go big in the 2027 draft.
In less words: There's no real pressure to make a late-season push from an objective point of view. But Coach Saleh doesn't see it that way at all. In fact, he believes the final nine games after the bye will go on to define the next decade of Titans football.
That leaves a huge gap between "we've got the pieces to be better next year" and "it's pivotal that we turn this thing around right now."
"The next nine games are going to define the next 10 years of Titans football," Saleh began. "The expectation is that we come back, we play with the effort and the tenacity of everything we got... we continue to build on what we're trying to get done here."
"Whatever happens happens, but at the end of the day, I do think we are getting better."
Is this so-called "coach speak" that will lead to the Titans dumping veteran assets and hoping a high pick will speed things up next year? Or does Tennessee hang on to their waning playmakers and try and make a statement in the second half of this season, potentially losing a higher pick as a result?
It's not like this Titans team hasn't come close to more than their fair share of wins. Tennessee's six one-score games through eight weeks is the primary beacon of hope of Saleh's that Brian Callahan didn't have.
The November 10 trade deadline is sure to make the Titans' actual intentions clear either way. If Tony Pollard, Amani Hooker, Jacob Martin, and others are kept around, expect a potential flare of second life from this group in the second and final stretch.
However, a few of those pieces go, and all of the sudden we're looking at a roster built to be retooled the moment Tennessee plays their final game this season. As far as Saleh is concerned, it makes sense that his urgency is higher than the franchise's relatively low perceived panic.
The aforementioned Callahan's tenure proved that winning is all that matters, in the end. Saleh has shown a lot of promise thus far, but the Titans' rebuild isn't tied to him being on the sideline. The last nine games may not be pivotal to the franchise necessarily, but they're hugely important for Saleh.

title: How Rookie Nick Singleton Could Get a Shot at RB1 if the Titans Trade Tony Pollard
full_text:
As of this morning, we have a reported price tag for Tony Pollard. The Tennessee Titans could potentially be convinced to move the rising veteran RB for a fourth-round pick. That may have seemed high for Pollard prior to this season, but his fiery stretch as of late makes sense of it.
Where would that move leave Tennessee's backfield? Well, with Tyjae Spears consistently missing practices, and struggling mightily when he does touch the field, the mutli-year Titan no longer looks like a viable option for replacement.
I pitched Tennessee taking a first-round back with the later pick they acquired in the Jeffery Simmons trade. But until we reach that reset point in 2027, the rookie RB sitting on Tennessee's bench right now has a rightful claim to the opportunity.
If Pollard is moved, Nick Singleton should get his shot.
Singleton has just seven carries for 12 yards this year. He's appeared in only two contests, most recently notching four carries for 10 yards in the Titans' Week 4 loss to the Baltimore Ravens.
Even more recently, Robert Saleh said outright that veteran back Michael Carter has greater three-down value than Singleton right now, and has been given complimentary minutes as a result. That outlook is bleak for the rookie, but a Pollard trade changes things.
Moving your current RB1 essentially hits the big red button on the backfield. Of the three guys that are fighting for two or three leftover carries a game right now, who gives your team the most if they're shoved into a leading role?
Spears might be the answer on paper, and Carter could be deemed safer than Singleton. But Tennessee has yet to see what they have in the rookie. If they sign or draft someone over him next offseason, Singleton may have missed his window.
Pollard being moved would open that window, and I can't imagine the Titans don't at least give Singleton a shot to jump through it. After all, why use a fifth-round pick on the guy if you're not going to give him an extended chance to prove his worth?
Seven carries through eight games is hardly enough to judge a player. After all, Singleton didn't just trot to setting Penn State's school record for career rushing touchdowns, total career touchdowns, and career all-purpose yards.
There's more to the rookie than meets the eye. Before the Titans bury him with the likes of Kalel Mullings and Julius Chestnut (the latter, to his credit, has made an impact on special teams), he should be given enough touches to see exactly what's on the table.
The deadline is just four days away now, so Titans fans won't have to wonder about the backfield scenario for long either way.

title: Tony Pollard, Calvin Ridley Trade Tracker: Titans' New Price Tag Complicates Move
full_text:
With the trade deadline only four days away now for the NFL, you can only really trust what's right in front of you. As far as the Tennessee Titans go, a 1-7 team is bound to make some noise on the market. But after trading Jeffery Simmons last week, things have come to a halt.
However, the trade train may not have completely pulled into the station for Tennessee. This morning, Sports Illustrated's Albert Breer dropped an update on the Titans' price tags for a few of their veterans, as well as the team's general attitude toward their state of affairs right now.
"After the Simmons trade, the Titans like the way their team is playing," Breer began, going on to note that the team is still evaluating Cam Ward, and won't simply "give away" guys like Tony Pollard and Calvin Ridley. Although, everybody has a price in this league. The Simmons trade proved that.
"But they have listened on both players." The temperature right now suggests that it would take at least a fourth-round pick to "pry" Pollard away from the Titans, while Ridley could potentially be drawn away for something like a sixth-rounder.
If Pollard is truly on the market, this is a price that could bring things down to the wire. For Ridley, on the other hand, a sixth may be the sweet spot to move the seasoned WR.
Regarding the former, Pollard is really only a primary options for teams that are out on Indianapolis Colts star Jonathan Taylor. As Breer puts it: "Pollard has drawn interest from teams looking for running back help that don’t want to pay the freight for Taylor."
But Pollard's mid-season development into a pure RB1 workhorse has changed things. Initially, trading the 29-year old rusher in the final year of his contract seemed inevitable. Yet now, as long as he's assisting Ward's growth, Pollard looks like a more important player for Tennessee.
He's likely gone after this season either way, which is likely why this move is still on the table. However, it may take dire need for a team to cough up a fourth for a back in the unique age and contract situation that Pollard is in.
Ridley, on the other hand, is much easier to part with. The 31-year old receiver has passed his prime of production in Nashville. Mostly healthy and with a little gas left in the tank, Ridley could realistically be pitched to a contender as some late-season WR help.
The Titans, however, just don't have a spot for him anymore. It'll be interesting to see if any team believes it's worth a late pick to pluck Ridley from the Titans. It wouldn't be all that surprising if Tennessee came down from their standards in Ridley's case specifically, either.
Does Tennessee move off of Pollard at the right price and try and patch up their backfield until the 2027 draft? Would they trade Ridley at a lower late just to clear out their overstuffed WR room? We'll know the answer to both and more in just a few more days.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Cam Ward’s Rise in QB Rankings After Career-Best Performance Gives Titans Something to Build On During Bye
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans lost their seventh game of the 2026 NFL season last Sunday against the Cincinnati Bengals, but in defeat, quarterback Cam Ward posted the best game of his professional career.
Ward, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, threw for a career-high 304 yards, completed 65% of his passes (26 of 40), and tossed two touchdowns with no interceptions in Tennessee's 43-36 loss to Cincinnati. Ward has gone through a lot of downs so far this season, but Week 8 was a major high point in his development.
Though the Titans enter their Week 9 bye with a 1-7 record and face an uphill battle to even get back into the playoff picture, Tennessee finally has something to look forward to for the rest of the season as the franchise continues its rebuild.
CBS Sports released its latest power rankings of each NFL starting quarterback , and Ward came in at No. 25. The Titans signal-caller was dead last in the rankings a week ago.
Author Garrett Podell noted Ward's excellent performance against the Bengals, where he went toe-to-toe with one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, Joe Burrow, and flourished without his top target, rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate.
"Cam Ward nearly outdueled Joe Burrow in Cincinnati in a 43-36 overtime defeat in Week 8. He threw for a career-high 304 yards, a career-high two passing touchdowns and no interceptions on 26-of-40 passing. Ward also did this without No. 1 rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate. Ward now has something to build on entering the Tennessee Titans' Week 9 bye week. (+7)," Podell wrote.
Ward still has a lot to prove before establishing himself as the Titans' 2027 starter , but if the Miami product can build on his performance from last week coming out of the bye, he will construct a compelling case to remain QB1 for the future.
It's known that Ward has the talent to be a productive starting quarterback, but the 24-year-old must continue to take steps in the right direction in his development and play clean football for the remainder of the year. Despite starting the season off with lackluster performances , Ward can still be Tennessee's franchise signal-caller that drives the franchise back to relevance.
The Titans will host the Jacksonville Jaguars at Nissan Stadium coming out of the bye. The division test would be a fantastic contest for Ward to show more growth and possibly lead Tennessee to an upset.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Carnell Tate's Latest NFL Accolade Broke a 7-Year Drought Titans Fans Likely Forgot About
full_text:
Over time, a rebuild will sweep a lot of positivity under the rug. The Titans haven't had the benefit of a winning season since 2021, when a division-winning Tennessee team went 12-5 before falling to the Cincinnati Bengals in the divisional round. Since then, it's been almost all downhill.
That's why news like Carnell Tate being dubbed the NFL Offensive Rookie of the Month for October can't be taken lightly. With LB Anthony Hill Jr. earning the honors on defense last month, it's the first time in Titans history that two players on either side of the ball have checked that box in the same season.
But that isn't even the wildest stat at our disposal here. The last time a Tennessee player won the honor on offense was 2019. That player was short-lived superstar (as far as his Titans tenure goes) A.J. Brown.
If there's any shaft of light to run to in this 1-7 season, it's the development of Tennessee's rookies. Tate specifically is trending toward a franchise-changing plane, on which the Titans haven't had a receiver since Brown.
A look at the stats reveals a gap in production between the two players, but their scenarios are plenty different, too.
Tate was given the honors for October after netting 290 yards on 21 catches. Tate caught his first career touchdown during that stretch too, lifting Tennessee to their only win of the season over the Indianapolis Colts on the road.
Meanwhile, Brown also had 21 catches... but his went for 470 yards and, get this, five total touchdowns. One of those scores was on the ground. Tennessee did finish that year 9-7, led by longtime QB Ryan Tannehill, and upset their way to the AFC Championship Game.
It's not entirely fair to compare these numbers for that reason. Tate likely would've been elevated in the same scenario as Brown, and even if he still didn't reach those heights, the wider point here is that the Titans finally have a budding superstar at WR again.
After years of rebuilding on the whole and signing underwhelming veterans at the position, Tate promises a more reliable solution for Tennessee. Even with plenty to figure out elsewhere, the Titans' fourth overall pick clearly went to good use.
Joining A.J. Brown in the Titans' historic ranks is no easy feat. The best part is, it seems that Tate is only just getting started.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Outlining a Perfect Trade Deadline Outcome for the Titans: Only 2 Players Ultimately Go
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline is just five days away now, meaning every single rumor related to the Tennessee Titans will have to give in one direction. That’s good news for fans biting their nails over the eventual outcome.
But what would the best possible version of that outcome look like? Where could the Titans ultimately land that would satisfactorily cover every single base heading into the second half of the 2026 season?
I’m here to (try to) answer that question today. With less than a week until we’ll know for sure, here’s a guide to what I believe would be the ideal trade-deadline outcome for Tennessee.
Believe it or not, trading a guy like Jeffery Simmons will shift your outlook a little bit. What looked like the makings of a fire sale for Tennessee prior to Week 8 now appears to be a much safer, much less drastic result. That's what 36 points and two new first-round picks will do to a franchise.
This block of no-trade hopefuls all have an active role in Tennessee's rebuild. Veterans like S Amani Hooker and EDGE Jacob Martin are almost solely keeping a Simmons-less defense alive, while EDGE Jermaine Johnson and CB Alontae Taylor each have the potential for long-term roles under Robert Saleh.
Tony Pollard has been the big-ticket trade piece all season, but he might be the most crucial keep in this bunch right now. The 29-year old RB has taken immense pressure off of Cam Ward, and his recent dominant uptick directly allowed the second-year QB to have a career-best game last week.
There's a system that's beginning to work on the offensive side of the ball, and Pollard is a necessary cog until the Titans find a real replacement for him. As for the defensive pieces, through a broader lens, it would be unwise to rock an already leaky boat any further after moving Simmons.
The two pieces I would like to see Tennessee find a way to move are WR Calvin Ridley and LB Cody Barton.
Ridley's case is self-explanatory, and it's a drum we've hit over and over again already. He's long faded out of the Titans' offense, and is vying for a role in what may be the team's deepest position group. He doesn't fit the vision in Nashville any longer and, at basically any cost, would be worth moving.
Barton, on the other hand, looked worse than fellow LB Cedric Gray last season. He then played complimentary snaps to rookie Anthony Hill Jr. while Gray recovered from his concussion and got used to Saleh's defensive changes.
Now that Gray's snaps are back on the rise and Hill continues to impress, Barton looks out of place. Gray already has more tackles than Barton ( 37 to 34 total ), in spite of playing significantly less snaps.
Similar to Ridley, I'd be fine with the Titans taking any pinch of draft capital to clear out their LB rotation and hone in on the better, higher-potential players therein.
Tennessee doesn't need to move off multiple key playmakers to have a successful trade deadline; in fact, they'd be better off holding on to the majority of them. It's about committing to a fresh identity and trading out pieces that either don't fit that mold, or won't for much longer.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Déjà Drop: Can Titans Stop Wan'Dale Robinson From Becoming Their Next Calvin Ridley?
full_text:
Calvin Ridley's four-year, $92 million deal back in 2024 was surprising even then. Going on 30 years old at the time, Ridley's NFL career had already left a lot to be desired over two teams; the veteran receiver was already two years removed from his best season, and yet, the Titans paid up.
Since, it's basically been nothing but regret in Nashville. Ridley, playing on a restructured contract with little to no hold in the offense, is perhaps the team's most obvious trade target ahead of next Tuesday's deadline. Yet, even if the Titans move Ridley, a similar problem seems to be rising.
Wan'Dale Robinson was brought in on an eerily familiar four-year, $70 million contract this past offseason. Reunited with newly-hired OC Brian Daboll, the fifth-year pass-catcher was signed to be Tennessee's working WR1. But he hasn't met that mark.
Robinson's three touchdowns are the most among any receiver, but his opportunities have mostly come in short-yardage scenarios. The former New York Giant appeared to break out with his first 1,000-yard season last year, but that's looking more and more like a fluke right now.
The key difference between Robinson and Ridley, however, is that Robinson is only 25. For as long as he sticks around, the Titans need to find a way to maximize Robinson's potential as arguably better pieces rise around him.
Robinson dropped two passes against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 8, losing a fumble along the way as well. His touchdown catch represented the best of his game, while the aforementioned struggles signaled the worst.
He's a mechanically sound pass-catcher with good control and, obviously, speed. But Robinson is struggling to get any looks or momentum downfield. His average 7.5 yards per reception this season is tied for a career low. In spite of 35 catches, he's only collected 262 yards.
For comparison, Elic Ayomanor has 13 receptions for 211 yards. Carnell Tate has 34 receptions for 413 yards. Robinson has found himself to be the beneficiary of Cam Ward's targets in the red zone, but elsewhere, his impact has been painfully minimal.
The good news is that it's only Robinson's first year, and Ward just threw him a score in the latter's best game of the season. Their chemistry is there, which is something that couldn't be said of Ridley. That's a plus.
However, with someone like Chimere dike hauling in five receptions and a score of his own in what is essentially the lone opportunity he's had to make a dent this year, Robinson won't have forever. Younger players like Dike, Ayomanor and, of course, Tate, are only getting more involved.
Tennessee will keep looking for ways to prop Robinson up, but just as it was with Ridley, he could absolutely be played out of the lineup. You could argue that the Titans may be able to scheme for him, but two drops and a fumble in a road defeat aren't exactly the best sign to look someone's way.
The Titans will host the Jacksonville Jaguars after the bye break.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders News: Adam Peters Won’t Let Rams Game Decide Trades | Burgundy Roundup
full_text:
The Commanders ruled out Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown on Friday, leaving Jayden Daniels with only two available receivers who have caught a pass for Washington this season. Burks missed all of practice this week with a foot injury. Brown hurt his calf Thursday and did not practice Friday. With Terry McLaurin already on injured reserve, Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams are the two. Van Jefferson and Luke McCaffrey are also on the active roster, while Jaden Bradley remains an option for a practice-squad elevation. Quinn also praised Bradley’s work as a featured receiver on the scout team, though Washington had not announced an elevation Friday. Peters shared better news about McLaurin: his surgery to repair a torn patellar tendon was successful, and he has been around the team facility. Peters said Washington continues to field calls ahead of Tuesday’s trade deadline , though he did not see anything heating up Friday or Saturday. He left Monday open. He also pushed back on the idea that the Rams game will decide whether Washington buys or sells. “The results of the game aren’t going to dictate what we do,” Peters said. He wants a move that makes sense for the team and its value, regardless of Sunday’s score.

Cornerback Jaylen Watson is out, while Trent McDuffie and safety Kam Curl are questionable. Those absences could give Washington chances downfield, depending on what its depleted receiver group can do with them. Matthew Stafford practiced fully for a third straight day despite his right elbow issue and has no game designation. McVay also said the Rams plan to activate running back Ronnie Rivers from injured reserve before Sunday. Karty handled kickoffs last week while Brandon McManus took field goals and extra points. title: Commanders-Rams Final Injury Report Rules Out Two Receivers, Leaves McDuffie Questionable
full_text:
The Washington Commanders released their final injury report Friday ahead of their matchup with the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. The report listed two of Washington's receivers, Treylon Burks (foot) and Dyami Brown (calf), as officially OUT against the Rams. Burks missed practice all week with an injured foot that he's been dealing with since the 49ers game, while Brown was added to Thursday's report as limited before missing Friday's practice. With Terry McLaurin already out for the season, Washington will need more from Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams, who led the team with seven targets and five catches for 54 yards against Philadelphia . Van Jefferson could see more work, and Luke McCaffrey is another option. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn spoke Friday about Jefferson's readiness: "I liked his approach. I liked his readiness, and so when called upon, I'd expect he'd play well." Rookie Jaden Bradley could also be elevated from the practice squad, although Washington hasn't announced that move. Elsewhere on the report, Jer'Zhan Newton is questionable with his pectoral injury despite practicing fully all three days. Newton is still in his 21-day practice window and must be activated from injured reserve before he can play. That decision carries some weight with Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw now on IR . Shy Tuttle (shoulder) was limited all week but carries no game designation, while Sam Cosmi (knee) returned to full participation Friday. John Bates (shoulder) was limited throughout the week but has no game designation either. Los Angeles has some injury problems of its own, particularly in the secondary . Cornerback Jaylen Watson (shoulder) is out, while Trent McDuffie (back) is questionable after missing every practice this week. Former Commanders safety Kam Curl (foot) is also questionable after returning to limited practice Friday. The Rams could be short-handed in the secondary, although McDuffie's and Curl's availability won't be settled until closer to kickoff. The Rams also listed long snapper Joe Cardona (ankle) as doubtful, with tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs), linebacker Grant Stuard (hamstring), and receiver Jordan Whittington (back) questionable. Quarterback Matthew Stafford practiced fully throughout the week, while head coach Sean McVay expects Myles Garrett to play Sunday, pending his activation from injured reserve. Tight end Terrance Ferguson (ankle/hamstring) was ruled out after injuring his hamstring in Friday’s practice .

title: Puka Nacua Can Hurt the Commanders Before Matthew Stafford Even Throws
full_text:
Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua presents a difficult matchup because of his physicality and versatility, but his movement across formations is really what causes issues. Having your best cornerback follow him wherever he goes might seem like the obvious answer, but Washington Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones explained Thursday why that approach can create problems of its own. Nacua has 56 receptions for 565 yards and three receiving touchdowns in six games this season, and is averaging 5.8 yards after the catch per reception, according to Pro Football Focus . PFF also shows him lining up wide on 75.3% of his passing snaps, with another 24.2% coming from the slot. Those numbers don't account for how often McVay puts him in motion before the snap. Los Angeles also uses him as a physical contributor to its running game. If you were playing in an online "sim-Madden league," Sean McVay would have been suspended long ago for spamming receivers, but it still works, quite well, I might add.
Asked whether having one cornerback follow Nacua would help, Jones explained, "They move Puka so many different places. Having some experience playing against him a couple years ago, tried that, and they're jetting him across left and right. They're inserting him into the line of scrimmage, and so you have a corner trying to track that. It becomes difficult because now he's in a space that he's not used to. He's gotta fit the run, and he's not a linebacker, and you wanna keep certain guys out of that." And Stafford doesn't even have to throw it Nacua's way for any of that to matter. That leaves Washington's linebacker corps with a big part of the job. Frankie Luvu didn't describe Nacua like a typical receiver. "Puka, he's like another running back," Luvu said, pointing to the screens and perimeter plays the Rams use to get him the ball. His solution wasn't complicated. "We've just got to keep him in the phone booth, and we'll be all right." Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles sees the same problem. "He does a really good job with yards after the catch," Styles said. "So, it's going to be a big assignment in terms of getting him on the ground." Jones said that responsibility extends beyond the secondary. Linebackers and even edge rushers dropping into coverage have to know where Nacua is before the snap. Washington still has to get him on the ground once Stafford delivers the ball. The Commanders have already seen what happens when an opponent's top receiver gets going. Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught 10 passes for 128 yards and two touchdowns against Washington in Week 3, despite the Commanders winning 33-31. Jones specifically pointed to Seattle's success late in that game as something Washington cannot repeat against Nacua. "Our premium awareness has to be at an all-time high," Jones said. K'Lavon Chaisson sees the defensive front as another part of the solution, with Washington needing to create problems for Stafford before he can get the ball out.
Slow down Puka Nacua. Slow down Matthew Stafford. The Commanders defense knows what they have to do on Sunday vs. the Rams. K'Lavon Chaisson said, "it's going to start up front. Creating as much havoc as possible." pic.twitter.com/wK63EhNtAI
Having Trey Amos back gives Washington more flexibility at cornerback, while Nick Cross can work closer to the line of scrimmage or deeper in coverage. Washington has also removed some of the layers from its defense to help players communicate and react faster. The unit showed progress against Philadelphia, but McVay and Nacua will present a different challenge Sunday. Keeping everyone on the same page, regardless of where Nacua lines up, will be just as important as the coverage itself. title: Commanders Daily: The Rams Have More Than Film on Jayden Daniels
full_text:
While Sean McVay always brings back memories of "the one that got away" every time he visits as an opposing head coach, he's not the focus of former coaches coming to town this week. McVay has two former Commanders coaches on his staff who were with quarterback Jayden Daniels in 2024-2025: Kliff Kingsbury and Brian Johnson. Kingsbury served as the team's offensive coordinator, while Johnson was the assistant head coach/pass game coordinator. Washington's current OC, David Blough, worked under them as the Commanders' assistant quarterbacks coach before being promoted this past offseason. When asked if Kingsbury and Johnson could share their knowledge of Washington’s personnel with the Rams’ defense, Blough's response was direct: "I think so. I think everybody in every role shares information. And yeah, they certainly know our guys. We know what they know about our guys, and we kind of go from there." There's no getting around the fact that the Rams will come equipped with information on Washington's strengths and tendencies from a year ago. Kingsbury and Johnson helped prepare Daniels each week, which gave them a chance to see what he handled well and what needed more work. That experience can help the Rams make sense of what they’re seeing from him in Blough’s offense now. They will certainly know the assistant that Blough was; hell, they'll know Dan Quinn even better. That's the type of familiarity Washington's staff will need to account for. Blough still has plenty of appreciation for the coach whose job he now holds. “It means a lot. He gave me so much in just two years of coaching underneath him. I’m incredibly gracious for my time under him. He’s one of the most gracious people I’ve ever met. And even if it’s a text of encouragement, call it at different low points of the season, he’s reached out. We’ve stayed in contact,” Blough said.
Washington has changed quite a bit since Kingsbury and Johnson left, though. Stefon Diggs, Rachaad White and rookie Antonio Williams all arrived this year, and Blough is running his own system with more work under center. He described Daniels as learning “a new language” Thursday, so Los Angeles still has to prepare for how Washington is using those players now. When asked whether he finds himself watching what Kingsbury and McVay are doing on offense, Blough brought it back to the defense his own group has to face . “I mean, we’re all focused on handling the front this week. And you see some of the concepts and plays that they’re running throughout different tapes of the week. But we’re all focused on today, specifically trying to pick up their third-down pressure package.”

full_text:
We want to hear from you! Each week, we invite you, the Burgundy and Gold faithful, to send in your Washington Commanders questions about everything going on in Ashburn/Landover. We want to make sure everyone gets a chance to have their take heard in the HTTR4LIFE Mailbag, so we'll answer questions on either Monday or Friday, depending on the volume of responses each week. You can send your Washington Commanders questions for the HTTR4LIFE Mailbag to hailbng+si@gmail.com . Washington’s top receiver is out for the year, yet Luke McCaffrey remains outside the main receiver rotation. This week’s mailbag examines what’s blocking his opportunity and how much confidence Dan Quinn’s Eagles win should restore.
Question from Nigel F. via email That's a great question that I've written about here before . From what I can tell, the staff likes McCaffrey, or he wouldn't be on the roster, but he somehow keeps falling outside of the group that gets the main share of the offensive snaps at receiver. Against Philadelphia, McCaffrey played just three offensive snaps. Antonio Williams played 50, Treylon Burks 40, and Stefon Diggs 39. The team loaded up at receiver this offseason, giving the staff options even after McLaurin went down.
#Commanders WR Luke McCaffrey’s two great returns set the team up in great field position On the kickoff return for 44 yds, that was his longest of the season. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/BPqPWQGC3b
The receiver room may not be big on names outside of McLaurin and Stefon Diggs, but rookie Antonio Williams is emerging fast , and whenever Treylon Burks can stay healthy, he routinely produces. Add in the attention tight end Chig Okonkwo gets, and there's not much left for McCaffrey, Dyami Brown, or Van Jefferson. On film, McCaffrey gets open, so offensive coordinator David Blough has to make the scheme work with the talent they have. With injuries playing a factor, McCaffrey will likely get his shot to show what he brings to the field before the end of the season.

title: Commanders Daily: A Hall of Fame Rule Change Could Help Doug Williams Reach Canton
full_text:
The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced its five remaining Contributor nominees for the Class of 2027 on Wednesday, including former Washington Redskins quarterback Doug Williams, who currently serves as a senior advisor to Commanders GM Adam Peters. The field started with 42 nominees and has been reduced to this group, which includes Robert Kraft, Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, and John Wooten. The Contributor Subcommittee must still choose a single candidate who advances to the full committee. The Hall announced revised bylaws on September 4 for the Class of 2027 selection process. Under the old Contributor definition, candidates were judged on contributions outside of playing or coaching. The new rules allow their playing and coaching careers to be considered, too. The Hall of Fame's website has this nugget now buried in its bylaws. "Moving forward, a nominee’s full resume, including years as a player and/or coach, may be taken into account." Williams became the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, earning MVP honors after throwing for 340 yards and four touchdowns in Washington’s 42–10 victory over Denver on January 31, 1988. He also helped the Tampa Bay Buccaneers make their first three playoff appearances. Over nine NFL seasons, he passed for 16,998 yards , threw 100 touchdown passes along with 93 interceptions, and rushed for 884 yards and 15 touchdowns. Williams also had two stints as head coach at Grambling State, winning four Southwestern Athletic Conference titles. Williams also co-founded the Black College Football Hall of Fame with former NFL quarterback James “Shack” Harris in 2009. His NFL scouting and personnel experience includes Jacksonville, Tampa Bay, and Washington. He returned to the Redskins front office in 2014. His current work alongside Peters includes the draft, free agency, and scouting, but he carries a special relationship with the players, many of whom he mentors. The Contributor Subcommittee will meet virtually on November 17 to select one candidate from the remaining five. That candidate would then advance to the full committee for consideration, where they would need at least 80% approval to be elected. The Class of 2027 will be announced at NFL Honors in February, with enshrinement in Canton in August.

full_text:
The Washington Commanders released their first Week 9 injury report as the team gears up for its matchup with the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday. Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton practiced fully on Wednesday after being limited throughout last week. A day after the team placed both starting defensive tackles on injured reserve , Shy Tuttle was limited with a shoulder injury. Newton returned to practice last week as the team opened his 21-day practice window while he recovers from a torn pectoral muscle. Treylon Burks was another name missing from Wednesday's practice, as the receiver continues dealing with the foot injury that left him questionable against Philadelphia . He played anyway and led Washington with 81 receiving yards on three catches, including a 53-yard gain. With Terry McLaurin out for the season, the Commanders need Burks available, but missing Wednesday's practice doesn't necessarily mean he'll be unavailable against Los Angeles. Stefon Diggs also sat out Wednesday, although his absence was listed as rest rather than an injury. John Bates (shoulder) and Sam Cosmi (knee) were limited, while Jayden Daniels (left elbow) and Colson Yankoff (knee) practiced fully. Thursday's injury report should provide a clearer picture of where Burks and Tuttle stand heading into the weekend.

title: Commanders' Unique Usage of Safety Nick Cross Could Have Long-Term Implications
full_text:
Washington Commanders safety Nick Cross has greater alignment diversity than any NFL defender, according to SumerSports data through Week 8. The interesting part is that Cross’ position designation captures only part of what defensive coordinator Daronte Jones asks him to do. So, then the real question becomes: What does Washington gain by moving him around this much? Cross gives Jones a 212-pound safety who can play closer to the run game and be used as a blitzer. He can also move back to a deeper alignment on the next snap. Washington doesn’t have to take him off the field to change his job.
There is no defender in the league who has more alignment diversity than Nick Cross. Daronte Jones has him lined up all over the formation for the Commanders (Data from @SumerSports ) pic.twitter.com/JHgTvkubeU
Washington has more than doubled Cross’ slot-alignment rate from his final season with the Colts, according to Pro Football Focus . His work is now split almost evenly among free safety, the box, and the slot. Last season, nearly half of his snaps came in the box.
Source: PFF. Percentages calculated from 1,111 defensive snaps in 2025 and 233 through Week 8 of 2026. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn discussed Cross’ role Monday after Washington’s 27-10 win over Philadelphia . “And then Nick in this game, I thought, did a really good job, especially when he was playing at Nickel, and he was down by the line of scrimmage. We blitzed him some, John; I thought he had a really good third-down run stop,” Quinn said. Cross earned his two highest overall PFF grades of the season against San Francisco and Philadelphia. The Eagles game was also his strongest in run defense and tackling, backing up what Quinn saw near the line.
Good third-down pressure to get Washington's defense off the field. 7-man pressure front vs. 6 blockers. Philly adjusts for the DBL-A mug and Sonny Styles, while Washington bluffs Sonny and drops Dorance Armstrong. Nice fire zone, creating a free rush for Nick Cross. pic.twitter.com/HlvLQrvai3
Washington showed seven possible rushers against six blockers, but Jones didn’t have to send all seven. Sonny Styles bluffed his rush, Dorance Armstrong dropped into coverage, and Cross came free. As the film above shows, the protection accounted for defenders who weren’t coming, giving Cross a path into the backfield without having to beat a blocker.
Source: PFF. Grades and defensive stops cover all of Cross’ alignments. Quinn emphasized Cross’ communication against Philadelphia. “But most importantly, I really felt his communication in this game, the urgency of what we're looking for from that," Quinn said. "So I thought that was a good step forward as well.” Moving Cross around only helps if the other ten defenders are on the same page. Cross’ work at nickel also gives Jones an alternative to Mike Sainristil , who didn’t play a defensive snap against Philadelphia. Cross still has something to prove in coverage. PFF has charged him with 10 receptions on 11 targets for 69 yards and one touchdown across four appearances, with a 56.2 coverage grade. Those catches averaged 6.9 yards, so opponents haven’t piled up yardage in that sample. The figures include all his coverage work, not just his plays from the slot. If Cross proves he can cover consistently from the slot, Washington could have less need for a dedicated nickel corner. That would give general manager Adam Peters more flexibility to prioritize outside corners or depth elsewhere in the secondary. The Rams game is the next test. Cross’ work over the rest of the season could help determine whether Sainristil has a regular role on defense and which positions Washington needs to address in the offseason. title: Commanders Daily: Washington’s Depleted Front Has More Than Kyren Williams to Handle Against the Rams
full_text:
After missing the 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday night, Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw were both placed on injured reserve Tuesday . Reportedly, it marks the end of the season for Payne, who is dealing with a Jones fracture in his foot; Kinlaw underwent season-ending MCL surgery Tuesday, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Wednesday. It should be noted that without the starting two defensive tackles, the Commanders held the Eagles' depleted team to 91 rushing yards on 29 attempts, including 30 yards on 13 carries from Saquon Barkley, who has been dealing with back and hamstring issues, although he held no game designation against Washington. In place of Payne and Kinlaw, Tim Settle Jr. played 42 snaps (61%), and Shy Tuttle played 32 (46%), along with Byron Cowart, who played 11 (16%) after being elevated from the practice squad to the active roster. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn acknowledged the front seven's work: "I knew the run game on the defensive side was gonna be an important one, so I liked what that looked like of guys setting edges," Quinn said.
The Rams have a couple of backs that need some attention. Sunday, Blake Corum rushed for 73 yards on 11 carries, and Kyren Williams added 56 and a touchdown on 16 carries against the Chargers. Corum added 93 rushing yards the week before against the Raiders and has now scored a touchdown from scrimmage in four consecutive games.
one thing I loved is how mcvay stuck with the hot hand this entire drive, didn’t rotate in kyren at all and just let blake corum take over, whether it’s kyren, or blake… you need to ride the hot hand… pic.twitter.com/vMF4b0Zzwe
Corum can dump yards in spurts. On Sunday, he gained 55 rushing yards on five carries in the opening possession of the second half against the Chargers, including the 23-yard touchdown that gave the Rams a 17-9 lead. The Commanders' rotation will have to stay focused, as the Rams have multiple backs who need the front seven's full attention and aim to wear them down over four quarters. Corum understands what his coach needs out of him: "Our big thing here, Coach McVay always says, is stamina. And so I knew one of them was going to crack," Corum said Sunday . With Payne and Kinlaw both done for the year and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton still in his 21-day practice window, Washington is thin up front. Cowart reverted to the practice squad Monday; his Eagles elevation doesn’t automatically make him available against the Rams. The key in this coming game, and in the weeks ahead, is the Commanders establishing a rotation that can effectively stop the run, without getting gassed in the process.
